The war on drugs was not, is not, and never will be about protecting society (it demonstrably achieves the exact opposite); it exists solely for power. Those whose current careers depend on fighting drugs will never admit such a thing, of course—yet the Global Commission on Drug Policy, a body composed of former powerful officials who devoted their careers to the war on drugs but no longer make a living from it (including former presidents of South American countries, a former US Secretary of State, a former head of the UN, a former NATO Secretary General, and a former EU High Representative), openly declares: "The global war on drugs has failed, with devastating consequences for individuals and societies around the world."

Drug prohibition is the exact same nonsense as Alcohol Prohibition in the 1920s United States; the only difference is that it affects fewer people, so its catastrophic consequences are not visible at every turn. In a stateless society, however, one can imagine drugs being sold just like any other commodity, which would undoubtedly improve not only the purity of those substances—among other things, it would also spell the complete end of drug cartels, which are created solely and exclusively by the war on drugs. After all, what would be the point of smuggling or secretly manufacturing and stockpiling something that is freely available in stores?

It is to be expected that in a stateless society, everyone would arm themselves according to their own judgment and financial means; private landowners could certainly set whatever rules they wished on their own property, including restricting the carrying of weapons, though such restrictions would only be local in nature. The idea that practically anyone could carry a firearm anywhere else is none too pleasant for many of us, because we have grown accustomed to regulations whose creator—the state—instills in us from childhood the belief that without it and its laws, society could not function and we would all shoot one another.

Empirical data from both the past and the present clearly show that this is nothing more than sheer scaremongering. On one side, then, stand strong emotions whipped up by state propaganda, thanks to which everyone "knows"—without ever having truly thought about it—that complete gun deregulation would bring about an apocalypse, while on the other side we have the facts; it is up to each of us which side we choose. In the past, firearms were an ordinary part of people's lives and were typically regulated minimally or not at all—for instance, in the United States before 1934, anyone (regardless of age or any government permit) could buy any weapon (including heavy ones), and in our own lands restrictions were negligible until 1918; yet no catastrophes occurred—not even massacres in schools, which were not "gun-free" back then—and people did not go around shooting each other on sight (even children were used to guns and learned how to handle them, so accidents were rare).

Many will object that without gun regulations we would end up with a "Wild West," which we know from Westerns as a very bloody time and place. Yet the catch lies precisely in the sources used—few people bother to look up historical data when they think they already know what things were like back then. In this case, however, reality is a far cry from romanticized depictions; take the toughest of the tough frontier towns (which inspire many Westerns to this day): Abilene, Ellsworth, Wichita, Dodge City, or Caldwell, where between 1870 and 1885 there were 19 murders per 100,000 inhabitants annually—which is less than in present-day Washington, D.C.—not to mention that population statistics from that era omit various transient individuals (once those are included, the annual murder rate per 100,000 drops from 19 to just over 1). Or consider the most famous gunfight of the Wild West, the shootout at the O.K. Corral (also great fodder for Westerns), in which a grand total of nine (!) people took part, six of whom survived; and compare that celebrated battle with today's gang wars.

Whenever I mention the Wild West, someone often brings up that the genocide of Native Americans took place during that period; yes, that is indeed true. But who carried it out? It was not the farmers and free settlers—who, though well-armed, made (more or less non-violent and mutually respected) agreements with the indigenous peoples—but the state army, whose officers launched the largest and most horrific massacres in order to prove their indispensability in the territory. Anyone who wants to learn more about this period should read the book "The Not So Wild, Wild West" by Terry Lee Anderson and Peter Jensen Hill.

But back to the present. Supporters of regulation like to cite statistics showing that the more accessible firearms are, the more people end up being shot; and they are right—this is indeed true, yet... irrelevant. Where rifles and pistols are hard to obtain, people certainly do not get shot as much, but they stab, strangle, bludgeon, and hang themselves all the more (anti-gun advocates typically include suicides in those statistics). Why, though, should we care only about the number of people shot? What matters is how many people lose their lives (by any means), and on that metric firearms have no demonstrably negative effect; as for the total murder rate, their effect is actually positive. Looking at all countries in the world for which data are available (as a source, I recommend the "Small Arms Survey"), we find that statistically there is less murder where the population is more armed (while one can find pairs of countries whose comparison suggests the opposite, far more confirm this conclusion); meanwhile, the availability of firearms neither decreases nor increases the suicide rate (it affects only the method used).

This observation leads to a very important (and not particularly surprising) conclusion: people typically do not start plotting whom to kill because they acquire a firearm; rather, they first decide to commit murder and only then choose an effective tool. If a firearm is at hand, they will reach for it because it is effective; in its absence, however, they will not turn their nose up at a knife, an axe, or a car. This brings us to the main reason why regulating weapons makes no sense: a human being can be killed with a stick or a stone (to say nothing of a hammer or a screwdriver)—tools whose blanket ban no state can realistically enforce, so anyone intent on murder will find a way.

On the contrary, regulation actually helps murderers. Weapons are a means of equalizing natural imbalances of strength; some of us are physically weaker by nature (especially women and children), while others are stronger. With weapons (and especially firearms, since melee weapons still depend heavily on the user's strength), even those not endowed with great physical power can defend themselves effectively; banning them therefore severely disadvantages the weak against the strong. And that is not all! If I have the element of surprise and the opportunity for an ambush on my side, the effectiveness of my weapon matters far less than when a fight breaks out and I need to defend myself (in a surprise attack from behind, it is easy enough to succeed even with a knife, whereas defending against it is very difficult); banning firearms thus harms defenders more than attackers.

And unfortunately that is still not all: gun regulations restrict law-abiding citizens far more than criminals. Certainly, banning firearms complicates life for criminals a little, yet given their disregard for the law, it comes nowhere near disarming all of them; it does, however, disarm every single law-abiding citizen—precisely because of their respect for existing legislation. As a result, another imbalance of power emerges in favor of "the bad guys." When criminals know their victims have no way to defend themselves, they can do whatever they please (because law enforcement simply cannot be everywhere, even if it tried), which is not the case where almost everyone carries a boomstick; an armed society is a polite society.

Many people feel an aversion toward firearms that is usually induced solely by the actions of the state, which demonizes these tools; yet this propaganda is nothing more than another (unfortunately quite successful) attempt to consolidate state power and drum into subjects the idea that they cannot defend themselves and need the state to do it for them. Not to mention that a disarmed populace has no way to resist government oppression (and it is no coincidence that dictators—Stalin, Adolf Hitler, Mao Zedong, Pol Pot, the Kim dynasty rulers of North Korea, and others—have always confiscated people's weapons); the Founding Fathers, for example, were well aware of this, which is why the U.S. Constitution includes the Second Amendment (which seeks to preserve the "anarchist freedom" of bearing arms even for citizens subject to state power).

A weapon in the hands of an individual has one more crucial significance: thanks to it, the person must take on greater responsibility; using—or failing to use—a weapon in a crisis is an act whose consequences often cannot be undone, and one can only learn to live with them. While at first glance this may seem like a disadvantage, someone who chooses to remain unarmed makes that very same decision—in advance, without knowing the situation in which they might find themselves; yes, they will probably find it easier to rationalize to their own conscience that they "couldn't do anything anyway," when in reality they could have, had they only thought about it beforehand. Either way, carrying a weapon has the exact opposite effect of suppressing responsibility, the consequences of which are discussed in the fourth chapter of this book.

Related to this is the fear of firearms in the hands of teenagers or various lunatics; even today, they occasionally cause enormous harm with them. Yet this happens today precisely because the attacker is surrounded by unarmed people who cannot effectively defend themselves, turning them into tempting targets. A person with a gun poses the greatest threat where nobody else has one; otherwise, they can hardly do more damage than someone today who attempts a massacre with a knife or an axe—they kill one or two victims before others stop them (in an armed society, a shooter can be neutralized just as quickly, putting murderous madmen at a disadvantage compared to today).

"But what about heavy weapons?" the reader may object. "Why not regulate them?" Mainly because in order to do so, the state must possess even heavier weapons, which—given how it is funded—is immoral, to say nothing of the direct infringement on property rights. Moreover, such regulation makes no sense even from the standpoint of "protecting society," because anyone with enough resources to buy heavy weapons who wants to cause harm can already invest those resources far more effectively today; compared to the price of, say, a modern tank, an attack using poisons or explosives (which can be manufactured from legally available materials) is a cheap affair. Furthermore, in the U.S., for example, the sale of all weapons was completely unrestricted until 1934, and thanks to the Second Amendment, weapons purchased back then could not be confiscated from their owners, so some people there still own (legally inherited) artillery—outdated, yes, yet still capable of attacking densely populated cities even today; nonetheless, nobody uses it to commit crimes. And nuclear weapons? There, state regulations lose all meaning, for anyone rich and powerful enough to acquire them has no trouble whatsoever bypassing the law (and possesses a vast array of other ways to cause harm).

Thus, even though governments try to persuade us of how desperately we need their regulations—for it is in their interest that we believe them and offer no resistance—let us never stop trying to see things as they truly are. Let us not close our eyes to the facts (in the area of weapons, the statistics speak very clearly), even when emotions triggered by omnipresent state propaganda can severely distort our perception. Recall, for instance, the relationship between the number of guns and the number of people shot that I mentioned above; although that information is true, it comes nowhere near revealing the whole truth—on the contrary, it serves to distort it.

Who would finance research without the state? Companies often earn a direct profit from applied research, so they would certainly invest in it; but what about basic research, whose results typically appear only after a very long time? Who would invest their resources in something so uncertain? Inquisitive free people, of course—that is my answer. Yet Jeff Vail once said, "The free market will ignore solutions that are not capable of generating a profit." Wasn't he right?

Yes and no. From the context of his work, it is clear that by profit he meant only financial profit; and in that case he is definitely wrong, because the end consumer (the customer) on the free market typically seeks non-financial utility. The person who mines quartz sand presumably does so for monetary gain; the manufacturer who turns that sand into rods of pure silicon certainly has the same motive; the one who stamps microchips from those rods likewise wants to make money; and it will be no different for the one who uses those chips to build a mobile phone... Yet many buyers of that device derive no financial benefit from it whatsoever—they simply want to stay in touch with their loved ones; this decision (buying a phone) is not profitable for them in monetary terms (quite the opposite, it costs them money), yet they choose it anyway because it brings them great non-financial utility.

If, therefore, we include absolutely everything in the concept of "profit"—not only money, but everything a person gains (including non-financial benefits)—then Jeff Vail was completely right, yet the statement above ceases to be a criticism of the market; on the contrary, it becomes its ultimate defense, because ignoring solutions that bring utility to no one is precisely what reduces waste in a world of scarce resources. But how does this relate to science? Well, research need not be merely a means of making money; it can also be an end in itself, an obsession, a passion. Humans have been deeply curious since time immemorial, and a great many scientific discoveries (including in basic research) came about simply because someone wanted answers to their questions—and this applies not only to the scientists themselves, but also to wealthy patrons of their research.

Many will object that in today's society, although plenty of entities fund applied research, far fewer flock to basic research, so the state "must" step in; the catch, however, is that when the state first takes away most of what people produce and then finances research itself, people's incentive to fund it out of their own pockets drops sharply—both because they have far fewer resources at their disposal and, above all, because they have no reason to pay out of pocket for something that will be paid for with "public" money anyway.

After all, the Czech state consistently subsidizes research and development at roughly two percent of its budget—hardly an amount people would be unwilling to pay voluntarily if they were not being so massively robbed by the state; the poorer among us might well contribute even less or nothing at all, while on the other hand many wealthy individuals would undoubtedly contribute not only a larger sum, but also a higher percentage. Not to mention that everyone could contribute where they themselves saw fit, and there would be no need to fund all sorts of perverse projects just because someone knows how to skillfully apply for grants. Understandably, there are concerns that the general public might not appreciate the importance of certain research—which is a very good reason to spread awareness, though certainly not a justification for violent coercion; if some line of research is truly important, it is surely possible to explain why—and if it proves impossible to popularize it and collect a hundred crowns apiece from the broader public, one can persuade a few wealthy donors to make larger contributions. If neither succeeds, one must ask whether (and for whom) the research in question is really so important when no one is willing to bear the costs voluntarily.

Naturally, one might argue that some discoveries will only matter in the distant future and people do not think that far ahead. The simple (and, in my view, not very convincing) answer is that the state, too, is run only by people, and there is no reason why these particular individuals should be more "enlightened" than anyone else (especially when we look at them and see what sort of people they are). In my opinion, however, there is another flaw in this argument: it assumes that "thinking far ahead is good" and, by extension, the further ahead, the better. Yet what if I said I wanted to plan ten thousand years ahead? And that I needed your money to do it... Most people would probably disagree with that. But why?

Although my example of ten thousand years may look like a reductio ad absurdum, I am aiming at something slightly different. How far ahead does it make sense to plan development? Ten years? Definitely. Fifty years? Probably yes. A hundred years? Hmm, maybe, though that is already quite a stretch. A thousand years? Definitely not. Yet what answers would people living in the Middle Ages, at a much lower technological level, have given to this question? Their time horizons would most likely have been shorter. And what about prehistoric humans who were only just learning to use tools? For them, it made sense to plan perhaps for the next day—and who knows if even that. I would not be surprised, however, if in a few hundred years technology had advanced so far that planning development over millennia began to make sense. A superficial conclusion might be that prehistoric humans were doing it wrong and that the further into the future we plan, the better off we are; in reality, it is rather the reverse—the wealthier and more technologically advanced we are, the further ahead we can afford to plan. How would a prehistoric human have fared if, instead of worrying about what to eat today (or tomorrow), he had focused on planning the future for his distant descendants? He would most likely have starved to death.

In general, the wealthier and more technologically advanced a society is, the further into the future it can afford to plan—partly because it possesses more knowledge and information on which to base reasonable predictions. But who is to decide what the "right" degree of future planning is? Politicians? No. This is not an objective matter; everyone has their own priorities and needs—some are happy living day to day, while others prefer building a family legacy; one cannot objectively declare the latter "better," since time preferences are purely an individual affair. So let people fund whatever research makes sense to them. Although development can be artificially accelerated, it is always at someone else's expense—an extreme example is war, which is commonly said to speed up research, often truthfully, yet at what cost? And when states likewise accelerate development through the violent plunder of resources, it is the very same principle—merely applied on a smaller scale.

Various educational institutions (much like universities today) would have an additional incentive to pursue basic research on the free market; why would they do so? Well, how better for an institution focused on specialized education to build a name and reputation than by employing leading scientists, publishing papers in the field, and delivering the latest discoveries? Of course, it is possible that only prestigious, top-tier institutions could afford this "advertising" on the free market, yet precisely in science and research that is enough—for here, more than anywhere else, quality matters far more than quantity.

It would no doubt be interesting to go through individual scientific disciplines one by one and speculate on how they might be funded on the free market, but we lack the space for that here. What I consider more important is the insight that people will voluntarily pay for what matters to them; conversely, anything they do not pay for is clearly not something they consider important enough (or rather, they prioritize other things over it)—and whoever dislikes that may try to change their minds, but should not force them to do anything by violence.

In a free market without regulations and the state, there can of course be no labor code; everyone would thus be free to enter into whatever contract they agree upon with the other party. In such a society without legislative restrictions, employers could refuse to hire anyone and would owe an explanation to no one; the termination of employment would likewise be governed solely by the contract agreed upon by the parties for the work in question. Quite understandably, such an idea evokes uncertainty and perhaps even fear in some people; in most of them, state propaganda has fostered the impression that without regulations, workers on a free market would be completely lost. I will try to debunk this myth—along with several others—in this chapter.

Right at the outset, I would like to state that the labor market is a market like any other! Some offer their time and skills on it; others buy them. Buyers here stand in a position vis-à-vis sellers similar to that of customers toward shops: they too can simply choose not to buy what does not suit or please them. And there is nothing wrong with that at all. By contrast, I find it utterly reprehensible if anyone should be threatened with violence in order to force them to buy something they do not want, or at a price they do not agree to. After all, everyone understands that even desperation does not entitle a failing pub owner to force anyone to become his patron, or to pay him more than they are willing; so why should the desperation of an unemployed person be a reason to use force against a potential employer in order to secure better terms?

To speak more concretely, let me give a few examples: the minimum wage, mandatory breaks, maximum working hours, minimum days of paid leave, and many others; the labor code is full of such mandates. And what exactly does this legislation mean in practice? Offensive violence may be used against employers who offer their employees different terms (regardless of whether those employees agree to them or not), and in extreme cases the state will shut down their business. I consider something like this deeply unethical and entirely comparable to the aforementioned pub owner forcing someone to come drink beer at his place instead of at a competitor's.

Here too—perhaps more than anywhere else—morality goes hand in hand with efficiency. However, this is not obvious at first glance, because the most common objection against a free (state-unregulated) labor market goes something like this: "In theory, the labor market may be a market like any other, but in practice employers hold a much stronger position than poor employees, who often have to accept terrible jobs simply because they have no better option." I agree with this observation; however, we must ask what causes that state of affairs. Incredible as it may seem, state regulations are once again to blame here: they place enormous obstacles in the path of anyone interested in becoming self-employed or an entrepreneur, which swells the ranks of those seeking jobs while shrinking the number of those offering them. We often forget that employees and employers are not fixed classes of people; a single person can be an employee, a sole proprietor, or an employer—and chooses among them based, among other things, on the conditions attached to each option.

Without legislative barriers, nothing would stop a newly laid-off shop assistant from getting up the next morning, buying some ingredients, cooking something with them, and selling it along with beer from a street stand, whereas in today's overregulated world she would have to register a trade license, obtain a permit to handle food, meet formal hygiene standards, keep books, electronically report her sales, deal with bureaucrats, and pay absurdly high taxes; and if she somehow succeeded anyway and wanted to hire someone to help out, she would run straight into all the legislative hurdles designed to "protect" employees. Most people have no desire to go through all that, so they look for a job instead; and because there are so many of them (and so few employers, for the exact same reason), they have poor bargaining power. Ultimately, then, every measure protecting the employee against the employer has one fundamental effect: it incentivizes people to be employees rather than employers, which—by the market law of supply and demand—strengthens the position of employers and weakens the position of employees in the labor market. An interesting paradox, isn't it?

Yet that is not all. For it to make sense for an employer to hire someone, that person must be able to pay for themselves (that is, generate value for the employer that the employer values more than the money paid out in wages). However, "employee protection" raises the costs associated with hiring someone, or lowers the value they bring to the employer; in the end, this inevitably hurts their pay or reduces potential employers' willingness to hire them. A good example is the reluctance to hire women, for whom employers are required to hold a position open throughout maternity leave.

Another way the state tries to help workers is the minimum wage; yet its consequences are not as positive as they might appear either. Those whose pay is already high enough are completely unaffected (it neither harms nor helps them); however, those whose labor has a market value below the minimum wage are fatally harmed, since virtually no one will have an incentive to hire them. If an employee's work brings the employer value worth ten thousand crowns, then a minimum wage of eleven thousand means only one thing: employing that person is equivalent for the employer to flushing a thousand crowns down the toilet every month—something the employer presumably does not want to do... And how will he solve that problem?

Since I have already touched on the cost of an employee's labor, I cannot fail to mention taxes, which massively inflate the cost of hiring someone. If an employee can produce, say, fifty thousand crowns' worth of value per month, that figure is the maximum an employer can pay for him without taking a loss. Yet how much money does an employee who costs his employer fifty thousand actually receive? Currently in the Czech Republic, a little over half—specifically around twenty-seven thousand; the rest is swallowed up by the voracious state in various taxes (including those called "insurance," though in reality they are taxes), not to mention that when spending that money, the state takes VAT as well (thus robbing the worker in total of far more than half of what he earned). And that is still assuming a scenario in which the employer does not make a single crown in profit.

Other laws force companies to guarantee employees certain workplace conditions; once again, this may seem noble, yet there is a catch. Essentially there are two possibilities: either the employer would provide such conditions voluntarily, in which case the legislation has no effect; or he would not provide them because the associated costs are simply not worth it to him, and the state forces him to do so. Yet someone must bear those costs, so they will very likely be passed on to employees' wages or to final prices for customers; thus, the state does not provide this improvement at its own expense—it pays for it out of all our pockets, including the pockets of those it supposedly seeks to protect.

The so-called protection of jobs—whether against cheap labor from poorer countries or machines that "take people's jobs"—does indeed protect certain workers, yet it harms society as a whole and holds back its development. Labor is a means to prosperity, not an end in itself; and if we can get work done more cheaply (whether thanks to machines or lower-cost workers), we are all better off, because the saved resources can be invested elsewhere. And what will become of the people who lose their jobs as a result? They will go do something else that is currently in demand. Although this may sound like mere theorizing, it is a time-tested reality: in the Middle Ages, almost everyone worked in agriculture; today, thanks to technological progress, a tiny fraction of us suffices to do that work. Is that a bad thing? After all, practically the entire population "lost its job" during that transition—and what happened? Those people moved on to other work, and society as a whole is far wealthier, despite the doomsday predictions that began spreading during the Industrial Revolution and, with minor variations, continue to spread today.

Under no circumstances should we forget that when someone accepts a job—even an extremely hard and poorly paid one—they demonstrate the following (assuming they are not coerced by violence): by their own standards, their previous situation (when they did not have that job) improved upon accepting the offer; whoever made them that offer clearly helped them (and of course themselves as well). Were that not the case, the worker would have declined the job; by taking it, they show that it is the best option available to them in their circumstances. When someone then rails against evil corporations exploiting workers, they are (provided those workers were not forced into the job by violence) actually cursing an entity that—unlike the person doing the complaining—at least did something for them.

We can observe a similar hostility in our society among people who condemn corporations for using cheap labor from poorer countries; in doing so, however, they forget that even the modest wage paid to workers there is manifestly more than they can earn elsewhere (if it were not, they would not work for the multinational corporation, but would go do something else—people always choose what they consider the best option available). One might object that such firms are taking advantage of others' misery, yet what would happen if they stopped? The plight of those poor people would get even worse! How do I know? Well, if they had a better alternative than working for that corporation, they would already be taking it; since they are not, it means that job was the best option available to them, ergo its disappearance would force them to fall back on their second-best option—which means making them worse off.

An unregulated free labor market is nothing to fear; even though the prospect may fill some of us with nagging uncertainty, it is the best possible arrangement. On the one hand, it is more efficient than state interventions and delivers greater benefits to people—customers, entrepreneurs, employees, sole proprietors, and employers alike—than coercive regulations; above all, however, it does not require initiating offensive violence against those who wish to run their businesses differently from what politicians dictate. Leaving people free to make decisions about their own lives is not only efficient, it is also moral.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Economics
subtitle_en: If the state (the competition authority) does not protect us, entrepreneurs will wipe out competitors through predatory (dumping) prices; once the competition is eliminated, they will raise prices and the customer will suffer.
text_en: Eliminating competitors through predatory dumping prices can certainly happen, yet it must be remembered that whoever sells at dumping prices loses money by doing so (while customers, by contrast, get to buy at low prices); when (or rather, if) the competition actually goes bankrupt and the profit-seeking entrepreneur raises prices again, those profits will attract new competitors into the industry, and he can start all over again.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Economics
subtitle_en: If the state (the competition authority) does not protect us, entrepreneurs will wipe out competitors through predatory (dumping) prices; once the competition is eliminated, they will raise prices and the customer will suffer.
text_en: Not to mention that if the targeted competitor has at least some capital, it can directly buy up the rival's cheap goods at dumping prices and later sell them at a profit once prices return to their original level or higher; and it should be realized that virtually anyone with wealth can pursue this strategy, not just competitors within that specific industry.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Economics
subtitle_en: If the state (the competition authority) does not protect us, entrepreneurs will wipe out competitors through predatory (dumping) prices; once the competition is eliminated, they will raise prices and the customer will suffer.
text_en: Despite all this, it is of course possible that even on a free market—under very specific conditions—a strategy of predatory dumping prices could be used to drive out competitors; however, it is a very risky strategy that is by no means guaranteed to succeed, and the entrepreneur employing it bears the risk himself. In no case, however, does the customer suffer, since at worst he simply gets to buy at low dumping prices for a while.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Economics
subtitle_en: If the state (the competition authority) does not protect us, entrepreneurs will wipe out competitors through predatory (dumping) prices; once the competition is eliminated, they will raise prices and the customer will suffer.
text_en: A well-known example of an entrepreneur who allegedly destroyed competitors this way was John Davison Rockefeller, owner of Standard Oil; yet customers certainly did not suffer from these practices—quite the opposite: during Standard Oil's operation, the price of kerosene fell dramatically. There were even competitors who rebuilt their businesses over and over again and made money by selling their infrastructure to Standard Oil at a profit.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Economics
subtitle_en: If the state does not protect us, entrepreneurs can form cartel agreements; through them they will dictate prices, while the customer suffers.
text_en: The motive behind cartel agreements is, of course, primarily the desire for profit—yet that very same desire is usually what leads to the (sometimes secret) breaking of those agreements; naturally, each member of the cartel will still try to capture as many customers as possible for itself, which will very likely bring about the cartel's collapse.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Economics
subtitle_en: If the state does not protect us, entrepreneurs can form cartel agreements; through them they will dictate prices, while the customer suffers.
text_en: Even if that were not the case, any large profits earned by cartel members begin attracting other entrepreneurs into the industry, for whom the most profitable move is to set their price slightly below the cartel's agreed price—allowing the newcomer to start stealing the cartel's customers; the only way the cartel can prevent this is by cutting its own prices, at which point the entire agreement loses all purpose.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Economics
subtitle_en: If the state does not protect us, entrepreneurs can form cartel agreements; through them they will dictate prices, while the customer suffers.
text_en: The only way a cartel can genuinely exist over the long term, function effectively, and generate astronomical profits by fleecing customers is when the state prevents new entrepreneurs from entering the industry (usually through laws prohibiting business in that field without a state-granted license). For the reasons outlined above, free-market cartels do not really form, or else they collapse very quickly.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Economics
subtitle_en: If the state does not protect us, entrepreneurs can form cartel agreements; through them they will dictate prices, while the customer suffers.
text_en: The most commonly cited examples of cartels are South American drug mafias, which genuinely do form cartels. The reason, however, is that drugs are officially illegal under local jurisdiction, which blocks new entrants from entering the industry (as explained in the previous paragraph). Large, powerful mafias can defend their position against the state, whereas new (weak) competitors cannot.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Economics
subtitle_en: If the state (the antitrust authority) does not protect us, monopolies will emerge on the market; they will dictate prices, while the customer suffers.
text_en: A true monopoly—one that can dictate prices—arises only when other actors are barred from entering an industry, which is the consequence of state action (specifically, laws banning business in a given field without a state-granted license), not of the free market. When entry into an industry is not obstructed, a monopoly in the true sense of the word cannot emerge.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Economics
subtitle_en: If the state (the antitrust authority) does not protect us, monopolies will emerge on the market; they will dictate prices, while the customer suffers.
text_en: Even on a free market, a firm can certainly win the majority of customers in an industry (which some people call a monopoly), but only by offering better service than its rivals; if this "big player" ever tried to hike prices and reap sky-high profits, those very profits would lure competitors into the industry to take away its customers (unless the state outlaws competition).

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Economics
subtitle_en: If the state (the antitrust authority) does not protect us, monopolies will emerge on the market; they will dictate prices, while the customer suffers.
text_en: Probably the best-known example of a free-market "monopoly" was the oil company Standard Oil, which was broken up by the United States government in 1911 even though during its forty years of operation the price of kerosene fell almost continuously (and no competitor could keep pace with Standard Oil); prices only began to rise after the state—in the name of "protecting consumers"—dismantled Standard Oil.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Economics
subtitle_en: If the state (the antitrust authority) does not protect us, monopolies will emerge on the market; they will dictate prices, while the customer suffers.
text_en: An occasional objection is that these theories would cease to hold if someone acquired a unique source of some natural resource for which no substitute exists; everyone would then have to obtain that resource solely from its single owner. That objection is valid, yet such a situation has never occurred in practice, and I cannot imagine any realistic scenario in which it could.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Economics
subtitle_en: How could free-market education or healthcare work? Just look at private schools or hospitals—they are no better than the state ones!
text_en: This very common objection certainly does not apply only to education and healthcare; it is often aimed at other fields that are controlled by the state, even though under certain conditions the state allows private institutions to operate there as well. The rules and regulations binding such institutions are typically very strict, since the entire sector remains firmly in the hands of the state.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Economics
subtitle_en: How could free-market education or healthcare work? Just look at private schools or hospitals—they are no better than the state ones!
text_en: To address this objection, one must first realize that "private institution" is no magic incantation guaranteeing success; while the strength of the free market does partly lie in private ownership of firms, it lies above all in the fact that millions of entrepreneurs around the world test their own solutions, with those who do it well prospering and the rest going bankrupt (this is how the market "filters" out the right solutions).

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Economics
subtitle_en: How could free-market education or healthcare work? Just look at private schools or hospitals—they are no better than the state ones!
text_en: If, however, these private institutions are heavily regulated by the state, that main advantage of the market disappears, because their owners have almost no room to devise unconventional solutions to problems, as those often run afoul of various regulations; the difference between a state institution and a private institution bound by strict state rules and mandates is therefore relatively small, if not negligible.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Economics
subtitle_en: How could free-market education or healthcare work? Just look at private schools or hospitals—they are no better than the state ones!
text_en: There are also many other (in my view, less important) reasons why private institutions generally fail to deliver very good results for customers in an overregulated state environment: barriers to entry prevent natural competition, artificial state competition offering its services "for free" makes it impossible to compete on lower price, and so on (the list is far from exhaustive).

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Economics
subtitle_en: The activities of speculators impoverish decent people; whatever money a speculator made from his trades, he must have taken from someone else!
text_en: Hatred toward speculators stems from Ricardo's long-discredited cost theory of value, which Carl Menger refuted back in 1870 when he introduced the subjective theory of value; yet many still mistakenly believe that the value of goods is fixed. In reality, people assign value to goods, ergo value is subjective and changes over time. Things can gain or lose value without changing in any physical way.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Economics
subtitle_en: The activities of speculators impoverish decent people; whatever money a speculator made from his trades, he must have taken from someone else!
text_en: Speculators use this property to enrich themselves: they buy cheap in order to sell later at a higher price. Does this harm others? To answer that question, we need to understand why the prices of goods fall and rise: a fall signals a surplus, whereas a rise signals a shortage. To turn a profit, then, a speculator must buy surplus goods and sell scarce goods; what are the consequences of such activity?

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Economics
subtitle_en: The activities of speculators impoverish decent people; whatever money a speculator made from his trades, he must have taken from someone else!
text_en: In times of surplus, speculators help producers avoid bankruptcy; in times of scarcity, they supply buyers with scarce goods, thereby driving their price down. In essence, they "smooth out" price fluctuations over time. That is what the profitable ones do: they help society and are rewarded for it. Those who lose money, on the other hand, do cause harm (and pay the highest price for it themselves)—yet, surprisingly, hardly any of that anger is directed at them.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Economics
subtitle_en: The activities of speculators impoverish decent people; whatever money a speculator made from his trades, he must have taken from someone else!
text_en: The market is not a zero-sum game! One person's gain does not mean another's loss; that would only be true if the prices of goods were objectively fixed. That is not the case, however, because in a voluntary exchange each party values what it receives more than what it gives up (otherwise the trade would not take place); when someone gains something, therefore, it does not follow that someone else lost. Speculators do not profit at the expense of others.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Economics
subtitle_en: Even if the market worked in every other respect, it cannot handle the problem of public goods well; we urgently need a (democratic) state to provide them and secure payments.
text_en: Public goods are goods from which everyone benefits, whether they pay for them or not; street lighting is a classic example. A problem arises if the following mindset becomes widespread among individuals: street lighting will benefit me whether I pay for it or not; by not paying, however, I save money, and the chance that the lighting will end up missing specifically because of my absent contribution is minimal.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Economics
subtitle_en: Even if the market worked in every other respect, it cannot handle the problem of public goods well; we urgently need a (democratic) state to provide them and secure payments.
text_en: Financing goods from whose consumption it is difficult to exclude free riders can be challenging on a free market (though solvable, since everything is privately owned); it is claimed that the state can "solve" this problem. Not only is that untrue (those who own nothing pay no taxes and are free riders on the state), but above all, the state "solution" creates far greater troubles—especially in a democracy.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Economics
subtitle_en: Even if the market worked in every other respect, it cannot handle the problem of public goods well; we urgently need a (democratic) state to provide them and secure payments.
text_en: A major problem with democratic elections is that for a citizen to make an informed decision about whom to vote for, he would have to spend an enormous amount of time studying party platforms, both in terms of practical consequences and credibility; and even if the voter invests that time, the chance that his single vote will change anything is vanishingly small, ergo the rational strategy is to ignore elections unless one happens to enjoy them.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Economics
subtitle_en: Even if the market worked in every other respect, it cannot handle the problem of public goods well; we urgently need a (democratic) state to provide them and secure payments.
text_en: Does this remind you of anything? For a minuscule chance of influencing the outcome, a person must pay a relatively high price; naturally, this causes many individuals to prefer not paying that price (whether it is dozens of hours spent studying political party platforms or a contribution toward street lighting). Democracy thus offers merely the transformation of a relatively small problem (public goods) into a massive one (an entire government), rather than its solution.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › History
subtitle_en: All those anarcho-capitalist theories are nice enough, but show me a single real, functioning anarchist society; such a thing can never exist.
text_en: Anarchy has already proven itself in history. Take Iceland, which was an anarchy for nearly a thousand years after its settlement; although after a few centuries it was formally annexed by Norway and Denmark, in practice its population lived in anarchy. The Icelandic national assembly, the Althing, is sometimes called Europe's first parliament, yet it was more like a "council of elders" that did not issue laws binding on all inhabitants.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › History
subtitle_en: All those anarcho-capitalist theories are nice enough, but show me a single real, functioning anarchist society; such a thing can never exist.
text_en: Another example of functioning anarcho-capitalism was the United States during the colonial era. Despite what Westerns depict, crime at that time was significantly lower than it is today—not only in absolute numbers, but even per capita. Settlers got along well with the indigenous population (buying land from them and making treaties that were honored) until European states sent in armies.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › History
subtitle_en: All those anarcho-capitalist theories are nice enough, but show me a single real, functioning anarchist society; such a thing can never exist.
text_en: Another example might be medieval Ireland, though there is debate as to whether that society can properly be called anarchist. On the one hand, there was no Irish central government; on the other hand, many different territories at various times were controlled by local warlords, with the degree of freedom enjoyed by people in those areas varying dramatically—sometimes genuinely high, other times not.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › History
subtitle_en: All those anarcho-capitalist theories are nice enough, but show me a single real, functioning anarchist society; such a thing can never exist.
text_en: Until recently, the best-known example of anarchy was Somalia; admittedly, compared with modern, developed states, Somalia stands no chance of looking impressive. On the other hand, no sensible anarchist claims that just any anarchy is better than just any state—only that in any given time and place, anarchy is better than a state, which Somalia also confirms: the situation in that territory without a government was significantly better than with one (even though worse than, say, here).

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › History
subtitle_en: All historically known anarchies functioned only under specific conditions; that does not mean anarcho-capitalism could be viable today, in the modern world.
text_en: This objection is undoubtedly completely valid; it is merely an objection against an argument that is not used to defend anarcho-capitalism. The expectation that anarcho-capitalism would function in today's world follows from elaborate and hitherto unrefuted theories built on a few axioms (derived from economics—praxeology—and ethics), from which they are deduced through pure logic.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › History
subtitle_en: All historically known anarchies functioned only under specific conditions; that does not mean anarcho-capitalism could be viable today, in the modern world.
text_en: Examples of functioning anarchies in the past certainly support these theories, yet they do not form their foundation; nor is anyone trying to hold up those historical anarchies as proof that anarcho-capitalism is feasible today. The theories of anarcho-capitalism are definitely not based on the fact that anarchy worked well somewhere at some point in the past.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › History
subtitle_en: All historically known anarchies functioned only under specific conditions; that does not mean anarcho-capitalism could be viable today, in the modern world.
text_en: It is also true that all functioning anarchies of the past shared certain common traits, notably low population density (though that is partly because overall population density in the past was practically everywhere much lower than today) or a relatively "remote" geographical location; however, it does not follow from this in any way that anarcho-capitalism could not function under other conditions.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › History
subtitle_en: All historically known anarchies functioned only under specific conditions; that does not mean anarcho-capitalism could be viable today, in the modern world.
text_en: Furthermore, one must realize that things cannot be declared impossible simply because they are not currently implemented anywhere; if they could, nothing new could ever come into existence, because we would dismiss everything as pointless for lacking a real-world example demonstrating that the idea works (and it is precisely this argument that prevents such an example from ever being created).

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Human Action
subtitle_en: Entrepreneurs pursue only short-term goals and make only investments with a quick payback period; for genuinely long-term projects, we need a government.
text_en: First of all, it should be noted that politicians aren't much of a catch when it comes to the long term either, since they are typically elected for four years and their interests rarely extend any further; if they do invest for the long term, it is mainly because the money they are investing is not their own—so the decision about what to invest in depends less on whether the step is actually needed than on how many votes it will win the politician.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Human Action
subtitle_en: Entrepreneurs pursue only short-term goals and make only investments with a quick payback period; for genuinely long-term projects, we need a government.
text_en: The problem with long-term investments lies mainly in the fact that it is very hard to tell which ones are the "right" ones and which are not; and since it is possible to invest in an endless variety of things, it is probably most sensible to leave it up to free people to decide what they want to finance with their own money and what they do not—after all, it is their money, which they managed to earn, so presumably they can figure out how to spend it too.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Human Action
subtitle_en: Entrepreneurs pursue only short-term goals and make only investments with a quick payback period; for genuinely long-term projects, we need a government.
text_en: People sometimes judge that the more "long-term" an investment is, the better; that need not always be true. Generally speaking, the greater current wealth is, the more it "pays off" to invest for the long term, which applies both to individuals and to society (when we are "starving," we usually save less for retirement than when we live in abundance); there is no need, however, to "manage" this in any way—people behave this way quite naturally.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Human Action
subtitle_en: Entrepreneurs pursue only short-term goals and make only investments with a quick payback period; for genuinely long-term projects, we need a government.
text_en: A good example of such a botched "long-term investment" is the decades-long massive subsidization of biofuels in the name of fighting global warming, which ended up causing deforestation (something its architects could have foreseen had they not been incentivized to ignore it); such waste of resources is typical when dealing with "public" funds, where the person making the decisions is not the one to whom the resources belong.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Human Action
subtitle_en: If the state did not finance certain projects, they would never exist, because people would not voluntarily contribute to them on their own; therefore the state must subsidize these projects!
text_en: The first possible answer to this objection is that the statist raising it is simply mistaken; many projects generally assumed to require state financing just to survive have already existed in history without any state intervention. Naturally, it is in the state's interest to claim otherwise, as that is a very effective way to preserve a corresponding monopoly without anyone raising an objection.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Human Action
subtitle_en: If the state did not finance certain projects, they would never exist, because people would not voluntarily contribute to them on their own; therefore the state must subsidize these projects!
text_en: The second possibility is that the statist raising the objection above is right: the project in question really would disappear without state support. What does that mean? Well, simply that people are not interested in that project—or rather, they prefer to invest their money in something else they consider more important, and no one can properly judge that importance better than the people directly affected.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Human Action
subtitle_en: If the state did not finance certain projects, they would never exist, because people would not voluntarily contribute to them on their own; therefore the state must subsidize these projects!
text_en: If, therefore, the state carries out a project that would not exist without it, it is actually doing people a disservice, because it takes their savings and invests them in something instead of which those people would rather have acquired something else that matters more to them (if that were not so, the project would have come into being even without state intervention); it is thus simply a waste of resources on less important things at the expense of more important ones.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Human Action
subtitle_en: If the state did not finance certain projects, they would never exist, because people would not voluntarily contribute to them on their own; therefore the state must subsidize these projects!
text_en: A frequent counterargument is this: "People do want the project, but they are living in abject poverty, so they simply cannot afford it." Upon closer reflection, however, we find that this fits what was described above all the more: the people in question are poor, so they prefer to spend their money on food and other basic necessities, leaving them unable to afford the project; forcing them to pay for it anyway through the state certainly will not help them.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Human Action
subtitle_en: The state must provide people with things they are unwilling to pay for voluntarily (to the given extent)—for instance, subsidies for public transit, firefighters and rescue services, certain forms of art, and the like.
text_en: First of all, it must be said that statist scaremongering about all the things that supposedly wouldn't exist without the state is a very popular pastime for some people, yet it is rarely grounded in any real evidence; if we look at historical anarchies, we find that many services the general public assumes cannot function without the state were already being provided without the state in the past.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Human Action
subtitle_en: The state must provide people with things they are unwilling to pay for voluntarily (to the given extent)—for instance, subsidies for public transit, firefighters and rescue services, certain forms of art, and the like.
text_en: This is because whenever there is demand for a service in society and people are genuinely willing to pay for it, an opportunity arises for entrepreneurs who can provide that service and turn a profit; thus, supply emerges to meet every demand, and the more urgent the demand, the more people are willing to pay, which correspondingly increases the incentive for providers.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Human Action
subtitle_en: The state must provide people with things they are unwilling to pay for voluntarily (to the given extent)—for instance, subsidies for public transit, firefighters and rescue services, certain forms of art, and the like.
text_en: It is important to realize that if a service currently provided by the state genuinely would not arise on the free market, that means only one thing: there is insufficient interest in that service, because operating and providing it consumes more resources than the utility it delivers to people—meaning that if those resources were invested in another (profitable) way, society's overall utility would increase without providing that service.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Human Action
subtitle_en: The state must provide people with things they are unwilling to pay for voluntarily (to the given extent)—for instance, subsidies for public transit, firefighters and rescue services, certain forms of art, and the like.
text_en: Incidentally, this refutes a favorite argument statists like to invoke to defend various social experiments (often in transportation, though not only there): "Even if it saves just a single human life, it is worth it." Not necessarily; resources are scarce, and another investment could save more lives—or bring people greater utility in some other way.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Human Action
subtitle_en: Just look at "ordinary people"—they simply need the state to take care of them; they make plenty of foolish decisions, and if it weren't for the state, they would starve to death in the streets.
text_en: It is a fact that some people behave irresponsibly and often fail to think much about their actions. Yet the reason they are like this lies primarily in the fact that they can afford to be, because they rely on the protection of an all-powerful state; and the more the state convinces them that it guarantees them "safety" and "security," the less need these people will feel to look after themselves and bear responsibility.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Human Action
subtitle_en: Just look at "ordinary people"—they simply need the state to take care of them; they make plenty of foolish decisions, and if it weren't for the state, they would starve to death in the streets.
text_en: From a very young age, right from school, the state instills in its citizens the idea that one of the duties of a proper state is to look after the weak, the elderly, the helpless, and everyone else who "was unlucky in life"; in doing so, the state effectively assures its citizens that whenever they run into trouble, it will take care of them and provide for them, thereby taking over their responsibility for their own lives and turning them into dependent individuals incapable of managing their own affairs.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Human Action
subtitle_en: Just look at "ordinary people"—they simply need the state to take care of them; they make plenty of foolish decisions, and if it weren't for the state, they would starve to death in the streets.
text_en: The sad truth is that whenever the state mitigates the consequences of any kind of irresponsible behavior in any way, it simultaneously incentivizes people toward that behavior; being irresponsible and worrying about nothing is obviously very comfortable (compared with building savings and preparing for hard times), so people will gladly refrain from doing so if someone promises to do it for them (with other people's money, of course).

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Human Action
subtitle_en: Just look at "ordinary people"—they simply need the state to take care of them; they make plenty of foolish decisions, and if it weren't for the state, they would starve to death in the streets.
text_en: People are not incapable of taking care of themselves. With a strong state at their backs, they simply have very little reason to even try; before the state took over responsibility for people, they took care of themselves—even under conditions far worse than those we live in today. People are not helpless idiots; they are simply lazy by nature, and most of them do not want to bear responsibility when they don't have to.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Money and Banking
subtitle_en: Banks must be regulated by the state to hold fractional reserves; if they were not regulated in this way, they would issue an unlimited amount of money (after all, without state laws, anyone could print money).
text_en: The reason this fallacy is relatively widespread is extraordinarily sad. It stems from the fact that the state has already distorted most people's understanding of the nature and purpose of money to such an extent that almost nobody can even imagine free-market, non-state money anymore; out of this confusion arise notions that private money could not work because anyone could just print it.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Money and Banking
subtitle_en: Banks must be regulated by the state to hold fractional reserves; if they were not regulated in this way, they would issue an unlimited amount of money (after all, without state laws, anyone could print money).
text_en: The catch, of course, is that the state has declared a particular currency official and forces people to accept it—so if anyone had the ability to issue that money without restriction, it would indeed be a catastrophe. On a free market, however, there is no compulsory currency whose acceptance is enforced by violence, ergo untrustworthy money that someone just prints out of thin air will simply not be accepted by the market.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Money and Banking
subtitle_en: Banks must be regulated by the state to hold fractional reserves; if they were not regulated in this way, they would issue an unlimited amount of money (after all, without state laws, anyone could print money).
text_en: Another reason banks on a free market cannot afford to keep fractional reserves too low is so-called hostile clearing—a form of competitive struggle in which banks buy up as many of a rival's banknotes as possible and then demand that the rival redeem those notes for gold; it is essentially an artificially induced bank run on a competitor, and if the rival does not hold enough gold, it goes bankrupt.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Money and Banking
subtitle_en: Banks must be regulated by the state to hold fractional reserves; if they were not regulated in this way, they would issue an unlimited amount of money (after all, without state laws, anyone could print money).
text_en: Historically, too, free-market banks functioned well and private money caused no problems; as long as currency was backed, business cycles did not occur. Examples include the "Bank of Scotland" and the "Royal Bank of Scotland," which in the eighteenth century maintained very high gold reserves without any regulation (precisely due to hostile clearing), thereby preventing the economic crises that afflicted neighboring England.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Money and Banking
subtitle_en: Banks must be heavily regulated, because their deregulation caused the economic crisis; moreover, that crisis is a demonstration of free-market failure.
text_en: If there is a law that restricts the free market and individual liberty, it is a regulation. If a second law is then passed that restricts that first law in some way, that second law can be described as deregulation. And if the government then introduces a third law that limits the validity of that second law, this third law is once again regulation, not deregulation.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Money and Banking
subtitle_en: Banks must be heavily regulated, because their deregulation caused the economic crisis; moreover, that crisis is a demonstration of free-market failure.
text_en: With the first law, the state forced people to accept a single national currency—an utterly illegitimate act of violence that governments mostly justified by the need to finance war efforts (which are typically nothing more than further unnecessary violence)—and granted selected banks the privilege of printing and creating this currency (under certain rules). That was a regulation.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Money and Banking
subtitle_en: Banks must be heavily regulated, because their deregulation caused the economic crisis; moreover, that crisis is a demonstration of free-market failure.
text_en: With a subsequent law, the state imposed stricter rules on banks governing how they could issue new money and extend loans; although some label this law regulatory and so-called "pro-market," given that it curbed the power granted to banks by the state in defiance of the free market, that label is completely misleading. That law was therefore deregulatory.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Money and Banking
subtitle_en: Banks must be heavily regulated, because their deregulation caused the economic crisis; moreover, that crisis is a demonstration of free-market failure.
text_en: Finally came a law that relaxed the rules for banks so they could issue more money and make more loans; yet if free-market currency is typically 100% backed by precious metals, whereas state currency is backed only by a fraction, further reducing that backing ratio is definitely not deregulation—not a step toward the free market. Ergo, the laws that caused the economic recession were regulations, not deregulations.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Money and Banking
subtitle_en: Libertarians so often defend that outdated, old-fashioned gold standard; if we went back to it, would we have to start carrying pouches and paying in gold again?
text_en: A currency backed by gold or silver is certainly not something that "was long ago superseded and discarded as a bad concept"; in reality, backed currency was not abandoned by free people, but forcibly abolished by states that needed to print unbacked money to finance their military ambitions (with politicians not infrequently promising that after the war, the state would return to the gold standard).

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Money and Banking
subtitle_en: Libertarians so often defend that outdated, old-fashioned gold standard; if we went back to it, would we have to start carrying pouches and paying in gold again?
text_en: Even setting aside the fact that by issuing money through banks the state robs its subjects (engaging in practically the same activity as illegal counterfeiters), making it effectively another form of taxation (from which this time banks profit as well), this does not change the fact that unbacked fiat currency is the cause of business cycles and depressions (which began to appear only with unbacked currency; for an explanation, search online for "ABCT").

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Money and Banking
subtitle_en: Libertarians so often defend that outdated, old-fashioned gold standard; if we went back to it, would we have to start carrying pouches and paying in gold again?
text_en: There is essentially no sensible reason why the state should hold currency in its hands; unlike other sectors of the market, where various pseudo-reasons centered on "protecting ordinary people" are offered, nothing of the sort exists for money (aside from the popular habit of dismissing backed currency as a "long-outdated concept"). Currency backed by precious metals (including private currency) functioned smoothly around the world for centuries.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Money and Banking
subtitle_en: Libertarians so often defend that outdated, old-fashioned gold standard; if we went back to it, would we have to start carrying pouches and paying in gold again?
text_en: Upon the (re)introduction of a gold standard, it would of course not be necessary for every payment to be made by weighing out grains of gold (though coins, especially silver ones, would likely find their place); in today's age of modern technology, it would obviously be possible to deposit gold in banks that would manage our accounts, enable card payments, and the like—the units simply wouldn't be crowns, but grams of gold.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Polemics
subtitle_en: In anarcho-capitalism, situations can arise where injustice, inefficiency, lawlessness, and all sorts of evils occur; so it won't be such a wonderful social arrangement after all.
text_en: Naturally, such things will happen in anarcho-capitalism, just as they do in every social arrangement. No sensible person offers a recipe for a world that is perfect and ideal in every respect, and anarcho-capitalists are no exception. There is no point in hunting for hypothetical situations in which a social system might fail; rather, we should look for the arrangement in which such situations occur least often.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Polemics
subtitle_en: In anarcho-capitalism, situations can arise where injustice, inefficiency, lawlessness, and all sorts of evils occur; so it won't be such a wonderful social arrangement after all.
text_en: No sensible anarchist regards anarcho-capitalism as a panacea for all the world's problems; they claim only that anarcho-capitalism is a better social order than any state. It is therefore of little value merely to point out potential flaws of anarcho-capitalism without naming another system (whether the current one or some hypothetical one) capable of handling those flaws better.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Polemics
subtitle_en: In anarcho-capitalism, situations can arise where injustice, inefficiency, lawlessness, and all sorts of evils occur; so it won't be such a wonderful social arrangement after all.
text_en: There could even be anarcho-capitalist societies whose overall condition is worse than that of some state-governed societies: if poor, uneducated barbarians live in anarchy, their standard of living will be lower than that of educated, wealthy people living in a state—yet it can still be expected that both of those societies would function better without a state than with one.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Polemics
subtitle_en: In anarcho-capitalism, situations can arise where injustice, inefficiency, lawlessness, and all sorts of evils occur; so it won't be such a wonderful social arrangement after all.
text_en: Merely pointing out the flaws of anarcho-capitalism without specifying any social arrangement that can solve the problem better (while not creating other, worse problems) is effectively equivalent to comparing anarcho-capitalism to an ideal—nonexistent—society that solves every possible problem in the world.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Polemics
subtitle_en: Anarcho-capitalism is nothing but social engineering; and that must be unequivocally rejected, because it is a nasty piece of work.
text_en: If anarcho-capitalism is social engineering, then designing any social order whatsoever must be social engineering. Building a state means manipulating people via social engineering into submitting to that state; if people are manipulated toward anything by the theories of anarcho-capitalism, it is only toward being free and responsible for themselves.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Polemics
subtitle_en: Anarcho-capitalism is nothing but social engineering; and that must be unequivocally rejected, because it is a nasty piece of work.
text_en: Social engineering is typically used to manipulate people so that someone in particular benefits from the manipulated masses doing what that person wants—most often submitting, allowing themselves to be ruled by him, paying money for something they would not want to pay for without that manipulation, or changing their behavior for the supposed "good of the whole" or "welfare of society."

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Polemics
subtitle_en: Anarcho-capitalism is nothing but social engineering; and that must be unequivocally rejected, because it is a nasty piece of work.
text_en: Anarcho-capitalism rests on the exact opposite: people refuse to be ruled by anyone, they are free, and they take responsibility for themselves. The so-called "benefit of society" is simply the sum of the benefits of all its members, which each individual secures best for himself, since he alone knows best what he actually wants. There is no need for anyone to rule such a society or to serve as the beneficiary of supposed social engineering.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Polemics
subtitle_en: Anarcho-capitalism is nothing but social engineering; and that must be unequivocally rejected, because it is a nasty piece of work.
text_en: The term "social engineering" can carry many different meanings, and it cannot be ruled out that for some people anarcho-capitalist theories fall under it; if so, however, they must consistently include virtually any proposal to change our social order under that term, in which case it can hardly be anything bad in principle.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Polemics
subtitle_en: Anarcho-capitalism is a lovely theory, but then again, so was communism; in reality, neither would work.
text_en: First of all, it must be said that communism is definitely not a good theory, because it is built entirely on the teachings of Karl Marx, who relied on Ricardo's cost theory of value, which was refuted by Carl Menger back in 1870 when he introduced the subjective theory of value; the fact that this was ignored by those still trying to build a bright future a hundred years later does not make communism a good theory.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Polemics
subtitle_en: Anarcho-capitalism is a lovely theory, but then again, so was communism; in reality, neither would work.
text_en: Communism is by no means an example of a system that works well in theory yet proves unworkable in practice; the theory of communism had been refuted long before a bunch of ignoramuses tried to put it into practice. Anarcho-capitalism has not yet been refuted on a theoretical level; yes, that could happen, yet until it does, we ought to treat it as an unrefuted theory and not equate it with communism.

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Polemics
subtitle_en: Anarcho-capitalism is a lovely theory, but then again, so was communism; in reality, neither would work.
text_en: Regardless, anarchist societies have already existed in history and were stable and successful; examples include medieval Iceland, as well as the United States during the colonial period or medieval Ireland (in the last case, there are doubts as to whether it was truly an anarchy—some call that state of affairs anarchy, while others argue it was a large number of mini-states on a small territory).

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Polemics
subtitle_en: Anarcho-capitalism is a lovely theory, but then again, so was communism; in reality, neither would work.
text_en: One can naturally object that this was long ago and that no modern functioning anarchy exists today; while true, that in no way invalidates anarcho-capitalist theory or puts it on the same footing as the refuted theory of communism (communism has failed in practice every single time; there is no anarchy in modern society, yet we know of no case where it failed—historically, on the contrary, it worked).

title_en: AMEN: Analysis of Many Statist Objections › Polemics
