If you are among them, try imagining an analogous situation in which someone advises a victim of domestic violence to be grateful to her abuser for not beating her (too) badly (and perhaps even points out that all her previous partners beat her worse). Where is that likely to lead? Naturally, to deeper oppression; whenever anyone thanks someone (even if only silently) for not hurting them, they accept oppression as the norm. People who accept this and grow accustomed to their own subjugation gradually become blind to it; that is why supporters of democracy see nothing strange in expressing gratitude to the state for refraining from aggression—just as many victims of abuse see nothing strange in doing so toward their abusers.

title_en: AMEN: aphorisms manifesting the essence of disobedience
subtitle_en: "Be the change you wish to see in the world." – Mahatma Gandhi / "Freedom cannot be imposed; freedom must be lived." – Urza / "We change society by sharing, not leading." – Athena (ChatGPT)
text_en: All of these aphorisms highlight the absurdity of anyone (a politician, for instance, or anyone else) planning or organizing freedom for anyone other than themselves; if we want a freer world, let us live freer lives. If it proves worthwhile, others will gladly draw inspiration from us once they see the results; the more of ourselves we share with others, the better chance we give them to find something to latch onto and follow (if they themselves wish to). Yet I consider it absolutely essential to leave the decision up to each person and never force anyone into anything; besides, forcing it wouldn't work anyway—we need to grow into freedom (within ourselves). This does not apply only to political or other coercion by force; even non-violent forms of pressure tend to produce the opposite effect in the long run—attempts to persuade someone of something often provoke resistance. Seeing the solution to one's own lack of freedom (or other problems) in what others should or should not do corresponds to a victim mentality; a creator, by contrast, understands that they hold their life in their own hands (which is also the attitude far more likely to inspire others).

title_en: AMEN: aphorisms manifesting the essence of disobedience
subtitle_en: "The spirit of the game stands above the letter of the rules." – Gary Gygax
text_en: Gary Gygax was one of the two creators of the original 1974 edition of the legendary game Dungeons & Dragons; it sparked the rise of the entire tabletop RPG genre and served as the template for many titles, including the Czech game Dračí doupě ("Dragon's Lair"), which I spent a large part of my adolescence playing and which shaped me to a great extent. Nearly every player of this or any similar role-playing game understands what Gary Gygax meant by his statement: rules are a tool for our enjoyment, and we should not become slaves to following them to the letter in every situation; at any point, we can agree to set the rules aside if we find that doing so improves the overall experience. However, I believe that the quote above can also be read as a metaphor—one that, in my view, reaches far beyond the gaming world of dragons and magic.

title_en: AMEN: aphorisms manifesting the essence of disobedience
subtitle_en: "The spirit of the game stands above the letter of the rules." – Gary Gygax
text_en: Beyond Ježek bez klece, where I have volunteered for years, my curiosity led me to dozens of self-directed schools and similar collectives, where I studied different ways of making decisions and establishing norms. Despite expecting the decisive factor to be the approval mechanism itself (consensus-seeking, majority voting over a minority, and so on), repeated observations pointed me instead toward the crucial role of how rules—and the procedures for creating them—are codified. The more precisely everything is defined (and written down), the more often everyone's attention shifts away from the meaning and spirit of the rules toward the letter of various provisions (including hunting for loopholes and ways to exploit them); conversely, collectives with very loosely defined (often merely oral) conventions focus most on their underlying meaning and spirit. I am not claiming that writing rules down can never be helpful; I am merely pointing out that most people fail to realize how much such codification diverts attention away from human needs and onto the rules themselves.

title_en: AMEN: aphorisms manifesting the essence of disobedience
text_en: Quotes from Jesus are rarely received warmly in atheistic Czechia; in anarchist circles this holds doubly true, since for nearly two thousand years all manner of authoritarians have abused his teachings to gain, maintain, and enforce power over their fellow human beings. For me, however, Jesus represents (among other things) a functional archetype of the loving and compassionate human being I aspire to become; even if I were ever to discover with absolute certainty that he never existed, it would change nothing about my effort to move closer to him (as an ideal). I enjoy reading the Bible; the older I get, the more passages speak to me—resonating with my growing life experience. I have no illusions that I will ever be able to fully understand it; yet it continues to enrich me, and in my view it also complements the Buddhist teachings I practice as well. This approach often provokes displeasure among Christians and condescension among Buddhists, while atheists think I have lost my mind; yet to me, this path makes complete sense.

title_en: AMEN: aphorisms manifesting the essence of disobedience
text_en: I know no one capable of constant, unconditional love for all people (including those "enemies"); nevertheless, I regard it as one of my life ideals. Why do I want to love every person regardless of what they do or who they are? Not primarily for others' sake, but above all for my own; the outer world can be ennobled by love, whereas the inner world can be completely transformed by it. Of course, loving everyone does not mean agreeing with everyone, let alone supporting their actions; nor does it imply that we cannot stand up to them or defend ourselves against them. Love, however, protects us from losing our way in the face of severe trials and trading our original (perhaps noble) direction for vengeance or delight in another's suffering; many people do not even notice such a shift happening, because they are too busy fighting and blinded by "righteous anger." Intellect will not help us much against these traps, because the sharper our mind, the more cleverly it can deceive us; there is immense strength in humility, compassion, and respect for every human being.

title_en: AMEN: aphorisms manifesting the essence of disobedience
subtitle_en: "If we cannot leave people their freedom, how can we entrust them with power?" – unknown author
text_en: I often hear the claim that humanity is not (yet) ready for anarchy; supposedly, once we become more responsible and less indifferent, we might be able to govern ourselves, but not until then. Personally, I see it the exact opposite way—the more "corrupt" a population is, the greater the danger posed by the concentration of power. Critics of anarchism—who often seek an illusion of safety in statism—unfortunately forget that a government is generally drawn from the very society it is meant to rule, and is therefore burdened with the same vices; moreover, those vices are typically amplified, since the opportunity to control the state apparatus tends to attract domineering and unscrupulous individuals. Freedom can be understood as a person's power over themselves; if we start from the premise that people are not (yet) capable of bearing even that, it surely makes no sense to entrust them with power not only over their own lives, but over the lives of others as well (not even indirectly through the power to elect representatives for such a role—someone unfit to handle their own freedom can hardly decide competently who would make a good leader for themselves and everyone else).

title_en: AMEN: aphorisms manifesting the essence of disobedience
subtitle_en: "Pain is inevitable, suffering is optional." – Buddha
text_en: For many years, I understood this part of the Buddha's teaching only on a theoretical level; I owe my practical grasp of it (and I genuinely feel that gratitude) to a paragliding accident I survived with twenty-five broken bones and internal injuries. After a few days in a hospital bed, it occurred to me to put this wisdom to the test; the hospital staff granted my request to discontinue the morphine so that I could have the chance to better understand what the Buddha meant. I came to understand that we have the ability to perceive pain as nothing more than a signal from the body; what we do with that signal depends solely on us—we can suffer, or we can choose not to—it is a choice (though not always a conscious one). I am not speaking of "overcoming" pain through sheer willpower (which I consider counterproductive in this context), but of simply accepting it; not everyone is always capable of this (even I cannot do it at all times or with any level of pain), yet it is something that can be practiced. How does this insight relate to anarchism? I regard it as crucial for working with inner freedom and fear; once we learn to accept pain, our tendency to succumb to fear (and thus slip into a victim mindset) drops dramatically.

title_en: AMEN: aphorisms manifesting the essence of disobedience
subtitle_en: "We cause our own psychological pain." – Marshall Rosenberg / "We cause our own pain." – Gabriela Ježková
text_en: Marshall Rosenberg's Nonviolent Communication changed my life (though I cannot claim any great mastery of it—I am still learning); with its help, this peacemaker managed to reconcile not only feuding families and workplaces, but also criminals with their victims, and even warring tribes that had been murdering each other for generations. He built his skills on an understanding of basic principles of the human psyche—among them the insight that we cause our own psychological pain. It is a reaction to the outside world—what hurts us is not its state as such (which is neither objectively good nor bad; it simply is), but our interpretation of it; different people evaluate the very same situation differently—it hurts some and leaves others unharmed (depending on the state of their inner world). There is nothing that wounds everyone psychologically; precisely because (unlike physical injury) what hurts us is our own reaction to a stimulus, not the stimulus itself.

title_en: AMEN: aphorisms manifesting the essence of disobedience
subtitle_en: "We cause our own psychological pain." – Marshall Rosenberg / "We cause our own pain." – Gabriela Ježková
text_en: The vast majority of people tend to dispute this thesis, so I have spent dozens upon dozens of hours defending it; all the more surprising was Gabriela's reaction, when she not only did not dispute it, but countered: "And why only psychological? I would say we cause all of our pain ourselves." In other words, she was probably pointing to the same thing the Buddha meant regarding suffering. Psychological wounds arise from our reaction to the outside world; physical injuries do occur directly, yet once we learn how, we can work freely with the pain associated with them (their other consequences, of course, can still be severe or even fatal). I consider working with pain an important (and likely essential) step toward overcoming the fear of it (and thus toward disobedience); taking responsibility for one's own suffering is the surest path not only to minimizing it, but above all to freedom.

title_en: AMEN: aphorisms manifesting the essence of disobedience
subtitle_en: "Everything you lose through your own authenticity is an illusion anyway." – unknown author
text_en: This is my translation of the English saying: "Anything you lose by being real is fake." In my view, this aphorism holds a deep truth about authenticity. The more clearly we say #no_to_obedience and live our lives on our own terms (rather than according to other people's expectations), the more we risk rejection, social condemnation, loss of reputation, and alienation from the people around us. Hard as it may be to deal with those consequences, we have not lost anything wholly real—by showing the truth, we cannot lose anything that was not at least partly built on an illusion; if someone turns away from us upon discovering who we truly are, for example, they never truly wanted to be with us in the first place. If we accept the pain that comes from such losses and do not resist them, the environment around us will begin to mirror our authenticity; and that will show in our relationships, projects, work, and hobbies—we can free ourselves on every front.

title_en: AMEN: aphorisms manifesting the essence of disobedience
subtitle_en: "The criterion of truth is that it works, even if nobody is prepared to acknowledge it." – Ludwig von Mises / "Truth prevails." – Jan Hus
text_en: The Austrian economist Ludwig Heinrich Edler von Mises viewed truth (and not only truth) very pragmatically; he believed it ultimately prevails simply because it yields better results than falsehood—regardless of whether society or individuals accept or reject it. In the context of his work, he was speaking primarily of economic laws; yet the validity of this statement extends far beyond them, as he was well aware. The more accurate (and therefore truer) our model of reality is for describing the world around us, the better we are able to achieve our goals; this means that true propositions enjoy a fundamental "evolutionary" advantage over false ones. It follows that sharing information more often leads to the triumph of truth than of falsehood; and if freedom is truly good for people (which I firmly believe), it also leads toward achieving freedom (which is indeed slowly happening over the long run).

title_en: AMEN: aphorisms manifesting the essence of disobedience
subtitle_en: "The criterion of truth is that it works, even if nobody is prepared to acknowledge it." – Ludwig von Mises / "Truth prevails." – Jan Hus
text_en: The Czech presidential standard bears the motto "TRUTH PREVAILS," originally attributed to Jan Hus, popularized by Tomáš Garrigue Masaryk, and expanded by Václav Havel into the sentence: "Truth and love must prevail over lies and hatred." Given that I consider this motto profoundly true, I find it amusingly paradoxical that Czech presidents invoke it and display it on a state symbol; for I believe that the triumph of truth (and love) will inevitably bring about the end of state oppression as well. The power of the state rests on deeply ingrained statism; the vast majority of us are indoctrinated into it by the current educational system, which relies on manipulation (typically through punishments and rewards)—something directly at odds with any genuine commitment to truth.

title_en: AMEN: aphorisms manifesting the essence of disobedience
text_en: ACAB is an acronym for "All Cops Are Bastards" (in Czech, "všichni policajti jsou parchanti"). Of course, I do not think that every member of the police force is necessarily an unscrupulous scoundrel; undoubtedly there are individuals among them who have no desire to deliberately harm anyone (perhaps they simply could not find better work on the labor market), or who even genuinely view their job as a way to help the weak and protect the defenseless. Yet it is important (regardless of whatever personal qualities they may have) not to forget that they remain agents of the largest legalized mafia. I am certainly not encouraging hatred toward individual police officers (they are human too); however, I do warn against the danger of interacting with them—they can sometimes be polite and pleasant, yet they remain public officials, meaning that anything we say to them they are permitted (and often legally required) to use against us, our loved ones, or anyone else (and of course they are allowed to lie about it—which they routinely do). I examine exactly what to watch out for in my lecture "Anarchocapitalism: How (Not) to Talk to Police (and Others)" ("Anarchokapitalismus: Jak (ne)mluvit (nejen) s policajty?"); a recording is freely available online on the Free Port channel (Kanál Svobodného přístavu).

title_en: AMEN: aphorisms manifesting the essence of disobedience
subtitle_en: "Life has more imagination than we carry in our dreams." – Christopher Columbus
text_en: One of my favorite quotes is commonly attributed to the skilled navigator and ruthless colonizer Christopher Columbus. Much as I disagree with many of his actions and his overall attitude toward people, I find myself living this statement constantly; it has resonated with me ever since I first came across it, nearly thirty years ago. It recently occurred to me that replacing the word "life" with "the free market" yields a libertarian aphorism illustrating how astonishing outcomes of human action can never be achieved through human design (as Friedrich August von Hayek put it: "the result of human action, but not of human design"). Above all, however, this quote speaks to me as a reminder to stay open to everything, avoid dogmatism, and humbly embrace all the wondrous beauty of the world; I have no idea what tomorrow will bring, yet today something is real to me that only yesterday was an unattainable fantasy.

title_en: Karel Šindelář: Freedom without a center – mind, nature and being (KSP26: Freedom yesterday, today and tomorrow)
text_en:
If you want to support this and the next Freeport Conference, please send a voluntary contribution in crypto or crowns!
Regular support and LN: https://opristavu.urza.cz/
BTC: 35othr5vCtcf1MiP2u3sReqBv3vqVWc5Pc

--------
The eighth speaker of the "Freeport Conference 2026: Freedom yesterday, today and tomorrow" was Karel Šindelář with his lecture "Freedom without a center: mind, nature and being".

Freedom can turn into a distant ideal, that the very idea of "one day I will be free" can create distance, desire, fear and the need for security - that is, mechanisms that paradoxically move us away from freedom. The same can also be a consequence of trying to define freedom firmly: Every definition creates a center, an authority or an arbiter. On the contrary, even one's own mind can be decentralized, similar to society. It is possible to release the inner "central authority" that evaluates, controls and directs. Indeed, the greatest lack of freedom can be rooted in our internal mechanisms of fear rather than in states and institutions. However, one can walk freely even in the midst of restrictions – much like the landscape, which is not the enemy but the environment. The lecture is not meant to bring ready-made answers, but to offer a common space for questioning our certainties, ideas and need for control.

Karel has long been devoted to contemplative practice and the themes of fear, death, love, life and freedom. The sixth speaker of the "2026 Freeport Conference: Freedom Yesterday, Today and Tomorrow" was Linda with her talk "Individualism".

Individualism is - in a nutshell - the ability to respect all emotions (and the resulting needs and preferences), both your own and those of other people. This is one of the basic building blocks of a satisfied and balanced society. Unfortunately, in today's world there is desperately little room for the expression of emotions - so in this lecture I will try to bring individualism to the awareness of more people. I will break down its principles, what it implies and why it is important to us as humans.

Linda is a graduate of the self-directed Jezek without a cage school. Although she went through six schools in her life, she does not consider her education to be the most important part of her personality. During high school, she started creating content for social networks, the main content of which was ecology, philosophy, art and mental health. After graduation, she also started a business on social networks, but it did not fulfill her in the long term, so she took a different path. Now she supports herself by working in a cafe and in her spare time she devotes herself to self-development, psychology and other social sciences. She works above all to make me happy and feel at peace in myself, which she succeeds in doing for the first time in her life. In the future, she would also like to help other people.

The fourth speaker of the "2026 Freeport Conference: Freedom Yesterday, Today and Tomorrow" was Urza with his lecture "Anarchoagorism: A Practical Path to Freedom".

Libertarians (especially anarcho-capitalists) understand that (and why) central planning doesn't work; however, this often does not prevent them from thinking of freedom as something that can be centrally planned - they desire to live more freely so much that as a result they fall into the same trap as statists, when they are too eager to believe that the answer to their needs can come "from above". However, we cannot talk our way into freedom; nor can it be imposed on anyone who is not interested in it - not only does the end justify the means, but centrally controlled decentralization doesn't even make sense, it's an oxymoron. What about that? The answer comes from anarchoagorism – by creating agoras (islands of freedom based on voluntariness and spontaneous order), disobedient individuals can locally shield the power of external authorities; the goal is not to defeat or dominate the state, but to exist in parallel independently of it.

Urza is an anarchist author; forms the autonomous educational initiative Svobodný přístán and operates in the self-managed Ježek bez klece school. Martin Čaban is a Seznam Zpráv commentator with a focus on politics and economics. He has been following the Czech political scene for more than 20 years, especially with an emphasis on the health sector, but also on budget policy, social issues and, above all, the pension system. Jan Čmolík works as a self-employed person in the role of interim manager, focusing on the restructuring of commercial companies. In December, Štěpán Drábek will speak as part of the Anarchocapitalism series with his lecture; will deal with the contributions of F. A. Hayek, an Austrian philosopher and economist with Moravian roots, to monetary economics. Specifically, he will focus on Hayek's early criticism of the stabilization of the price level (the work Prices and Production), which according to him initiates the economic cycle, and on Hayek's proposal to separate money from the state (the works Denationalisation of Money, Choice in Currency and others). I will also focus on the remarkable development of Hayek's attitude to the possibility of the existence of non-state money over time - from his work The Road to Serfdom, through The Constitution of Liberty to Law, Legislation, and Liberty.

On November 17, Czech citizens celebrate the holiday of democracy; so Tim and I joined, even though we're not exactly Democrats. Štěpán Drábek is a young economist (he calls himself a future economist), libertarian and bitcoiner; that's probably why Kicom invited him to his channel, where they talked about bitcoinization, the potential bitcoin economy, but also the deflationary economy in general.

The state is criticized from all sides – as dysfunctional, inefficient, unjust, authoritarian or blind to the needs of minorities. But what if all these complaints are not just random complaints, but a symptom of a deeper flaw in the way the state works as a process? In this lecture, we will look at specific problems that people of different value frameworks feel: from the alienation of the majority to the failure of the rule of law to the oppression of minorities. For each point, we will focus not only on its symptoms, but above all on where the very mechanism that should solve these problems fails. And we will also propose specific alternatives – small but significant interventions that could correct these defects.
Presentation: https://prednasky.urza.cz/grail/

– Teri “The Idealist” Paul; volunteer; defender of freedom; YouTuber

I have known Peter Ludwig for a long time as a promoter of critical thinking; however, lately I have been receiving contributions from him (mainly about Ukraine) that contradicted my critical thinking - so I decided to invite him to the Studio and discuss it with him.
What I really liked about the interview was Peter's humility, his willingness to learn and openly (publicly) admit that something is not clear to him; such qualities are rather rare in my opinion. We also addressed the warlike state of mind; and how explorers and warriors perceive the world differently.

From May, the cycle Anarchocapitalism moves to a new space; I will perform at The Grail. I'm going to talk about anarchoagorism, which is making more and more sense to me; it differs from anarcho-capitalism in that it doesn't recognize political solutions, which resonates with me quite a bit, although I probably wouldn't be as sharp about it. However, I would like to address why I don't think we will change anything by (obediently) voting or changing laws; central planning does not work not only in the economy, but also in efforts to achieve greater freedom, in my opinion. title_en: Urza and Lawrence "Larry" Reed on freedom and humanity
text_en:
If you enjoyed the lecture and found it valuable, please consider sending a donation!
Regular donations or LN: https://opristavu.urza.cz/
BTC: bc1qqs0sutxykl5h97xa0fcu4qaptvkvq5ecm52qn9
LTC: ltc1qpcnumcpvx2a77p0shkxwac555nepy25l0n090
IBAN: CZ72 2010 0000 0022 0135 9764
--------
Larry captivated me with his talk at LibertyCon; it was undoubtedly the best lecture of the event for me and perhaps one of the best I've ever heard. That's why I was delighted when he accepted my invitation to appear in the Free Haven.
We discussed his concept of human virtues as the foundation of liberty. I described my concept of outer freedom and inner freedom (limited by fear) — an idea Larry resonated with. We concluded by discussing how to practically cultivate these virtues in everyday life.
--------
Biographies I Recommend — by Lawrence W. Reed:
1/ Beneath a Scarlet Sky by Mark Sullivan—the story of World War II Italian resistance figure Pino Lella, who is still living today at 92.
2/ Bonhoeffer: Pastor, Martyr, Prophet, Spy by Eric Metaxas—about Dietrich Bonhoeffer, the Lutheran pastor who became a part of the 1944 plot to kill Adolf Hitler.  
3/ Destiny of the Republic: A Tale of Madness, Medicine and the Murder of a President by Candace Millard—follows the final two years in the lives of James A. Garfield, 20th U.S. President, and his assassin, Charles Guiteau.
4/ Longitude: The Story of a Lone Genius Who Solved the Greatest Scientific Problem of His Time by Dava Sobel—about how the clockmaker John Harrison won the prize for discovering how to determine longitude at sea.
5/ Ronald Reagan: How an Ordinary Man Became an Extraordinary Leader by Dinesh D'Souza—one of the best of many Reagan biographies.
6/ When Character Was King by Peggy Noonan—another great and inspiring Reagan biography.
7/ Bury the Chains: Prophets and Rebels in the Fight to Free an Empire's Slaves by Adam Hochschild—an excellent history of the British anti-slavery campaign, with special focus on the personalities of Thomas Clarkson and Olaudah Equiano.
8/ Amazing Grace by Eric Metaxas—the best biography of anti-slavery parliamentarian William Wilberforce.
9/ The Myth of the Robber Barons by Burton W. Folsom—excellent chapters on American business figures such as Cornelius Vanderbilt, John D. Rockefeller, Charles Schwab and others.
10/ Real Heroes: Inspiring True Stories of Courage, Character and Conviction by Lawrence W. Reed—contains 40 chapters on great men and women of politics, business, humanitarianism, etc.
11/ The Cross and the Switchblade by David Wilkerson—the story of a Pennsylvania preacher who attempts to change lives in inner city New York.
12/ Cicero by Anthony Everitt—the best biography of the ancient Roman statesman and orator.
13/ The Last Jeffersonian: Grover Cleveland and the Path to Restoring the Republic by Ryan S. Walters—about one of America's greatest but forgotten Presidents.
14/ Margaret Thatcher: Everything She Wants by Charles Moore—focuses on the Iron Lady's premiership from the Falklands War on.
15/ Sophie Scholl and the White Rose by Annette Dumbach and Jud Newborn—fascinating story of a brave college student who challenged the Nazi regime.
16/ The Final Race: The Incredible World War II Story of the Olympian Who Inspired Chariots of Fire by Eric T. Eichinger and Eva Marie Everson – about Scottish athlete and missionary Eric Liddell, a man who was about as good as it gets.
17/ A Man of Iron: The Turbulent Life and Improbable Presidency of Grover Cleveland by Troy Senik – America's 22nd and 24th president stood for sound money, free enterprise, low taxes and strong character.
18/ The Child is Father of the Man: C. H. Spurgeon by Tom Nettles – one of several good biographies of the most famous minister of 19th Century England.
19/ The Revolutionary: Samuel Adams by Stacy Schiff—a thorough recounting of the man and his principles that played a huge role in the founding of America.
20/ Red Scarf Girl: A Memoir of the Cultural Revolution by Ji-Li Jiang—a story of the horrors of Mao Zedong's murderous regime from one who experienced the worst of it.
21/ Founding Martyr: The Life and Death of Dr. Joseph Warren, the American Revolution's Lost Hero by Christian Di Spigna—a thrilling walk through the beginnings of the American Revolution and the story of a courageous man who gave his life for it at Bunker Hill.
22/ The Jazz Age President: Warren Harding by Ryan Walters—America's 29th president, often derided as among our worst, deserves far more appreciation than he gets, and Walters explains why.

– Lawrence “Lary” Reed; libertarian; free man; president emeritus of the Foundation for Economic Education (FEE)
– Urza (www.urza.cz); author of Anarchocapitalism; creator of Freeport; co-founder and head of the Ludwig von Mises Institute; member of the Freedom of Learning board; a teacher at the independent school Hedgehog without a cage

The April lecture in the Anarcho-Capitalism series will take place the day after April Fools' Day, which is a good thing, because otherwise you might think I'm joking; I want to calculate how much the state actually costs us. Being a theorist (which many consider a slur, but I certainly am not), you are used to theory from me; this time, however, we will look at the specific practice of the state - we will calculate not only individual taxes (including those called "insurance", fees and the like), but also other costs. The fourth speaker of the "Free Harbor Conference 2025: Culture Wars Yesterday, Today and Tomorrow" was Vláďa Krupa with his lecture "History of Culture Wars".

Political agitation since the mass expansion of suffrage takes place not only through direct methods such as election campaigns or advertising spots, but also through indirect influences that have a long-term and often subtle impact on public opinion. These indirect methods are, for example, novels, songs, plays, films and other forms of mass-consumed culture. These cultural influences often shape the political opinions of people who shy away from direct political messages. An example of the influence of these cultural methods is the process that took place in Great Britain in the 19th century. There, a combination of literary influences and the programs of the Fabian Society succeeded in transforming the ethos of classical liberalism into evolutionary socialism. Key figures of this change were, for example, John Stuart Mill, Bernard Shaw, Sidney Webb or authors such as Carlyle, Ruskin and Kingsley. This process of transformation of public opinion from the perception of state power as an inhibiting factor of progress to the perception of the state as a guarantee of freedom and an engine of progress was achieved to a large extent precisely through the non-violent path of cultural influences.

Vladimír Krupa is the co-founder of the Czech Mises Institute, an organization focused on spreading the ideas of the Austrian school of economics and individual freedom. As a prominent translator and author of articles, he has been devoted to the topics of economic history and monetary history for a long time, which enables him to look at the culture wars from a unique economic and historical angle.

The third speaker of the "2025 Freeport Conference: Culture Wars Yesterday, Today and Tomorrow" was Urza with his lecture "Culture Wars or Freedom?".

Conservatives feel that progressive "woke" propaganda is taking away their freedom (often through the state); progressives, on the other hand, are convinced that their freedom is limited precisely by conservatives (often through state intervention). And so culture wars arise... But which of the above statements is true? Unfortunately, both; and when two fight, the third laughs. Who is the third one? The state, of course... What about it? I'm afraid the only workable solution is to stop fighting, however tempting it may be to involve the state in the conflict; for the state is a bad servant, but a bad master. I find it infinitely naive to think that the culture war can be "won" with the help of state power without serious consequences for both sides; thus only authoritarians can win, while freethinkers will be defeated.

Urza is an anarcho-capitalist author and teacher at the self-governing Hedgehog Without a Cage school; wrote over a thousand libertarian texts on the web and in print media and the first Czech book on anarcho-capitalism. For fifteen years, he not only reads, thinks and writes about freedom, education, the free market and the role of the state in society, but also lectures, discusses, debates and makes videos. Together with his student Emma from the Hedgehog without a cage, he forms the Free Harbor; he heads the Czech and Slovak Institute of Ludwig von Mises, of which he is a co-founder; belongs to the board of the Freedom of Learning association and cooperates with many libertarian initiatives. You can find more about him on the Urza.cz website.

The first speaker of the "Free Harbor Conference 2025: Culture wars yesterday, today and tomorrow" was Roman Joch with his lecture "Why conservatism is for freedom and why progressivism is against it".

Conservatism wants the state to defend society, but not to interfere with its spontaneous, free development; progressivism wants the state to intervene and "improve" it, prohibiting and commanding people to do various things. Conservatism is for private property, progressivism not so much, or even against. Conservatism perceives man as a unique individual, an original; progressivism through the prism of gender, racial, sexual, cis- or trans-gender identity and intersectionality. Conservatism wants to protect (conserve) Western Civilization, the cradle of freedom; progressivism considers it uniquely evil and wants to "deconstruct" it and replace it with a new, "better" post-civilization.

Roman Joch (1971) is a columnist and university teacher. He studied general medicine at Charles University in Prague. He is the chairman of the Civic Institute. In the years 2010-12, he was an advisor to the Prime Minister of the Czech Republic for human rights and foreign policy, and in the years 2020-23, he was the director of the Institute for Work and Family Research in Bratislava, Slovakia. He is a teacher at the University of Economics and CEVRO University, where he also works as a Senior Fellow of its Center for Transatlantic Relations (PCTR). He is the author of several books and studies on political philosophy and politics, a contributor to the Czech and Slovak media. Among his books are "Rebellion Against the 20th Century Revolution," about American post-war conservatism, and "No, Mr. Prime Minister!" on the experience of the advisor to the Prime Minister.

In 2009, the EU fined Intel $1.1 billion for "conditional rebates" and "naked restrictions" (payments to those who do not buy from competitors); Intel sued the EU and won in 2022 because the EU's "conditional rebates" failed to prove a specific impact on competition (and the fine did not specify which part was for "conditional rebates" and which part was for "naked restrictions"). In 2023, the EU demonstrated the effects of "naked restrictions", for which it fined Intel $386 million; but Intel sued the EU for lost interest on the wrongful fine, which had risen to $536 over those 15 years. The entire court case therefore cost taxpayers $150 million - if we do not count the expenses for the European Union authorities, which messed up the decision and subsequently dealt with it for many years.

That story deserves (in addition to our money) Hitler's commentary with subtitles, don't you think?

If you liked the lecture and find it valuable, please send a voluntary contribution in crypto or crowns!

Account number: 2201359764/2010; variable symbol: 5

The students of the Brno Scio school have been dealing with alternative social arrangements for the past month; so far, they are most interested in ankap and non-growth. They originally wanted to hold a debate of the representative of the ankap against the representative of the spawn; it ended up falling apart because we couldn't find a date, so they invited us one after the other.
The format was a talk; and with good questions from the audience (many focused on ecology). In the end, it turned out that I only convinced one of the students directly about the ankap; on the other hand, during the discussion, several of them dropped their sympathy for infertility, which surprised me, since we did not deal with it much.

– Urza (www.urza.cz); author of Anarchocapitalism; creator of Freeport; co-founder and head of the Ludwig von Mises Institute; member of the Freedom of Learning board; a teacher at the independent school Hedgehog without a cage

I know Lenka Zlámalová from her appearances in the Czech media, where she is often the voice of (libertarian) reason; has a negative attitude towards regulations, but above all warns against the ever-increasing dependence of citizens on the state. However, she recently filmed an interview where she questioned the importance of cryptocurrencies.
First, we addressed the economy and market laws for small and large companies, big tech and the connection between corporations and states; then we got to crypto-currencies – or rather Bitcoin – and their real importance for the economy, which I hope I managed to convince Lenka Zlámalová in the end.

I like hackerspaces; that's why I was pleased by the invitation from Brno's Base48 to come and tell them something about the basics of anarcho-capitalism (even for people who have never heard of it - although most have). I really enjoyed lecturing between 3D printers, milling machines, CNC machines and all sorts of other hardware.
First, I described the ankap for about a quarter of an hour, then I answered questions from the audience; we mostly focused on the hegemony of power, the potential monopolization of security agencies and structures, but there were also many other topics from ecology to socialism to economics - yesterday, today and tomorrow.

Ivan Bartoš was the chairman of the Czech Pirate Party practically throughout its existence; now he is a pirate MP. Since I have been criticizing the Pirates for a long time, I decided to discuss it directly with Ivan Bartoš personally in the Studio; I'm glad he accepted my invitation.
We talked about the vision of his political career and the meaning of the founding of the Pirates; we discussed freedom - we probably perceive it diametrically differently. Of course, we did not forget the digitization of the state administration, which is important to me!

text_en:

Martina from Erazim caught my attention at the Association of Free and Democratic Schools when she talked about her approach to self-management - hers and her children's. Since then, we have met several times in Ježek or Erazim, which led to my invitation to the Studio.
Martina lives self-management quite radically; when her three-year-old daughter was in danger, she did not take her to the hospital until she had her consent. In her own words, this experience taught her that a child has the right to die; these words alone make this one of my rawest conversations about self-management.

– Martina; a person who lives self-directed education; teacher in Erazim, Opava
– Urza (www.urza.cz); author of Anarchocapitalism; creator of Freeport; co-founder and head of the Ludwig von Mises Institute; member of the Freedom of Learning board; a teacher at the independent school Hedgehog without a cage

In November, we will focus on the economy in the cycle Anarchocapitalism; this time the people's creative economy. Some argue that economic science is intuitive; others do not find it intuitive, or even perceive it as counterintuitive. I think that although they all have some part of the truth, I would like to deal mainly with those parts of economics that work differently than one would expect without a deeper study; because from these arise all sorts of false assumptions, on the basis of which we can, for example, during democratic elections, vote for politicians who directly harm our interests, although we can believe that the opposite is the case. I will also try to explain where these economic fallacies come from; because I believe that they arise completely naturally and inevitably.
Presentation: https://prednasky.urza.cz/bbc/

– Urza (www.urza.cz); author of Anarchocapitalism; creator of Freeport; co-founder and head of the Ludwig von Mises Institute; member of the Freedom of Learning board; a teacher at the independent school Hedgehog without a cage

Ondřej Stárek responded to an interview about Objectivism with Jiří Kinkor; he wrote a text clarifying some of Mr. Kinkor's theses in a way that I could understand. Based on our subsequent conversation, I decided to invite him to the Studio; I think that his explanation of objectivism could be closer to you as well.
We devoted ourselves to objectivist morality and a bit of political philosophy; but we also dealt with the basic axioms and principles of objectivism, including the derivation of other consequences and implications. This conversation probably brought me the closest to Objectivism; I don't agree with everything, but at least I understand something.
– Ondřej Starek; objectivist
– Urza (www.urza.cz); author of Anarchocapitalism; creator of Freeport; co-founder and head of the Ludwig von Mises Institute; member of the Freedom of Learning board; a teacher at the independent school Hedgehog without a cage

One lecture at the Cherubín teahouse eventually became a whole series; I like to go back there because the place has the right tea tree and a great atmosphere (and a Buddha statue with the inscription: "When the god said: "Let there be light," the sound already existed.").
I have been dealing with freedom basically all my life; and even though in recent years I have been mainly dealing with inner freedom, I don't want to stay only with it, although I also touched on it in the lecture. Above all, however, I devoted myself to exchanging freedom for security, which Benjamin Franklin had already talked about; it has a lot of interesting implications, but above all the reasons why people do it in the first place...

With Emma, we consider self-ownership to be one of the fundamental pillars of freedom and libertarian ideas in general; that's why we decided to dedicate an entire section of the Free Port Studio to it, in which we analyze its consequences and practical effects on our freedom.
We dealt with suicides and respect for the decisions of people who choose to end their lives; we talked about assisted suicide and euthanasia, which some countries allow (the Czech Republic does not, although it circumvents the ban); finally we discussed abortions and surrogacy.

In October, Tim Kožuchov will give a lecture as part of the cycle Anarchocapitalism; he has been dedicated to minority rights for a long time. We often hear that liberal democracy is there to protect minorities. But does it happen in practice? In which cases does the state harm and in which cases does it protect minorities? The lecture is mainly focused on various marginalized groups - i.e. Roma, homosexuals, transgender people and the like. We will also talk about the experiences of specific members of minorities with the state.

Children are the most oppressed group in our current society, whose rights are systematically (and institutionally) still massively trampled upon; they do not have direct representation in decision-making processes, as their parents act for them - just as in the past men acted for "their" wives or masters for "their" slaves or subjects. Four reasons for separating the judiciary from the state!
Like any monopoly maintained by force, the state judiciary provides expensive and poor quality services.
Just as other professions compete in the free market, so can judges. Where there is a demand for justice and dispute resolution, there is also a supply. 
The impartiality of state judges is only illusory. The state pays them and appoints them to positions, so at least they cannot be impartial in disputes with the state. Moreover, instead of finding justice, judges only interpret the intentions of the state to organize social relations.
Only a decentralized judiciary allows each dispute to be judged by someone who does not belong to either party; more information can be found, for example, in the recordings of lectures on polycentric law; you can listen to them here - on the Freeport Channel.

Josef Tětek will give a lecture in May; his topic will be – unsurprisingly – Bitcoin, as he has been intensively devoted to it for many years. Although there are many Czech promoters of this cryptocurrency, Pep's anarchist view of the (Austrian) economist stands out among them; it does not deal too much with the technological (undoubtedly also fascinating) side of Bitcoin (and certainly not with the development of the price on the stock exchange), but it describes very well its (economic) consequences for our entire society. A great deal of understanding of the past (and present) of this digital money also lends a lot of weight to Pep's predictions of the future; you can use this when asking questions. Pep's trips to Africa are also interesting, where he observes with his own eyes - and also contributes to - the bitcoinization there.

The April lecture from the cycle Anarchocapitalism will be about different (non)paths to (non)freedom; both on an individual and societal level. We will talk not only about what steps in my opinion lead to freedom (and here I develop a lot over the years, I reevaluate my views - perhaps as a result of a deeper understanding of freedom), but also about which paths do not lead to freedom, or may even cause the opposite of the intended result (here I am fairly constant over time, although I notice certain - rather minor - changes of opinion in this as well). Moreover, it is possible to aim at two seemingly different goals - freedom for oneself as an individual and freedom for society; here the first makes more and more sense to me, but I also perceive an increasing "overlap" of both approaches.

The sixth speaker of the "Freeport Conference 2024: Technology yesterday, today and tomorrow" was Jan Romportl with his lecture "How AI has burned into us through ChatGPT".

The ChatGPT system, which was presented to the public by OpenAI at the end of November 2022, achieved several major results. For example: (1) planet-wide ChatGPT fetishism; (2) the emergence of an incredible number of new "AI experts" whining about language models and whose jobs those models will take away; (3) popular influencers, who until recently unboxed, tested and commented on new iPhones and filmed themselves doing so on YouTube, are now unboxing new AI products in the same style and spreading consumer awareness about them to the lay public; (4) alerting an unexpectedly large number of people that there really might be some kind of AI; (5) the strained argumentative gymnastics of AI opponents who rely on the notion that ChatGPT is just a "statistical parrot" that, unlike a human, does not "truly" understand the text; (6) OpenAI suggests that they are indeed starting to approach Artificial General Intelligence (AGI), and that we should finally start paying attention. So... So how are we really doing now? What piece is still missing between big language models and AGI? Why is A(G)I one of humanity's main hopes and at the same time a fundamental existential risk? You can look forward to all this in the lecture.

Jan Romportl, founder and former CEO of Dataclair.ai, is now an independent AI consultant and runs his own startup that focuses on solving the problems of today's online world with AI. A PhD holder in Artificial Intelligence and Philosophy, he has over 12 years of university research and teaching in the areas of Artificial Intelligence and Human Machine Interaction. His experience also includes a leading position in the Department of Human-Machine Interaction at the University of West Bohemia in Pilsen and cooperation with the Center for Theoretical Studies of Charles University and the Association for Effective Altruism.

The third speaker of the "2024 Freeport Conference: Technology Yesterday, Today and Tomorrow" was Urza with his talk "Fear Against Freedom".

Human history is full of fascinating inventions and innovations that have often changed people's lives and society beyond recognition; of course, most such changes did not come without massive fears about the future - human progress is fringed by fear of the unknown. The older generations have been cursing the younger since time immemorial; many people in virtually every historical epoch feel that the real or metaphorical end of the world is approaching. Nevertheless, we always manage in the end; and not only that, as a company we are constantly developing and improving in the long term. However, fear is immutable; the rulers have long since understood that it can be used to rule and control the masses, so they like to feed it. How can one approach this? Is there anything we can do? And if so, what exactly?

Urza is an anarcho-capitalist author; wrote over a thousand libertarian texts on the web and in print media and the first Czech book on anarcho-capitalism. For fifteen years, he not only reads, thinks and writes about freedom, ethics, education, the free market, the economy and the role of the state in society, but also lectures, makes videos and is invited to various programs and panel discussions. Co-creates Freeport; teaches at the free school Ježek without a cage and has been actively cooperating with many libertarian initiatives for a long time.

In the public debate (and in the Freeport Study by some opponents) it is heard that health care is prohibitively expensive, so that the "normal person" cannot afford even a routine operation if it were not for the state; this belief spreads throughout society and becomes a universally accepted norm.
I have tried to debunk this myth several times in different ways, but maybe an example from practice (and my own life) will help. --------
Four reasons for free market legislation!
The Department of State Analysis of the Institute of State and Law of the Academy of Sciences found that in 2010 there were about 1.6 million legal norms in the Czech Republic, and in the long term they are increasing by 55 thousand per year. So today we probably have over two million valid orders, prohibitions, regulations and legislative orders.
Although ignorance of the law is no excuse, there is no one who knows all the laws. Lawyers are also represented by colleagues if they are conducting a dispute outside their field of law. Officials often do not even know the few laws under which they are supposed to work.
Because of the state, we live in a legislative jungle; we have become accustomed to solving all problems with laws that politicians churn out like on a treadmill. The state thus controls our lives more and more, which is a sure way to totalitarianism.
Free market law does not allow anyone to spout laws so easily, as it arises from below and is not centralized. You can learn more on the Freeport Channel in the lectures on polycentric law.

Four reasons not to trust the government!
We recognize the propaganda of historical or foreign regimes easily because we are not used to it. In contrast, we tend to ignore the propaganda that we are exposed to all the time.
Propaganda does not belong only to totalitarian dictatorships; all governments – even democratic ones – have a need to shape their citizens in a certain direction.
From an early age, we were all continuously indoctrinated in schools with theses about the necessity of the state, the correctness of democracy or the dysfunctionality of anarchy; the result is the inability of most people to think critically about these topics.
Schools are not the only vehicle for spreading propaganda; the media - especially the public ones - or the ubiquitous signs announcing what the EU has financed, as well as a number of so-called fact-checkers, in addition to information, push us emotions and the "right" view.

Although decentralization tends to be better accepted by people than anarcho-capitalism, it nevertheless raises a number of concerns; these mainly revolve around the impossibility (or considerable complexity) of controlling decentralized systems (compared to centralized systems). In September, Markéta Čermáková will lecture on anarcho-capitalism; he will talk about the fact that the state guarantees children the right to education by imposing it on them as an obligation. The state promises to take into account the educational needs of the individual, mutual respect and tolerance, tolerance of opinions, solidarity and dignity of all participants in education. Among other things, it imposes on educators the obligation to create a positive and safe climate in the school environment and to support its development through their approach to education and training. We will look at the ways in which legislation and school practice most often differ. And also to the main thing - why education, as it is set up, does not take into account the real needs of children, and how else (and why) children can be educated happily and effectively.

--------
The video was produced in collaboration with the Libertarian Institute; you can support him here:
https://www.libertarianskyinstitut.cz/jak-nas-podporit/
--------
Four reasons why the state should not restrict freedom of speech!
All communication platform rules should be determined by their owners; including any restrictions. State intervention in any direction contradicts property rights.
If we ban the public presentation of some opinions, they will not disappear from society anyway; on the contrary, it will be much more difficult to oppose them than if we let them be heard.
I believe in finding the truth through dialogue. If we suppress criticism of a position, we limit the possibility of its constant review and possible reevaluation.
Words have great power to do much harm; however, they have exactly the same power in defense against such damage. Let us fight against word with word, against sword with sword.

title_en: 4D: Why the state does not have to build roads!
text_en:
If you want to support the Free Port, you can do so in both crypto and crowns!

--------
The video was produced in collaboration with the Libertarian Institute; you can support him here:
https://www.libertarianskyinstitut.cz/jak-nas-podporit/
--------
Four reasons why the state does not need to build roads!
People want to be transported; and where there is demand, there is also supply in the free market.
The state has no additional resources available to it beyond those it collects from taxpayers. To give an idea: No company in the Czech Republic has such profits as the state earns from motorists after accounting for all costs. 
Notoriously known corruption - connected precisely with the construction of the road network - is, in principle, only possible where someone makes decisions about other people's finances - just like the state about taxpayers' money.
The private investor is motivated to manage and operate roads to the satisfaction of their users; not according to current – often ideological – political demand.

The May lecture from the series Anarchocapitalism will be devoted to the popular (dis)argument against ankap; namely, that it is a nonsensical fairy tale that does not hold up in the real world. Whether it is a comparison with communism as a "nice theory", the homo economicus model, the demand for a "new anarcho-capitalist man" and a change in human nature, or the idea that evolution shows the dysfunctionality of an establishment that has not historically prevailed, it seems to me that many - although certainly not all - efforts to refute (or perhaps overthrow) anarcho-capitalism are burdened by ignorance of the topic. I would like to elaborate on some of them; as part of this, I also intend to outline realistically functional (albeit slow) paths to freedom (and eventually a stateless society). I will be very happy for your questions, polemics and this time more than ever for comments and suggestions.
Presentation: https://prednasky.urza.cz/decentrala/

The April lecture from the Anarchocapitalism cycle will be devoted to how the state harms the poor; and this despite the fact that as part of his propaganda he constantly convinces everyone of the opposite. In today's age of various state restrictions, at the moment there is a unique opportunity for every individual to equip himself with an air gun, which he could not own until about a year ago without having to own a firearms license and register the weapon. These highly accurate and at the same time relatively powerful weapons can be perfectly used for sporting purposes, but in extreme cases also for survival or self-defense.

Ondřej Plachý is the founder and chief developer of Altaros Air Solutions, which manufactures PCP air rifles and their accessories. He also developed unique technologies for the production of lead bullets for air rifles, which are produced using the machining method on specially modified CNC lathes. He set the world record with a PCP air rifle of his own design and the already mentioned CNC turned lead bullets.

Nowadays, we are experiencing a psychedelic revolution, a renewal of scientific research into this unique class of substances after many decades when research in this direction was not possible for political reasons. New studies show the great potential of psychedelics to help treat a number of mental disorders. Although this represents new hope for people suffering from otherwise difficult-to-solve problems, question marks remain and it is important not to fall into the romantic notion of psychedelics as panaceas for all ills.

The third speaker of the "2023 Freeport Conference: Drugs and Guns Yesterday, Today and Tomorrow" was Urza with his talk "Time of Prohibitions".

What happens when we ban something? Regardless of the reasons or the meaningfulness of such a ban, most people have a need to believe that the ban in question is meaningful; without knowing anything about the given issue, they can retroactively "invent" why this or that was forbidden and what would "certainly happen" if it was not forbidden. There's just one catch - very often it's simply not true; however, this does not prevent states from exploiting this ignorance (and fear) in enforcing bans. Drugs and guns used to be common "everyday" items a hundred years ago; until quite recently they were stigmatized and banned - yet it seems that only without them can our civilization function. It's interesting that a lot of people who have learned the futility of drug or gun bans are vehemently pushing for the regulation of the other... Why?

Urza is an anarcho-capitalist author; wrote over a thousand libertarian texts on the web and in print media and the first Czech book on anarcho-capitalism. For fifteen years, he not only reads, thinks and writes about freedom, ethics, education, the free market, the economy and the role of the state in society, but also lectures, makes videos and is invited to various programs and panel discussions. Together with his wife Teresa, he forms the Free Harbor; teaches at the independent school Hedgehog without a cage; he heads the Czech and Slovak Institute of Ludwig von Mises, of which he is a co-founder; he belongs to the board of the Freedom of Learning association and has been actively cooperating with many libertarian initiatives for a long time. You can find more about him on the Urza.cz website.

We all grew up in a society that treats drugs as a phenomenon of the modern age, for which it is a scarecrow, and as responsible individuals we should fight against it by all means. From history, we may vaguely remember the hippie movement or the development of meth-cooking plants in socialist Czechoslovakia, but otherwise we consider the use of addictive substances by the lay public to be relevant especially for the present. Meanwhile, at the end of the nineteenth century, any citizen could buy marijuana, hashish tincture, cocaine, morphine, heroin, and sometimes even exotic psychedelics at a pharmacy. Drugs can also be medicine and have long been viewed as such. How is it possible that after more than a hundred years we have reached a situation where a medicinal plant that anyone can grow for their own treatment in the garden is threatened with prison?

The December lecture from the Anarchocapitalism cycle will be devoted to the regulatory principles of anarchocapitalism; despite popular belief among people who have heard little of anarcho-capitalism, anarchy does not mean the absence of rules, but only the absence of (forced and involuntary) rulers. However, people need - and therefore demand - rules for their daily lives, therefore they create them also on a voluntary basis; however, unlike central planners, the free market has the ability to flexibly create, change, and cancel these rules according to the momentary needs of its participants. In the lecture, we will focus on the most common principles on which market regulations work; and we will discuss them together.

text_en:

https://www.libertarianskyinstitut.cz/jak-nas-podporit/
--------
Four reasons why states and politicians always lose in the fight against corruption!
Space for corruption arises wherever someone makes decisions about other people's money. And deciding on foreign money is the very essence of the state.
Unfortunately, every control authority that should fight and combat corruption is also corruptible in principle. There is no reason why he shouldn't be; nor a way to ensure it.
In principle, incorruptible are those who manage their own – not other people's – money and property; bribing them then means nothing more than making a deal with them.
The only truly effective way to fight corruption is to eliminate public budgets and leave the money in the hands of those who earned it.

For several years now, every September lecture from the Anarchocapitalism series has been about education or children. However, we have not yet covered children's rights in anarcho-capitalism, as there is (surprisingly) not much demand for this topic; however, the time has slowly matured, so we will talk about children in a stateless society. Does self-ownership apply to them? Who has the authority to make decisions for them on issues they do not (yet) understand? Who will - as weaker individuals - protect them? What if someone abuses children? Can something be done about it even without the state? Can a child enter into contracts? And what if she decides to leave her parents and go her own way? Radim Passer entered the Guinness Book of Records by driving over 400 km/h on a German autobahn in his Bugatti; in fact, he did it twice, with Bugatti congratulating him for it in 2015 and disavowing it in 2022. Why? What has changed?

I believe that they are all heavily influenced by the degree of understanding of others' subjective preferences; and I am convinced that if they were not, we would live in a better society.

Four reasons why housing is so expensive!
Construction is such an extremely over-regulated industry that only entities large enough to dedicate enough people to just deal with the red tape can operate in it. This limits competition and raises prices.
Due to state regulations, construction procedures are extremely long, which increases costs. It is not built when the owner needs it, but when officials and politicians allow it. The offer then hardly responds to the demand.
The state's monetary policy consists in the permanent devaluation of the currency. Because of the state, money thus lost the ability to store value in the long term; people then store this in real estate, among other things, which increases their prices.
In addition to Czech regulations, European ones also affect us; of these, especially green policy requirements (for example, energy labels and the like) increase the price of housing.

Four reasons for the separation of healthcare from the state!
State socialist health care is killing people as a result of misallocation of resources; overworked, tired medical professionals or long waiting times for CT, MRI and other examinations can mean the difference between life and death.
Fees for true market health insurance would be based not on salary but on actual risks; people would thus be financially motivated to lead a healthy lifestyle.
During a pandemic, health insurance companies would be motivated to set up anti-epidemic measures for their policyholders as efficiently as possible, because every sick person costs them money; not like politicians who bear no material responsibility for their decisions.
The state prevents doctors and patients from having mutually voluntary relationships; some then get angry at others without realizing that the real problem is in the legislation and the setting of the entire system.

Four reasons why the state poses a great risk to our privacy!
Personal data protection has finally become a societal issue; people began to rightly ask what data private companies collect about them and what they do with it. Unfortunately, the state is completely neglected in similar considerations.
At the same time, we do not even have to give our data to private companies; on the other hand, the state assigns us a birth number at birth and then collects sensitive data about us without consent, from health documentation to records of economic activities.
We have to report a lot of sensitive data to the state under the threat of sanctions. We can only minimally influence the way the state will deal with them - and who will be able to abuse them.
If there is a change of political regime, all state data will remain; therefore, we give them not only to the current government, but also to all future ones. The Jews in Nazi Germany also acknowledged their origin to a government other than the one that exterminated them en masse.

Four reasons not to resign from responsibility for your life!
Freedom and responsibility are two sides of the same coin; a free man bears the consequences of his decisions, from which he constantly learns.
A state that seeks to babysit its citizens absolves them of responsibility for their lives; those concerned then lose not only their freedom of choice, but also the opportunity to learn from mistakes and the ability to make fundamental decisions.
In a society where the state has created a lot of irresponsible people, there is a growing demand for more state intervention; as a result of these, even more irresponsible people are born, who call for even stricter regulations and so on and on.
If people get used to making decisions for themselves and facing various risks, sooner or later the state will end up in the hands of someone who will abuse it against them.

The fifth speaker of the "Free Harbor Conference 2022: Money yesterday, today and tomorrow" was Mojmír Hampl with his lecture "Elastic money - the essence of the current monetary system".

It is surprising that we all use the monetary system on a daily basis, but often even the most educated people have only a vague or even zero idea of its nature and functioning. In the lecture, we will focus on how the current elastic money system is different from fixed money systems and explain how and where money is created and destroyed.

Mojmír Hampl is a Czech economist, banker and columnist with degrees from the University of Economics in Prague and the University of Surrey in Great Britain. He devoted most of his professional life to date to the Czech National Bank (ČNB), where he joined as an analyst after defending his diploma thesis with the then Vice-Governor of the CNB, Pavel Kysilka.
After a four-year break, when he worked as an economist at Česká spořitelna and later as a member of the management of the Czech Consolidation Agency, he returned to the CNB in 2006 when he was appointed to its banking board. Between 2008 and 2018, he held the position of Deputy Governor of the CNB. Throughout his life, he repeatedly returns to the topic of money, currencies and central banks in his works. This is also why he is known for his very sharp views on the subject of the euro and also European integration. He has published more than three hundred popular and professional articles in various areas of his broad interest - from macroeconomics, through economic history to contributions on the topic of cryptocurrencies. He lectured in many places around the world, especially on monetary policy and central banking.

The third speaker of the "2022 Freeport Conference: Money Yesterday, Today and Tomorrow" was Urza with his lecture "The Internet of Ancient Times".

I sometimes refer to money in my lectures as the "Ancient Internet"; it is a wonderful means of communication between people, which in addition to information also conveys motivation. In my opinion, this is one of the most important inventions of mankind; it allows us to efficiently allocate resources and send important signals to people whose existence we have no idea, but with whom we can still cooperate and coordinate our wealth-creating efforts through a system of prices. This way of communication is going great until states start disrupting it when they want to "aid and protect" their citizens; most people - politicians included - do not know or understand this invaluable function of money, so they will not even see the consequences of its (partial) paralysis.

Urza is the author of the first Czech book on anarcho-capitalism and more than a thousand libertarian texts on the web and in print media. He not only reads, thinks and writes about freedom, ethics, education, the market, the economy and the role of the state in society for more than ten years, but also lectures (for example, as part of the series Anarchocapitalismus in Parallel Polis and in (de)Central, but also in schools and at many conferences), makes videos and accepts invitations to various programs or panel discussions where he defends the freedom of the individual.
Together with his wife Teresa, he forms the Free Harbor; heads the Czech and Slovak Institute of Ludwig von Mises, which he founded together with other anarcho-capitalists; creates the Freeport Studio, the Freeport Sewers, the Freeport Channel and the Urza.cz website; belongs to the board of the Freedom of Learning association; he actively cooperates with libertarian movements promoting personal and economic freedom and writes articles for various websites dealing with the functioning of society.

The second speaker of the "Free Harbor Conference 2022: Money yesterday, today and tomorrow" was Lukáš Kovanda with his lecture "Bitcoin as a revolutionary stop in the dangerous evolution of fiat money".

Lukáš Kovanda, Ph.D., is a Czech economist and author of economic literature. He serves as the Chief Economist of Trinity Bank. https://www.libertarianskyinstitut.cz/jak-nas-podporit/
--------
Four reasons why to make free market decisions about recycling!
It makes sense to recycle precisely when the resources needed for recycling are less scarce than the resources needed to obtain new raw materials and process old waste.
The rarity of goods on the free market is reflected in their prices. The variant that consumes less rare goods is thus also cheaper. Recycling is therefore more gentle in an undistorted free market precisely when it pays off economically.
Otherwise, recycling is nothing more than a waste of human or natural resources. Depending on the technology used, recycling may consume too much energy, etc.
Artificial state support for recycling leads to a distortion of the market, as a result of which it can be worthwhile to recycle even where it means waste instead of frugality.

Four reasons for free international trade!
When goods cannot cross the border, soldiers will. It is not so easy for governments to make an enemy out of someone you know and who is beneficial to you. 
Division of labor means prosperity. Artificial efforts at national self-sufficiency create barriers to trade, thereby limiting the division of labor; both at the level of the individual and at the level of entire states.
While tariffs may help domestic producers, they harm all consumers as they artificially make goods more expensive. If tariffs were really beneficial, there would be no reason to levy them only between states; we could easily introduce them between cities as well.
Import quotas reduce supply, thus raising prices similar to tariffs. Competition is desirable in the market, and any restriction of it harms customers. This applies to competition from abroad just as much as to domestic competition.

Welcome to the Freeport Channel!
The Free Port is an anarcho-capitalist institution founded by the Urz couple for the purpose of spreading libertarian ideas, raising general awareness of the principle of non-aggression, anarcho-capitalism, economics and a free market stateless society, education and public enlightenment.
We are open to debate with anyone; our goal is not to get everyone to agree, but above all to discuss and think. We don't want a revolution, we don't force anyone to do anything by force (even political). We explain to people that the less state, laws, regulations and collectivism, the healthier society; and although many do not want to give up the state, we are happy for anyone who is willing to reduce it even a little.
So try to give anarcho-capitalist ideas a chance; you can possibly reject them at any time.

Four Reasons Why Central Planning Doesn't Work!
We live in a world of limited resources, where the fulfillment of one wish means that the wish of another cannot be fulfilled. And since no one knows the needs of others better than themselves, each central planner wastes public resources to implement less needed projects at the expense of more needed ones.
The information needed to produce anything is naturally decentralized in society due to the division of labor. The central planner has only limited and distorted access to them; therefore it is woefully inefficient.
In the free market, millions of entrepreneurs are simultaneously trying to do things as best they can by many different methods; the best will naturally take over and expand, the rest will disappear along with failing businesses. In central planning, there is no room for testing so many different approaches and solutions at the same time.
People working for themselves have incomparably more motivation to do good work than those in a socialist economy where "he who does not rob the state robs the family".

text_en:

--------
Four reasons for separating money from the state!
Money is one of the most amazing inventions of mankind; prices are used to transmit information about the rarity of goods between sellers and buyers around the world. Any artificial intervention in this system distorts information and sends false signals to all market participants, causing a waste of resources.
Interventions by central banks in the economy cause business cycles. Before the existence of central banking, economic crises used to have specific causes - for example, natural disasters, lack of crops and the like; due to interventions by central banks in interest rates, crises occur even without external causes.
Artificial inflation causes injustice because it takes away the value of savings, which is shared between banks and people with access to cheap credit. It makes it impossible to save money effectively and forces even those who do not want to undertake the investment risk.
If the state has power over money, it can at any time decide to devalue everyone's savings for its own benefit; this is how governments typically finance, for example, arming for wars, paying off excessive debts or other large expenditures.

Four reasons to take care of yourself and not try to control others!
People are different. Everyone finds pleasure and benefit in something different; everyone is bothered by something different and is afraid of something else. There is no one person who knows what the "right" rules are for everyone.
State-wide solutions may help someone, but always at a price that everyone will pay in the end; they are therefore always implemented at someone's expense. Instead of cooperation, people then focus on the state setting the rules that suit them the most.
Even the people to whom the state provided services that cost it more money than what they paid to the state in question did not have to earn from it. They lost the opportunity to spend their money first and foremost on what they need most. The same applies to European subsidies to member states.
The only way to find out if a service is really worth it to someone is to leave them with their money and the freedom to choose whether to buy it with that money, or make a different decision.

text_en:

--------
Four reasons why the state helps the rich at the expense of the poor!
Big companies can influence politicians and thus legislation. State regulations then effectively eliminate competition from smaller companies that do not have the means to meet often unnecessary standards and legal norms. 
Even a law adopted in good faith without corruption will rather be prepared with regard to processes in large companies, which are known to politicians and officials. In addition, corporations have entire departments of lawyers, accountants, and other personnel who can deal with regulations; in a small company, everyone is dedicated to the business itself.
Labor market regulations – such as the minimum wage – harm the least qualified, who then become unemployable, as the value of their work may not exceed the state-enforced minimum cost of their employment. Such people go into the gray area and live on social benefits. 
All state requirements for the minimum quality of services or goods make it impossible to sell products that are low-quality but extremely cheap. This makes life easier for the rich who wouldn't buy them anyway; however, the state deprives the poor of the opportunity to satisfy their needs at least somehow.
