One possible—albeit somewhat morbid—way to gauge population satisfaction is to track suicide rates; of course, it has its pitfalls (it only measures the number of the least satisfied and a lot of other factors affect it), but also advantages ("survey" will not affect any lying). And what does this metric say about some popular claims that we were better off "under the communists"? Well, under the previous regime, an average of 24 people per hundred thousand inhabitants were killed annually (in the five years after 1968, even 28); since the revolution we have an average of 16 suicides for the same number of people. So people committed suicide "under the communists" fifty percent more often than today! Of course, I am not saying that a person who would otherwise be happy will kill himself just because of who is in the government (I personally do not believe this explanation even with Palach); however, I believe that the political system affects people's lives enough to make some (not all) reasons for suicide.

Neoliberalism. The New Liberalism. What does that actually mean? The original meaning and many more recent ones can be found on Wikipedia; and a mention of how many times the meaning shift has occurred. Currently, the term is used almost exclusively by proud leftists, mostly as a slur. However, when you ask them for a definition, the answers tend to be non-existent or extremely vague (even the panel discussion on the topic "Diagnosis: Neoliberalism", for which I visited the Clinic, began with an explicit statement that they would not define the term, which they followed through), so when something comes out of them, it is usually a statement that it is a process of loosening state regulations, "free marketization" of society and privatization of state property; however, this contradicts the fact that by neoliberalism they often refer to the current reality, where the trends are exactly the opposite. So I ask—especially to proud leftists if they read this: Is the word “neoliberalism” more than a slur and a cliché?

Some people are appalled by the ingenuity of drug manufacturers, who from time to time come up with new narcotic substances, the destructive effects of which are often worse than those drugs that have been on the market up to that time; in recent years, for example, it is the crocodile substance, which got its name because it can damage its users in a similar way to a crocodile bite (pieces of their body fall off; and it is not surprising if we look at what this substance is made of). Where does such a demand for these drugs come from? Well, they are mostly created as substitutes for others that are more expensive (for example, some have started replacing cocaine with meth, and heroin with the aforementioned crocodile). And what causes such a high price when the production cost of drugs is negligible? Of course states and their regulation; she gave birth to all this crap"
the war on drugs
", without which no desperate person would want to inject the compounds of gasoline, thinner and hydrochloric acid into their veins.

Perhaps all libertarians will agree that the state should not interfere at all in marriages (heterosexual or homosexual), just let everyone deal with their own affairs as they see fit. Unfortunately, the situation today is that the state is usurping decision-making in this area (as in almost everything); and the rulers ordered that only two people of different sexes can marry (two people of the same sex can register their partnership, other combinations are not allowed). And some libertarians take the position that if the state shouldn't do weddings at all, we certainly shouldn't support gay weddings either, since that's closer to a "no state wedding" state; however, this does not make sense as long as the state disadvantages unmarried couples over married ones in many ways. Marriage currently, from a purely practical point of view, allows relaxation of some state regulations; and as long as these exist, we should not be able to deny marriage to anyone - regardless of gender or number of individuals.

title_en: Is stealing BTC a violation of the NAP?
text_en:
One of my readers asked me a question: When someone steals Bitcoin, they are in violation
non-aggression principle (NAP)
? The "theft" in itself (that is, sending a signed transaction that moves BTC from one address to another) is not, in my opinion, a violation of the NAP. No one can own a private key (it is a sequence of bits, in principle it cannot be owned, it can only be known and kept secret) or prevent others from signing transactions (thereby violating the NAP), therefore dealing with "foreign" BTC is not a violation of the NAP. The question, however, is how the "thief" got the key; there, most likely, a violation of the NAP has already occurred (even if he didn't break into anywhere, but hacked some device, it is still a violation of the NAP, because it involved dealing with someone else's property - that device - against the owner's will), although in theory it might not have to (if the "thief" had seen and remembered the key, for example).
You can watch the recording of my lecture on this topic from the Bitcoin is Retro conference on the Freeport Channel.

Dark Velvet – a bar/café combined – is hosting an anarcho-capitalist party tonight; In addition to the author's reading by artists Dominik Fiala and Sandra Dragoje, the program will also include my lecture with a discussion. There will also be a number of anarcho-capitalists that you can meet and chat with.
I'm looking forward to today at 19:00
in Dark Velvet
!

They say that in a blind test, people taste wine better when they think it was expensive; cheers! In the 1980s, the U.S. Army bought a toilet seat for forty-five thousand crowns, adjusted for inflation, and a hammer for thirty; if they told the soldiers, maybe they would shit and hammer better. When it broke, the taxpayers got screwed; however, they had to do so on boards two orders of magnitude (!) cheaper. I'm here some time ago
compared the budget of the anarchist Wikipedia and the state-owned Czech Television
; how did it turn out? Everyone understands why not spend thirty grand on a hammer; because we know the market price of the hammer. However, there was a time when it cost far more resources to make a hammer even on the open market than it does today; the toilet seat didn't even exist then. In light of this, I ask: How do we know that spending on public education, health, the judiciary and the police is not another hammer in thirty liters?
How much should they "correctly" cost?

Social engineers have a problem; and as it happens in a state-run society, we have it with them. In the Czech Republic, the birth rate is low, the population is aging, the nation is dying, the apocalypse is approaching; not that there would be any problem at all, if the comrades in the government hadn't invented an infinitely stupid pension system long ago, which assumes that this won't happen (and not that anyone would have noticed the whole thing at all, if it weren't for the CZSO and the state records of every fart). However it happened, the state (again) made a mistake; and instead of correcting it by phasing out the pension system, he is trying to save the situation with more mistakes.
Child allowances, maternity allowances, tax write-offs for children, and now perhaps even a reduction in social insurance for more children, these are all measures intended to stimulate citizens to have more intensive procreation; something like when a farmer has cattle and needs more cattle for economic reasons, somehow the lords of power look at us. They devised some pension system based on the assumptions that once held; and that would play so well that now the plebs are disrupting their plans, no such thing, you will give birth nicely!
By the way, what kind of people will the state's motivational methods be effective on? Do you want to increase the birth rate by giving financial benefits to people with children, dear social engineers? Holy goodness! At best, it will simply have no effect; in the worst case, it will mean that someone will start having children because they received subsidies from the state. People overflowing with love, who are able to pass on the best to their offspring and raise them to be decent people, will certainly provide excellent protection. As a result, the next generation will be even more dependent on the state than the previous one; and worse, I highly doubt that this is some diabolical plan, just the normal cycle of things where demented state solutions are quite naturally created and supported by stupid statists.
The next question is, of course, what is the correct number of people in the Czech Republic? Ten million? Eleven? Nine? Hundred? One million? Although our society with ten times or one tenth the population would look quite different than it does now, living conditions would change, but who knows exactly how? There is no one who could convincingly justify why ten million people in the Czech Republic is a more correct state than nine million there; the only argument for trying to get the ten (and more) is the poorly set pension system. But why use social engineering to mitigate the consequences of a bad decision when the right solution is
change this decision
?

From time to time, the Roma activist Ivan Veselý appears in my field of vision, who from time to time comments on various happenings in society; I remember his statement about the Germans, whom he does not trust and dislikes because of the Holocaust ("they killed our elites" - meaning Roma), and also about the Muslims, whom he would have impaled if he had to fight them. Let's say his second statement could only have been about those Muslims he would have gone to war with, however, he doesn't trust the Germans across the board (even without the war) because of what their - long dead - fellow citizens have done. Isn't that ironic? His theme in life is that people should not judge all gypsies based on bad experiences with some individuals, but he himself applies this approach publicly (albeit to another group); however, the person in question - like many others - unfortunately does not understand that the solution is not to "kick" for his group against others, but to get rid of collective guilt once and for all and set an example for others.

Some time ago, I met Teresa (who doesn't know which one, doesn't follow our channel, which
I recommend changing here
) attended a libertarian party; while I don't drink alcohol, Terezka likes beer, so she had two that evening (within a few hours). As I had scarcely slept the two previous nights, weariness fell upon me, and I did not want to drive at all; however, I was the sober one of the two of us and, according to the state, more fit to drive, although not realistically (not that I was so tired that I couldn't drive, but Terezka would have done better). Two beers (drinked during the evening) may slightly impair the driver's abilities, but less than my fatigue (not that I should fall asleep and crash, but I would react more slowly to crisis situations); not to mention that despite her age, Tereza is one of the best drivers I know (and I publicly admit that she drives better than me in my opinion). But we didn't want to risk her driver's license, so the one of us less qualified at the time (although still qualified) got behind the wheel; let him live
road safety in the hands of the state

Today is exactly three years to the day
opening Stok
. And you know what? We are still growing! And I don't just mean traffic approaching a thousand unique IP addresses per day (and often exceeding) and dozens of new authors, the number of which has almost doubled since last year (now we have exactly sixty - and all my thanks); above all, however, we only started as Stoky Svobodné přístov, when summarizing last year, I proudly announced that the
Freeport Channel

Free port
, who embarks on other activities! In particular, we are working on a big project that, when it comes out, the Freeport will not be just a virtual entity, but a truly tangible one in the real world.
We would never have achieved such successes without your support, which we value immensely (really, these are not empty words) and we thank you from the bottom of our hearts for it. You give us your time, strength, money, you motivate us; we have the best community one could ask for.
At the same time
we ask for further support
; we give so much to our ideas that we can't realistically take any more. And it has results; the number of libertarians in the Czech Republic and the awareness of anarcho-capitalism are growing rapidly, compared to previous years there are still more of us, but our representation in the entire population is still small. Let's change that!

The leading UK market research agency Ipsos MORI in their 2013 research “The Perils of Perception” revealed a phenomenon that I found very interesting; they asked people about the intensity of various problems (crime, unemployment, drug addiction, vandalism, immigration, garbage on the streets and others), how they perceive them in their surroundings and nationwide. The results were truly remarkable: All problems (without exception) were perceived by respondents to be more serious at the national level than in their locality; in other words, "I don't have those problems much around me, but others do." You know what that reminded me of? "
I can take care of myself, but others need to stand because they are too stupid.
Just as almost no one has crime, junkies, vandals and immigrants around them, but everyone knows that "somewhere in the world" there are clouds of them, almost no one is stupidly ignorant, but of course they know that the vast majority of others are.

title_en: Urza in deCentral: A school for authoritarianism
text_en:
The topic of the past
lectures on anarcho-capitalism at the (de)Centrála club
were human rights in a stateless society!
Today we will talk about indoctrination by statism in schools and the path to authoritarianism; because it is not only direct, but in general education is set up to lead us to conformity - is this even desirable?
You are also all invited to the next lecture, which will also be on the first Wednesday of the month, i.e. October 3; the topic will be the NAP (principle of non-aggression), which has been inflected so much lately, while we will also touch on animal rights or psychological violence.
I'm looking forward to seeing you tonight at 7 p.m
of the (de)Central club
.

The school year begins; the state forcibly forces parents to send their children to school where they will be
indoctrinated by propaganda
, which of them
will create obedient citizens
. Who would defy something like that and insist on it, the children will be forcibly abducted (!) by a social worker (with the possible support of uniformed monkeys, if necessary); the euphemism for this action - completely unacceptable for most of us, if the state did not do it (which clearly shows the power of that propaganda) - is compulsory schooling.
Let's get rid of her!
And there is another thing which is our children
indoctrinated similarly to the state; this is democracy
– the idol that, if you refuse to worship, you will become the object of ridicule of the believers of the most widespread religion, that is, statism. Anyone who is interested in the given topic more deeply should come to my lecture on Wednesday
of the (de)Central club

The holidays are over, so Stoky resumes its standard operation; and with Stokami, the entire Freeport.

my challenges

title_en: The beginning of the year in deCentral
text_en:
The school year is coming; on Friday, Stoky (and the entire Free Port) will be switched from holiday mode, on Monday the school year begins and on Wednesday the cycle of lectures on anarcho-capitalism continues.
Regular readers will surely not be surprised that education and the educational system is my topic, so the next lecture will cover it.
This time we will not discuss free market alternatives or free schools, but we will thoroughly focus on state schools functioning as temples of statism and cultivating conformity in us.
I look forward to seeing you in exactly one week on Wednesday, September 5 in the evening at 7 p.m
of the (de)Central club
.

When we founded the Ludwig von Mises Institute in 2010, we could not afford a part-time employee. In 2015, yes; she signed up
Teresa
(with whom, by the way, we run Mises together today).
One of her tasks was sorting articles for publication, which had previously been done by the authors themselves; I somehow didn't notice the change, so I constantly teased her about it with my texts.
It took about a year before she - as a new young part-timer in a well-coordinated team - spoke up; we soon met, got engaged in 2017, now we're getting married!
And we hope that one day the Freeport and the Ludwig von Mises Institute will be able to take over our children xD
At the ceremony, the marriage will be recorded in the blockchain in the OP_RETURN of one of the transactions at 1PPfW4rHery9apPL9pPQva6CWp44c9H5tQ.

The holidays are starting, which affects a good part of us in some way, whether it is school children, their parents, university students, teachers, visitors to various festivals and the like; website traffic with articles (even such non-articles) and comments is down, but my schedule will also be affected by the holidays. For that reason, I'm switching Stoky into vacation mode for two months, which means:
1/ Texts will not be published here with such regularity as before; they will be published rather randomly.
2/ I am asking libertarians who have more time for texts to Stok; send it to me by email (or publish it yourself; ideally hit the days when nothing comes out xD).
And above all, enjoy the summer!

Recently, we can hear here and there about the restriction and then the complete abolition of cash; what would it be for? Well, the state would have absolute control over all monetary transactions that take place; whenever you pay someone something, an electronic trail is left for the uniformed monkeys to follow if necessary. Then, in principle, even the EET would be useless, because the state would see much more. Of course, it won't happen overnight, people would chatter, but we are getting closer to it step by step (too large cash transactions are already restricted by law); and when some "Western developed country" abolishes cash, our politicians will start giving it to us as an example worth following, because "an honest person has nothing to fear." It's understandable to cry, but what about it? Fortunately, we still have cryptocurrencies; the abolition of cash could give them a huge scope.

You may have heard of LAMI (Summer Academy of the Mises Institute) in the past, which was transformed into MALI (Mises Academy of the Liberal Institute) in connection with the transfer of some events of the Ludwig von Mises Institute under the banner of the Liberal Institute; except for the name, practically nothing has changed, it is organized by the same people and the practical form also remains the same. This year, however, Tereza will be lecturing with me at MALI (and it's her first lecture in her life), so I'd rather you come; You can find out more about the event (including registration and list of speakers) when
you click here
. So don't hesitate and sign up!

Paradoxically, a common argument for the EU is the free market; thanks to our membership in the EU, we can benefit from the benefits of open borders and a free market, for which we supposedly "have" to pay the bureaucracy that regulates the markets (which is a paradox - regulate yourself to the free market). If we do not regulate, states will not be able to protect "their" companies from subsidized and favored competition; however, I maintain that nothing of the sort is necessary. If other countries subsidize their producers and the Czech Republic does not, Czech producers will become less competitive, but Czech customers will be able to buy cheaper (subsidized from abroad) goods; and if someone thinks even further and it happens that all Czech businessmen go bankrupt, their employees lose their jobs and have no money for anything, I recommend not to end the thinking here, but to think about one more step (his thorough thinking will explain why even that catastrophic scenario will never happen).

"That can never work," many argue; Public transport must be subsidized, otherwise it would not support itself from tickets. Why? Well... this argument is based purely on the fact that the way it is at the moment, the transport companies are unprofitable and perform horribly despite the subsidies; and when something is certain today, people tend to believe that it cannot be otherwise. But it doesn't make sense from the point of view, because people want to travel and there is no reason why it shouldn't be possible to make money from it (and if it really didn't work, it would mean that people are simply not worth the real costs of public transport, ergo it doesn't make sense to force them to pay). Anyway, years ago, for example, the subway in New York was private, today, for example, in Hong Kong, public transport is mostly private and works without problems; does that surprise anyone? Certainly not me; if we allowed private individuals to transport people en masse and unregulated, for example around Prague, I am sure that we would be very pleasantly surprised by the result.

Zdeněk Neusar from the Ministry of Transport threatens drivers with a driving ban for six months to a year for crossing out the EU flag on their registration plate. And you know what's interesting? As statists always defend laws (whether during their introduction or against their abolition) by their necessity; the license plate is said to be necessary, because how else will the heroic police turn out to be a criminal villain. Then some horror will appear in our legal system, from which, formally speaking, it follows that crossing out the EU flag on the registration plate can be punished by a driving ban. Such a thing is quite obviously at absolute odds with how the law was reasoned. But this is where the popular statist argument comes in again: "The law is the law." Badly made laws are constantly being forced upon us, which are supposed to prevent some evil, but in reality affect even things quite harmless; and when someone points it out, instead of dealing with a poorly made law, there is an appeal that we must obey even a bad law. And so freedom dies to the tumultuous applause of the crowds...

I make software for a living. I have devoted tens of thousands of hours in my life to programming, algorithmization, logic, databases, mathematics, computer networks, hardware and other related fields, during which I am still learning; it's a never-ending process where I make mistakes, learn, improve, and become more and more of an expert. People typically don't question my expertise; at most, sometimes another programmer disagrees with me, he has a different opinion on some things, which we sometimes discuss - and we don't always agree, but we both understand the topic, so it has its head and tail. Only once did someone who had spent no more than a few minutes or hours thinking about programming start to explain to me how I was doing it wrong; it was an aggressive pensioner and people tapped each other on the forehead. Even customers, if something doesn't work as it should, don't come to advise me how to program it correctly; because they know they don't have enough information and experience to make sense of it.
I spent no less time in my life studying anarcho-capitalism, political philosophy, ethics, Austrian economics, praxeology, the free market, the history of various forms of totalitarian regimes, and the like; I have also read dozens of books, thousands of articles, led countless discussions and written and created a few things myself, made mistakes, learned and am constantly improving my expertise. I encounter her questioning on a daily basis; most often by people who usually did not deal with the topic for more than a few minutes in total.
They don't take a second to study the historical polycentric legal systems before telling me they can never work. For some reason, they feel that they do not need knowledge and information here; they do not perceive that they are behaving like the pensioner mentioned above. Of course, I do not rule out the possibility that someone will study everything and still not agree; of course it happens, just as I don't agree with every programmer on professional issues. But at least the discussion makes sense.
I can be wrong and make mistakes in anything; be it anarcho-capitalism or programming. But in order for someone to be able to meaningfully point out these errors, they must first have at least a general understanding of the topic and familiarize themselves with what I am claiming and in what context. Everyone understands this about programming; however, masses of people who hear about anarcho-capitalism for the first time will react with rejection through some absolutely basic and countless times uttered argument like: "Without the state, who would build roads? Besides, justice, medical care, education and security would only be for the rich. And all this does not take into account the average person." Of course, I could have erred in refuting such arguments, but such an error cannot be detected by merely repeating the argument; you need to find out something about the given topic, study it, think about it and have a serious debate. Disproving a decades-old school of thought at first glance is about as likely as someone finding an error in complex source code because they've seen The Matrix.

MPs (and senators) have immunity, on the basis of which they can only be prosecuted with the consent of their colleagues (and offenses against them are dealt with only by colleagues); imagine if you were like that too, you can only be prosecuted if your colleagues at work agree. As an anarcho-capitalist, I only see it as

It is said that this is so that deputies (or senators) cannot be "bullied" by unnecessary lawsuits, which could paralyze the activities of the parliament (or senate); do you feel the mockery? The fight for freedom begins in the minds of the little ones; and we all know the establishment is winning across the board so far. Not only does it completely control education, but also the public media and pays for its own propaganda with our money. For example, look for the video "Democracy is cool" on YouTube - little kids sing about the fact that anyone who doesn't want democracy is a slob (financed by the EU and the Ministry of Education and Culture); regardless of whether you agree with that view, try to imagine the uproar and outrage over the abuse and manipulation of children if a church or political party tried such propaganda. However, the state and democracy are idols, in their name anything is allowed. Worse, however, is that similar propaganda is fed to our children by the public broadcaster CT; just try searching for the show "Bankovkovi", the episode "Taxes". Again, it is not so important whether you agree with the wording, but it is perhaps anything but "objective and balanced"; when providing information about the state, people subconsciously ignore this rule (and the law). In addition, verifiable falsehoods are heard in the program.
This time, though, I'd like us to do more than just state that it's wrong. I wrote CT
open letter, which you can read here
. The problem with open letters, however, is that no one cares, because everyone writes them, unless... people start talking about them. And once people start talking about them on social networks, in discussions and on their servers enough for the media to notice (and here I can reveal that I already have some media arranged; but we need more), the topic will resonate in society. And this topic is actually ankap itself and state propaganda; this is exactly what needs to be conveyed to the people. It's often said that you can't change anything by clicking, that you need to get up your ass and go do something; however, this does not apply here. If you really want to help, you can. It won't cost money, just a few minutes of time. Go spread the letter. Do you have your website? Favorite discussion forum? A social network? Newsletter? Please flood them. Elicit discussion, reaction; and disagree. If we do it thoroughly enough, it will attract the attention of the big media.

title_en: Piggy in a concentration camp; not to mention the state
text_en:
I'm watching Seznam duel, where there is a debate about Piggy in Lety; there used to be a concentration camp, and now the state is buying the place for more than a quarter of a billion to build a memorial there. This move is advocated by the populist Daniel Herman. As? By referring to the pieta, the suffering of the victims and so on, against which not even half a word can be said, because the Nazi concentration camps were really pure evil; the question is whether this is a seriously relevant argument. There is certainly interest in having a monument stand on the site; on the other hand, there is also an interest in having a piggy bank standing in the same place. What about that? The owner of the piggery makes a profit from it corresponding to how much benefit it brings to society as a whole (that is, to the people who eat the pigs); on the other hand, there is an intangible benefit to many people from a possible memorial. How to compare these two incommensurable values? Well, quite easily: Are those interested in the monument willing to fold and pay the owners of the piggy bank enough to give it up? If not, then apparently they want that memorial less than many want a piggery.
Unfortunately, nothing like that was heard in the duel. The opponent of the folklorist Daniel Herman was the Communist Josef Skála, who was only able to relativize the problem in an attempt to objectify the non-objectivable; his entire argument was more or less that there were other places where similar and worse atrocities were committed, so we should start with those. In principle, he makes exactly the same error in reasoning as his opponent: He puts his wishes and his subjective feeling above the preferences expressed by people through their actions in the market. If they consider Lety to be more important than other places, then it is not right to force them to build monuments elsewhere first. It is sad that two totalitarians clashed in the discussion, who, although they each have a different idea of what to spend the looted money they did not earn and on which they are parasitizing, but they agree on one thing: It is necessary to take that money from the people under the threat of violence, because a bunch of elitist politicians can make better decisions about it than the robbed people. It is sad that no one represented freedom in the debate.

Mon
lecture on free market internal security
a

what follows is perhaps the most difficult topic of the cycle Anarchocapitalism in Parallel Polis; this subject is nothing but the military and free market defense against an external enemy. At the same time, this is the penultimate lecture of this cycle; and I'm really glad you keep coming in such great numbers!
In today's lecture, we will talk about how an anarcho-capitalist free market society can defend itself against an external enemy, i.e. other states that might want to annex this territory. How would the security agencies fare against the regular army? What about the role of the militia in modern warfare? In almost all lectures, I talked about how the market is more efficient than the state; however, we must not forget why this is so and constantly subject this principle to criticism, which will result in an interesting insight in this lecture.
I also invite everyone to the last lecture, which will take place in two weeks (March 28 at 8 p.m.); there we will look at certain principles of anarcho-capitalism and place it in a wider context among other anarchist trends.
I'm looking forward to seeing you tonight at 8 p.m

Mon
a lecture on the judiciary
and the cycle Anarchocapitalism continues in the Parallel Polis after a longer pause, which is slowly approaching its end; that's why it tightens and the topics get harder and harder, this is one of the most explosive. I am very glad that you have been coming in such large numbers for almost a year and a half!
Today's lecture will directly follow on from the last one, where we discussed the resolution of disputes in cases where both parties more or less cooperate; today we will look at what possibilities the free market offers in situations where at least one of the parties is not interested in a peaceful and fair solution. Will people without a state resign themselves to justice and shoot each other in the street? Will the security agencies go to war with each other in a competitive struggle? What about the poor? If security is going to be a service like any other, what will those who simply don't have money do? Will they become free targets of sadistic killers? All this - and much more - we will discuss in the evening!
Everyone is invited to the next lecture (it will be in a month, i.e. on March 14), but above all to the launch of the book Anarchocapitalism! So come to Parallel Polis on March 1 (

title_en: Twenty-three years since the death of Murray Newton Rothbard
text_en: Today it is exactly twenty-three years since one of the greatest thinkers, economists, philosophers and geniuses left this world at the age of 69 - Murray Newton Rothbard, the "father of anarcho-capitalism"; his life's work was a consistent and logical introduction to the consequences of two trends that were seemingly not very related: anarchism and the Austrian school of economics. Anarchists were often wrong in economics, and the proponents of the Austrian school of economics did not apply their (correct) conclusions to the state; Murray Newton Rothbard corrected both and came to a brilliant conclusion: "Capitalism is the fullest expression of anarchism, and anarchism is the fullest expression of capitalism. Not only are they compatible, but you can't really have one without the other. True anarchism will be capitalism, and true capitalism will be anarchism." This knowledge and full understanding of it changed my life greatly; Thank you, Mr. Rothbard.

Well, although those in question are "just doing their jobs", they are destroying the lives of many under the guise of the war on drugs; and someone decided to point them out by name because we are all responsible for our actions regardless of excuses like "I'm just following the law". I believe that if cryptocurrencies become even more widespread in the future, similar projects will start to make a lot of sense; and even today, although they probably won't find mass use yet, they represent an interesting and functional concept. Thus, Judge Dredd embodies both a free market entrepreneur providing a real service, as well as a theoretical model and example of how the free market can replace some functions of the state.

In debates about the unnecessaryness of the state, one can relatively often encounter the question of what will happen to people who suffer from some serious and expensively treatable congenital disease, ideally one that can be detected before birth, which means that no insurance company will be interested in them; and what is my answer? Well, of course no one can predict the market, but I can imagine, for example, insurance for parents to whom the insurance company will offer a future contract for their child's insurance for an additional fee; I can also imagine insuring children even before conception and many other solutions. That similar services do not exist today? That is true, but why should they exist in a socialist health care system where everyone will be insured? Logically, there is no demand for something that the state offers for so-called "free"; if it stops happening, demand will arise - and where there is demand, there will also be an offer, because you can make money from it.
My fiancee called the principle "insurance against the uninsurable"; I consider this designation to be absolutely accurate. Insurance is similar to betting: If there is an event with a low probability of occurrence, I can bet for quite a bit of money that it will occur, and when it does, I can win far more (because the chance of winning was small); and as long as people are willing to bet, there is no reason why those bets should not be made by someone who calculates the statistical odds and designs favorable terms for himself. Why shouldn't it then be possible to bet that if a child is born to me affected by disease X, I will receive Y crowns, where Y is the price of treatment? If I am willing to bet significantly more than Y times the odds that the newborn will have disease X, someone rich will be found to make the bet because it is profitable; after all... if people come to you and offer 100 crowns for the fact that you will pay them 900 crowns with a 1:10 chance, will you refuse?

One does not have to go far for the idea that conscription should be reintroduced; however, I am not entirely sure that all those who ask for this really fully understand what they are asking for, because the state propaganda has gone so far that many people no longer even think about what is hidden behind each of the euphemisms used by the government. So what is conscription? So, above all, it is about slavery; true, typically time-limited, but the gist is that conscripts are forced (!) to submit to the whims of other people the military designates as their superiors. Whether they bully them or treat them quite "well" is irrelevant; a slave owner who does not abuse his slaves and is "good" to them as much as possible does not cease to be a slave owner. Are you, then, supporters of compulsory war, really supporters of slavery? I think mostly not, you just think it's an exaggeration to call military service that; but is it really so?
If you tell someone in an African country where female circumcision is a common practice that it is a disgusting barbaric atrocity, they will probably also find it exaggerated, because in their reality it is a quite normal thing; she will probably answer something along the lines of: "I went through it as a child too, and at least I'm not fucking myself." A chilling analogy to the notorious: "I was in the army, I was bullied, but it benefited me, at least I'm not such a slob like today's young people." What do I mean by that? That the way we perceive something emotionally is influenced to an extremely strong extent by how common that thing is in the environment where we live - if we get used to it, even absolutely horrible things no longer shock us; in such a case, let's forget about emotions and follow logic: Even if we don't have to perceive war as slavery, in reality it is (a person is forcibly forced to obey someone's orders); and how can such an atrocity be justified?

O
the state's war on drugs
(and actually about
drugs themselves
) I have already written a lot; from a moral point of view, there is no justification for the aggressive violence of the state against the producers and sellers of illegal drugs, nor for restricting the users' choice of how to dispose of their bodies, and certainly not for forcing the taxpayers to fund this aggression, while from a practical point of view, state intervention causes the increase in the price of narcotics, the crime associated with them, countless ruined lives as a result, and above all, it simply does not work (
a picture is worth a thousand words
), which
is well known
even to those who waged the war against drugs for decades. It is therefore an activity that costs a huge amount of resources, causes crime and unfathomable suffering, and moreover has no results; the ideal of fools and politicians, who already feed the public with fairy tales and lie to them about the benefits of the whole thing.
However, recently, while reading some text about the drug trade in prisons, one more thing occurred to me: The state is not even able to ensure that its prisoners do not fet! Even in maximum security prisons, where each cell is only a few square meters, with bars everywhere and guards who have the power to search Muggles' personal belongings at any time, order them around, manage their daily schedule and constantly check them, the state is unable to "win" the war on drugs; but if it fails even in an almost laboratory and ideal environment for exercising its power, how can anyone believe that it can succeed in the real world, where it has been wasting resources for decades without tangible results? We can discuss whether at least the set goal is correct (in my opinion it is not), but the fact that the chosen means do not lead to it, perhaps could not be more obvious...

Right-wing conservatives like to talk about the supposed favoritism of homosexuals in our society; I personally don't like this talk. On the one hand, in my opinion, this is not even true, but above all, I see the only goal in it, which is the release of antipathies in an artificial conflict about nothing. Paradoxically, it bothers them that a homosexual gets attention by coming out, although if nobody addressed homosexuality and everyone didn't care, it wouldn't attract any attention. Most normal homosexuals understandably do not deal with such things, but there are exceptions; for example, Matěj Stropnický tried to use his sexual orientation as a pre-election trump card. The result of the Greens suggests that homosexuality will probably not be such a problem socially; the fact that the person in question tried it shows both his desperation and ideological emptiness, but also how serious he is about the fight for minorities: If it brings political points, he is a great fighter; however, when it comes to votes, there is no problem with a well-timed coming out to put a gay stick in the hand of every frustrated person.

Many ask me who to vote for; I'm just saying that I don't know. I have no idea who you should vote for; I don't even know if you're supposed to vote. Although I certainly don't consider not voting to be stupid or wrong, I personally have always voted; and I will vote as long as the message I would send by not voting is perceived as disinterest, not disapproval.
I categorically reject the thesis that I would legitimize democracy or the state with my vote.
Although it is not clear to me who you should vote for, I dare to say that the most dangerous is the vote for Babiš; in my opinion, the choice of the People's Party or KSČSSD is slightly better (although still terrible); I consider voting for SPD or Úsvit, Zelené, TOPka or STAN rather stupid (but again slightly better); I don't consider the choice of the other parties to be so bad, because they are too small to cause real damage or a "lesser evil" (compared to the rest). I would just like to add to the Pirates that they are far from being as "anti-system" as they present themselves (on the other hand, still better than all the parties above); there are many socialists among them.
If you want to vote "against the Socans or Babiš" - or "so that the vote doesn't go to waste" - and you want to avoid voting for a small party, I would probably (with reservations) recommend the ODS, because it can perhaps be described as the least evil of the "big ones"; although in the past it has sharply shied away from the fight against a very large state (despite promises), thereby tripping up its voters, lately it is perhaps trying to make amends (I judge from watching their votes and speeches), but it will still take some time before they gain at least a shred of my trust. However, I consider the argument of the "loss" of the vote to be wrong, because the vote will almost certainly "lose" anyway ("it won't be lost" only if the election turned out at least a little differently without it, which is almost impossible). On the contrary, one strong argument for electing smaller parties is being forgotten: In addition to the fact that they can get money for votes, it is primarily a motivation for their members, for whom the difference between one and three percent can mean the difference between devoting their time to that party and to something else.
That is also why I will - with great self-denial - vote for Svobodné. I have a huge number of reservations about that side; unfortunately, there is no party I have less reservations about. I don't want to go into detail here about everything that bothers me about Svobodny, but considering how many libertarians there are among the readers, I would like to mention one thing: Two (unofficial) factions are fighting in Svobodny - libertarians and right-wing conservatives; and since the former are rather idealists (although many of them do the politics in practice), while the latter are "real politicians" (take that as a strong euphemism), unfortunately it is precisely the libertarians who leave the party more often simply because they have no stomach for some of the things that take place there (not that such things do not happen in every political party). What can a voter do about it? I can only think of one thing: circling. I'll throw it to the Liberals (although I don't seriously consider them "my representatives", but that's how it goes in a democracy) and I'll try to support the libertarians with preferential votes.
Some want to do the same, but they don't know the Liberal candidates, so they asked me for advice; I don't know who you should circle, but here is a list of those whom I would circle, because I consider them to be decent people or libertarians (the list is subjective and incomplete; I do not know all Svobodné): Tomáš Pajonk (not the first by chance), Jana Urzová, Zuzana Haberlová, Terézia Mlýnková Išková, Igor Bogdanov, Jakub Cyrani, Josef Káles, Jaroslav Suchánek, Pavel Mises (yes, he changed his name xD), Alois Sečkár, Jiří Kubíček, Ondřej Martínek, Michael Kopecký, David Král, Jiří Pánek, Martin Rumler, Petr Pořízek, Jan Šebelík, David Forbelský, Jan Matějka, Jiří Zapletal, Zenon Kuder, Jindřich Pilc, Miloš Bém, David Pokorný, Oldřich Peprla, Roman Bartolšic, Jan Mikula, Radim Smetka, Vítěslav Stanovský, Jaroslav Marsa. I would not choose from the Olomouc and Pilsen regions; I don't know much about the candidates from Olomouc, but unfortunately I do about the ones from Pilsen. Do with it as you wish. The choice is yours. I'm not too sure, maybe I'm wrong, so take me with a grain of salt.

Intellectuals like to gripe about how awful it is who people vote for; their votes can be bought for a doughnut, a sausage, a beer, a nice smile from a billboard... are voters that stupid? No, quite the opposite; they are smart and know what is best for them. What are the costs of making the "right" (informed) choice? Hundreds of hours of researching party programs, the credibility of politicians, the basics of economics, predicting the effects of this or that law; assuming you don't have this as a hobby, this is an extreme expense. And what is the profit from the "correct" (conscious) choice? Well, none; unless the "right" candidate loses by one vote (which has probably never happened anywhere), the outcome of the election is exactly the same for each individual regardless of how they voted. So if you don't care about politics, "sloppy" or no choice is a perfectly rational solution, not a mistake. And where is the mistake?
In democracy itself
; it just doesn't work for real people.

In the pre-election program, the bright socialists Greens expressed themselves clearly about the taxing of robots, the less clear socialists Pirates less clearly.
Anyone who thought this might be a good idea should read Bastiat's Petition of the Candle Makers (it is freely available on the Internet).
You know what's interesting? That work—over a hundred and fifty years old—explains why taxing robots is nonsense without mentioning robots at all.
And you know what's sad? That Bastiat is not cool enough for today's socialists to even bother to read his arguments.

Urza: You think Bitcoin will rise to a million dollars? If so, I'll sell one when it's at a hundred thousand; I will buy Tereza pilot training ATPL(A) and myself an Alfa 4C!
Martin Šíp: No, Urza. When Bitcoin is worth a hundred thousand dollars, you won't have to sell it.
At first I didn't even understand what he meant; this is a paraphrase (and Google says it's not the first) of this famous dialogue:
Neo: What are you trying to tell me? That I can dodge bullets?
Morpheus: Well, Neo. I'm trying to tell you that when you're ready, you won't have it.
Many of us use Bitcoin; and some even believe it will become a regular widely accepted currency (at $100k, BTC would be about one percent of the world's money supply, so it would probably actually be accepted everywhere). I like the optimism, although I fear that the moment Bitcoin becomes mainstream, states will start a campaign on the topic "BTC = child porn" (or something like that); the grand finale could then be a nationwide (perhaps even international) ban... something like "
the war on drugs
”, which would actually put him in the underworld (and the stores would also have to stop accepting him). What do you think about it?
And speaking of cryptocurrencies, I can't help but mention that one of the world's biggest congresses on this topic is starting today; takes place in Parallel Polis, where interesting speakers from all corners of our planet will gather. The tickets have long been sold out (although they weren't the cheapest, the whole event has a budget in the order of millions and it's not really state money), but it's held every year, so you can visit next time; in addition, I will have the great honor to give a lecture at this event, so I will at least provide a recording.

The last regular lecture from the Anarcho-Capitalism cycle was held in May and its topic was the popular statist question: "
Who would build roads without the state?
" When I have you on her
he called, I mentioned
that I will be silent for a long time, but most likely in the meantime some kind of ankap meetup will take place anyway. So indeed it happened in June; and now again - a fortnight before the first post-holiday regular lecture (it will be on an interesting topic - Social System).
Today's lecture is called "Aliens", so most people don't know what to imagine by that; well, I'm not surprised at all, so I'll tell you that at the lecture we'll talk a lot about argumentation, logic, but we'll also touch on emotions, and everything will be interspersed with the most bizarre arguments I've come across so far. Of course, we will also look at serious counter-arguments and frequent logical errors. And why is the lecture so strangely named? Come and find out! Yes, it's kind of comebait (derived from clickbait), but I think you won't regret it.
The next lecture (this time a regular continuation of the Anarchocapitalism cycle) will be in two weeks, on October 18 at 8 p.m.; its topic will be the social and pension system. In addition, I will post something interesting at the beginning of it, so be sure to come xD
I'm looking forward to seeing you tonight at 8 p.m
Parallel Polis
.

During the summer she was in
cycle "Anarchocapitalism" in Polis
pause; it technically ends on October 18th with a regular lecture on the topic "Social System", however, already on October 4th (so exactly in a week) we will start lightly with a lecture called "Aliens" xD
What do they have to do with ankap? Well, nothing much... However, I think the lecture will be interesting and the discussion even more interesting. So in a week at 8 p.m
Parallel Polis
!

title_en: Urza versus Bob Kartous in Polis
text_en:
As I already announced a fortnight ago, today at 18:30 in Polis the Freedom of Learning discussion is being held, to which I invited Bob Kartous based on the statement he made to DVTV: "It is necessary to be able to educate for citizenship and democracy against the background of what normally takes place in schools." Not that it hasn't happened a long time ago, and not that I haven't repeatedly criticized it; however, according to Bob Kartous, it's not enough and we should get even tougher, because according to some survey, only 58% of high school students think that democracy is the best form of government (which would be nice, but let's not rejoice, because he did the research... but I'll say more about that in the debate). I shall be glad if you appear in person; and even better if you contribute something to the discussion. And if not, I'll probably publish a video here in time.
I look forward to seeing you today at half past seven in the evening
Parallel Polis
.

title_en: Bad father? Three years in the cold!
text_en:
Some idiot encouraged his young daughter to hit a pillow with a baseball bat and imagine she was beating up gypsies or Muslims; the person in question is obviously a douchebag, so he filmed everything and published it on the Internet. And you know what? He is accused of inciting hatred and endangering the upbringing of a child, for which he can serve up to three years. I do not deny that the father is a dull brute for many reasons; but he didn't abuse his daughter, he just passed on his (albeit perverted) values to her. If we accept that the state should forcefully dictate to people how to raise children, we are heading straight for hell. And whoever thinks that he is not in danger because he is not such a limiter, I remind him of Martin Niemöller: "When the Nazis came for the communists, I was silent; I was not a communist. When they closed the social democrats, I was silent; I was not a social democrat. When they came for the trade unionists, I was silent; I was not a trade unionist. When they came for me, there was no one left to speak."
The point is certainly not that we should perhaps approve or even accept such a style of education as our own (I personally find it disgusting); but if the state will be the one who decides what is acceptable and what is not in education, it is not such a problem to change it so that next time something could be objectionable that we would not even imagine today and consider it completely absurd (parents of fat, aggressive, religious or vegan children can become persecuted, add anything). And the way to prevent this can hardly lie in trying to enforce across the board such prohibitions and regulations as suit us (because similar totalitarian practices always get out of control in the end), but in
absolute refusal to let a policeman, official or politician decide
about things for which children and their parents are ultimately responsible anyway.

It could certainly be worse (see DPRK); on the other hand, the state determines how we should educate our children, what we should lead them to, what values we must not pass on to them and which must be passed on to them through the education system; what goods we are allowed to sell, buy and under what conditions, what services we can provide and to whom, that we must register our potential company, report its earnings and pay taxes from them in the currency determined by the state, which they also force us to accept; it dictates who we may hire and whom we may not refuse, under what conditions people can work for us and for what reasons we can fire them; what we must not say publicly, what art and culture we must contribute to; how we are to pay for medical care, who may and may not treat us and what drugs they may use, and if that fails, who may not help us die; it also decides what substances we can inject into our bodies, from what age we can have sex and from what age we can watch it on the Internet; the official checks what we fuel with, what we drive; what means of transport we may own, under what conditions we may drive them and whom we transport; which weapons we may own and carry; the state determines how and where we can build our own house; what data we may send to the Internet; which pets we can keep... and that's it
very incomplete list
.

Today is exactly two years to the day
opening Stok
; and I'm glad that you come back here (mostly, perhaps even gladly). The number of visitors is still increasing, although not nearly as fast as at the beginning, as might have been expected; while in the beginning the point was to attract as many libertarians as possible, now it's mainly about creating new ones, which is a slow but ongoing process. In addition to large hundreds to small thousands of unique visitors per day, the SEWERS OF THE FREE HARBOR also received
FREEPORT CHANNEL
, where Teresa and I try to reach people through videos; we will be happy if you start subscribing to the Channel. However, what makes me most happy is how many new authors come to Stok; as of today, we already have thirty-three of them here. I thank each of them from the bottom of my heart; and thank you to everyone else who participates in the running of Stok, even by comments, and to all readers. Please bear with us; and if you can think of something on the topic (especially a positive one, but it doesn't have to be), don't hesitate and start writing too!

The EU banned roaming and the Eurocrats pretended that we should all kiss their ass for it, because they are saving us (with our money) from bad operators; and at first glance it may seem so serious to someone, but as I say: "You can't outsmart the market." In Norway (it is not in the EU, but the regulation also affected it) the prices of mobile services have risen by more than half, in Denmark by an average of 60 euros per customer per year, and the British are not much different (depending on the operator); Slovak operator Orange, on the other hand, charges for "overuse" of services abroad. I was in Belgium in July, where I didn't pay for roaming, but I didn't get data (which could be solved with the operator, but always only for a few hours; then he turned me off again). So rather than helping anyone, the whole event was EU PR; and I wonder how much better or cheaper services the operators could provide us if the money that the regulation cost went directly to them.

Nocebo is the opposite of placebo; while the placebo effect consists of healing based on the patient's belief that he is being treated (when in fact he is not), the nocebo effect worsens his condition based on perhaps expecting negative side effects of the drug (which he is not actually receiving). Disgusting pictures and warnings about all the horrible ways cigarettes can harm our health are now required by law to appear on every cigarette pack; why shouldn't the nocebo effect show up here? Every time a smoker takes his cigarette from a pack colorfully depicting the potential negative health consequences of his action, he is convinced that he will get sick; and if he believes it, his mind can seriously cause the disease. So not only the state
inexcusably violates proprietary rights
cigarette manufacturers when it regulates the appearance of their boxes, but even more so it harms the smokers it declaratively protects.

The school year begins; the state forcibly forces parents to send their children to school where they will be
indoctrinated by propaganda
, which of them
will create obedient citizens
. Who would defy something like that and insist on it, the children will be forcibly abducted (!) by a social worker (with the possible support of uniformed monkeys, if necessary); a euphemism for this behavior - completely unacceptable to most of us if the state did not do so (which clearly shows the power of
that propaganda
) – school attendance is compulsory.
Let's get rid of her!
And there is another thing which is our children
indoctrinated similarly to the state; this is democracy
– the idol that, if you refuse to worship, you will become the object of ridicule of the believers of the most widespread religion, that is, statism. However, there are still those who consider that propaganda to be insufficient and would like to toughen it up; I will face one of them – Bohumil Kartous – on September 18 in a debate in
Parallel Polis
. I hope to meet you there; and I wish the students the best of luck for the next school year - don't get too shaped.

The holidays are over, so Stoky resumes its standard operation.
Many thanks to all the libertarians who listened
my challenges
and delivered their texts over the holidays; please keep it up.

When I talk about the immorality of the state, I sometimes compare it to the mafia; although there are a lot of technical differences between those organizations, but from the point of view of ethics, they operate on the same principle: In some territory, they threaten people with violence to pay them. The victim then either has to move elsewhere, conceal income (with the risk of retaliation), pay, or be liquidated. The mob is typically weaker, so it unleashes terror, has less patience, and soon turns to violence; states tend to be stronger, ergo they can afford not to be so brutal, they proceed more slowly and do not intimidate so explicitly... at least that's what I'm saying; unfortunately, this is not always true.
I am posting a link to the article here
, which shows how it can also look like. This brings us to another difference: the Mafia does not have such good PR because it does not control the entire education system, so it cannot convince its victims that it is not actually evil; the state is very good at this - its victims feel that a mistake has been made, they find it "strange" (that's how a man whose life was destroyed by the tax office put it), but they don't reject the state as a whole.

Recently, the media has been informing us that the price of butter has risen; I didn't notice it myself, because I don't look at price tags when buying food, but judging by the comments, it caught the attention of many people. The chairman of the Agricultural Union of the Czech Republic, Martin Pýcha, said that people should get used to paying fifty crowns for a quarter of a kilogram of butter, because it is a normal price; however, many traders react by buying cheaper butter from other countries (which, by the way, shows how harmful high tariffs and protectionism in general could be). The real problem, however, is not slightly more expensive butter, but absurdly high subsidies and a huge degree of socialism in agriculture. No one has any idea how much butter is supposed to cost. Mr. Pýcha claims that fifty crowns is a "normal price", but he cannot know that, because the "normal price" is determined by supply and demand, which in our case, unfortunately, are massively distorted by taxes and subsidies. It's sad that nowadays
there is no way
, how to find the market price of butter; and almost everything else.

In the EU, they found out that French fries are unhealthy (wow, who would have thought) because they contain a lot of acrylamide (OK, I didn't know that), so no one should eat or sell them (and we are at home, social engineering is the main method and product of the EU). The representatives of the twenty-eight member countries of the European Union agreed that measures need to be taken to force people to submit to their next invention; this time in the name of reducing the risk of cancer: "Today we have taken an important step in protecting the health and well-being of citizens," said European Commissioner for Health and Food Safety Vytenis Andriukaitis. When smoking was banned, I argued that it would be possible to ban junk food with exactly the same arguments; what was described by my opponents as an absurd and impermissible sloping surface is now becoming a reality. How much freedom and responsibility will they take away from us? How much self-righteous idiots do they want us to be?

title_en: Discussion in Polis: LGBT Pride Week
text_en:
Today at 4 pm I will participate in a panel discussion in Paralelní Polis; the topic is quite controversial and the guest list even more so. We will debate about the march and the pride week of the LGBT community.
The aim was to invite people with a wide range of opinions to the same table - the nationalist and extreme opponent of LGBT Pavel Matějný was invited as the organizer of the protest march, the objectivist Luboš Zálom, the anarcho-capitalist Urza and the transsexual LGBT activist Marie Feryna from the radical left (Marxist), who accepted the invitation, but then withdrew her participation saying that she refused to sit at the table with Mr. Matějný, which caught many attentions other leftists (even the leftist media) who exacerbated the situation and tried to cancel the invitation to Mr. Matějný or the entire discussion through threats and intimidation, which of course they did not succeed (for the sake of fairness, I add that these threats were made by individual leftist radicals who apparently acted for themselves, not on behalf of any organization); instead of Maria Feryna, David Mařák, the president of the LGBT association Charlie, accepted the invitation despite great pressure.
The interest in the discussion is apparently considerable, the media and probably also a number of activists are expected to arrive; as some have expressed fear for their safety, professional security will oversee the smooth running of the event. The fact that the reactions to the entire event are more controversial than expected is also evidenced by the fact that I am writing here "pride week" and "pride march", but not its name, because the lawyer of that organization has already threatened me with a lawsuit for trademark infringement (and the absurdity is that the consultation with another lawyer shows that his threats may not be completely empty; what does this say about the legal system of the Czech Republic, you can guess for yourself).
I will look forward to seeing you;
come out

Everyone certainly has a lot of stories with the Czech Post (me too), so I won't go into detail about them here; however, what has fascinated me for years is the search in their information system (such a program from the days of MS-DOS), which has the remarkable property that it lacks the absolutely basic function that one would expect from such a tool - namely, to enter a name into it and find all shipments for the person in question. Instead, the recipient has to know whether they are looking for a letter, parcel, cash on delivery, registered letter, letter from abroad and the like - I don't know exactly how many of those categories there are - and the postal workers search in each one separately; is it really such a problem to write a function that finds any shipment with a given name? It certainly isn't, but why bother if the customer is going to wait; bearing in mind that the entire juggernaut is paid for by the taxpayer who
he has no choice
, the quality of service doesn't matter at all, so why bother...

A guy from Opava went to walk the dogs by car; he left the window open in the car to let it air out in the meantime. And what the hell, monkeys in uniforms were walking around; so the real, unadulterated police buzz began. The person in question coughed on them and drove off; A spokeswoman for the Flies commented: "He claimed it was his business, he had done nothing wrong and was not going to deal with anything. He then got behind the wheel and rudely drove away from the scene. If he hadn't done that, the incident almost certainly would have been resolved with a reprimand." That's how they steamed his band-aid. And for what? He was not conformist enough; if he licked the Bengs' shoes and kissed their ass, he wouldn't have to pay, which they openly admit. In other words, "Subject, we'll boo you, but show us the respect we don't deserve, or we'll force you to pay." And why all this? Well, because the law states: "A driver who intends to move away from the vehicle [..] must take such measures that the vehicle [..] cannot be used [..] by another person without authorization."
Boaters were buzzed by 279 uniformed monkeys all over the Czech Republic; checked 606 boats, 93 docks and gave 520 boaters a breather (boaters' buzzer we are here
repeatedly
solved
already last year; inclusive
breath tests
). What is it good for? The worn-out excuse like with cars doesn't really work here: "After all, the driver endangers not only himself, but also those around him!" But besides its crew, who does such a canoe really threaten? Sure, very hypothetically another canoe, however, if its crew is also not under the picture and if they use their brains, they will wash out as much as possible, which simply happens from time to time on the water and everyone expects it. But this is not about any security, protection or help, just like with the open windows in the car, it is only about keeping subjects under pressure, rebuking the egos of needy existences in the service of the police, reporting their activities and robbing some of that money into the insatiable maw of the state. Or does anyone have the feeling that the police are doing this for us?

Despite German libertarians, I know conspirators who believe that Germany is not really a state but a large corporation; as it happens, the clues to that belief are basically stupid, for example that German citizens are called Personalausweis, not Personenausweis (the former means something like an employee card, the latter should logically be a citizen, although it is not). What interested me about it? Proponents of the conspiracy theory and their opponents (although they disagree on whether Germany is a company or not) agree that it would be terrible if it were true. They live in a country controlled by some entity that somehow works; as long as the entity is called a state, everything is fine, but once it turns out to be a company, it would be a disaster, even if nothing changes in its functioning at all! Can you imagine a better example
state propaganda
? If an entity does something unacceptable, it is enough for people to perceive it as a state and everything is fine.

Two deeply depressed teenagers in Massachusetts shared their misery for several years; as is often the case with depressed people, they alternately gave themselves strength, alternately wanted to die, both were unstable and down. He then decided to kill himself with exhaust fumes, however he hesitated and called her; she just saw the world black (although they had previously tried to find a solution to their depression) so she told him to kill himself. He did it; she let him die, she didn't call for help. In terms of
principle of non-aggression
she did nothing wrong; freedom of speech includes this. From the human point of view I dare not judge; maybe at that moment she seriously believed it was the best solution (but I don't know). And from the point of view of the Massachusetts court? Twenty years in prison! Leaving aside the principle of non-aggression, I have two questions: How is the world supposed to be better after her imprisonment at the expense of the taxpayers? On the basis of this precedent, will someone be convicted, for example, for a depressing text on the Internet, if it inspires a suicide?

In Seattle, the minimum wage was raised to fifteen dollars an hour; unsurprisingly, it had exactly the negative effects that Austrian economists have been talking about for decades. Now, however, a study has been created for this, the results of which are "shocking", because they refute the results of some earlier studies that are supposed to "prove" the opposite. The creators of the study present the conclusions (long known to Austrians) that the minimum wage harms the least qualified workers (they start losing their jobs when they do not earn for themselves); for example, according to economist David Autor from MIT, a study can influence research in a given area and completely change the perspective on a given issue. On the one hand, it would be good to change it; on the other hand... why is that study needed? We still have valid laws of praxeology, ceteris paribus; so studies can show anything depending on other influences that cannot be eliminated or measured, ergo they neither disprove nor prove anything.

I will not be lecturing during the summer, however, as part of the "Anarcho-Capitalism" program in Polis, we are organizing a meeting of friends; but it also applies to people who are not exactly friends of this idea and just simply want to discuss the given topic. So there will be no lecture today, but we can all sit and chat; a small snack will also be prepared. I will be very happy if you give me ideas and topics for further lectures.
I look forward to seeing you tonight at 7:30 p.m
Parallel Polis
.

The holidays are starting, which affects a good part of us in some way, whether it is school children, their parents, university students, teachers, visitors to various festivals and the like; website traffic with articles (even such non-articles) and comments is down, but my schedule will also be affected by the holidays. For that reason, I'm switching Stoky into vacation mode for two months, which means:
1/ Texts will not be published here with such regularity as before; there will be an effort, but I don't know how successful it will be (expect outages).
2/ I am asking libertarians who have more time for texts to Stok; send it to me by email (or publish it yourself; ideally hit the days when nothing comes out xD).
And above all, enjoy the summer!

title_en: Up to five years behind bars for six cannabis seedlings
Anarchy in practice: the city of Gurgaon
text_en:
Gurgaon is an Indian municipal city, but in which only less than five percent of its area is subject to municipal authority; the remaining ninety-five percent are held by private individuals, and they provide all the services in question
we have been teaching since school years
, that the market cannot provide them – economist Shruti Rajagopalan wrote of the city: "It shouldn't exist, in theory." But there is; and it is successful - its population is growing by hundreds of thousands of inhabitants per year (it has already exceeded two and a half million people). Sure, it's in India, so it's no paradise on earth, but people definitely do better there than in other cities, as evidenced by the extreme migration to Gurgaon; if people have a choice, they choose the free market over the state. It probably won't surprise anyone that the biggest horror in the city takes place in the non-privatized part where public services and "social security" are provided; the market can simply do better. Want to know more? Martin Pánek translated
interesting article on the topic
.

In Pardubice, a transport hub will be built in front of the station, for which a large subsidy (108 mega) can be obtained; however, its condition is that noise limits must not be exceeded in any of the surrounding houses. This might make sense at first glance, but not in the case of houses that have to be demolished as part of the construction of that transport hub; however, the grant writer did not think of that, so... Pardubice must first soundproof the house, for which there is already a demolition plan, for almost two megabytes - and then demolish it. One would like to say that poorly worded eligibility conditions are to blame, but this is only partially true – poorly worded conditions cause less obvious inefficiencies to surface so that everyone can see and laugh at them (as many do); without it, the subsidy will also not be effective,
which is its inherent property
, but it stops being so obvious.
A centrally controlled economy is doomed to failure…

Socan Stanislav Křeček on Airbnb: "The situation is no longer tolerable. Cities must take measures to regulate. They must realize that short-term renting is not a normal way of using an apartment..."
Anarcho-capitalist Urza: "The state is not tolerable! You must realize, Mr. Křeček, that the owner of the apartment should decide on the use of the apartment, not the parasitizing members of parliament who live off the stolen taxes."
Křeček: "...and it harms the state's housing policy."
Urza: "Then the state's housing policy is bad!
The state is immoral
; but if you want to at least pretend to be there for the people, you can't at the same time claim that his policies are against their wishes.''
Křeček: "Apartments must serve people, not business."
Urza: "And who runs this business? Martians? Is this targeted manipulation, or do you really see it that way? Or are you just using the word people as a synonym for your interests?"
Křeček: "They also violate tax laws, the vast majority of entrepreneurs do not report income. Such activities should be monitored."
Urza: "So we're home! No people vs. business and such chatter; it's just that someone has a profit from which they don't pay protection money to the state for your salary, Mr. Křeček, so all hell breaks loose."

If we step on shit, we wipe it off and move on; not so socan Štěch, who stepped properly, but instead of wiping, he decided to get a little dirty in it. Instead of
after his statement about the use of self-employed people and their contribution to GDP creation
he kept his mouth shut, he decided to "improve" it by asking us to snap at the neighbors: "For example, in Denmark, if someone is unemployed and doing his own thing, the neighbor will just say so, because he is also being robbed of his money, which he puts into the system." Dude, seriously? For one thing... what kind of alien-grazing monster is this, why is he the president of the senate, why do I have to feed this parasite... but above all, what is the logic behind this "robbing"?
The state takes someone's money by force
and he claims that a neighbor did it, which is why he is being robbed, because the neighbor's state did not succeed in turning over so much. That it is the logic of a leech fed by forcefully collected money makes sense; however, the sad thing is how many
manipulated by propaganda
it eats citizens.

Wikipedia is not run by any government, it is funded by volunteers; anyone can write there, they don't need a license, they don't need to prove expertise, or they don't need anyone's permission. No one has a right to it, it is not guaranteed by any law; it is not copyrighted and has no regulatory authority. When it started, everyone "knew" it was going to be shit and everyone would just be trolling or writing nonsense. Yes, sure, sometimes someone really trolls and some nonsense can be found there, but it is still an amazing project with a huge benefit for clouds of people. This is how anarchy works in practice; even though everyone "knows" that "it can never work". And how much does it all cost? About sixty million dollars, i.e. a billion and a half crowns a year; by the way, this is several times less than the budget of Czech Television. How is that possible? Well,
CT does not have to - and cannot - be effective
, when it does not earn for itself and people are forced to pay it - no stranger's blood flows; unlike Wikipedia, which has to support itself somehow.

"The Airbnb application in Prague 1 has completely changed the conditions on the housing market. The phenomenon of shared accommodation, if not regulated, is very dangerous for every city," declared Prague 1 councilor Ivan Solil from the ČSSD; mayor Oldřich Lomecký from TOP09 (she takes notes with the ČSSD) confirms this: "We cannot allow the Prague 1 district to lose its function of housing, that is why we are calling for rules." Why can't you let it happen, you cocky paps? Do you know how people are supposed to live in Prague 1?
