Where do you get the smug belief that you know better than the owners of those apartments what is good for Prague? Even if everyone from Prague 1 decided to rent their apartments, what's the point? Nothing at all!
You are nothing but parasites
; you should be glad we feed you. Lomecký continues: "Tens, hundreds of apartments are flooded by someone we don't even know who he is." Well, what does anyone (except the owners) care? If you don't make a living as decent people, at least don't play savior.

Socan Milan Štěch has devised a way to drive tens of thousands of employees to companies: He wants to increase levies for self-employed people so that they can be employed; he says that no one knows what their contribution to GDP creation is (no bullshit; he actually said that), and they are not used effectively (which, according to him, no one knows). What would I say about that... I have no words. First of all, there is an audacity calling to heaven when a parasite, who has been straying in the senate for over twenty years, preaches about work
stolen money
, before the revolution he was in the Communist Party for ten years and in the meantime made a career as a professional trade unionist; how does this brute dare to evaluate the workers who feed him? Secondly, it is a typical populist social-democratic attempt to spit on the self-employed and compare them negatively with employees, but this time extremely demented; because few things will harm employees as much as tens of thousands of self-employed people who will become employees and compete with them in the labor market. Tykravol, may it happen to his constituents!

Tax Freedom Day is a date that divides the calendar year into two parts: From the beginning of the year until that day, people work for the state; only from that day until the end of the year can they work on themselves. For example, if we
the state took
half of what we earn, tax freedom day would be in the middle of the year. Since each person pays taxes a little differently, the result depends on the methodology used; for example, according to the company Deloitte, the day of tax freedom will be tomorrow, while such a Liberal Institute set it for May 29 this year. I'm trying
count everything
, what the state costs us, so my tax freedom day does not come until August; to different people on different days according to how much they pay in excise and the like. Whether that date falls in May, June, July, or August, the thought is appalling; let's realize how many months since the beginning of the year we've been working on a parasitizing state... and who happens to shorten it, the politicians (and, unfortunately, many citizens) will brazenly call him a thief.

Want to help me promote libertarian ideas? You can buy promotional items at
obchod.urza.cz
.
Answers to the FAQ: This is a module of an existing e-shop with which I agreed (I don't want to go through the bureaucracy myself), they handle orders, complaints, production and set prices; I make suggestions. We can arrange for me to design something especially for you; if you have ideas, write, I'll be happy to add them there.

The state is forcing its non-market money on us, causing an economic crisis
; the question is not if it will come again, but when the next crisis will occur. And as an anarcho-capitalist and holder of several cryptocurrencies, I can't help but ask: When the crisis comes again, what will it do to the Bitcoin (and other) exchange rate? I can imagine two fundamental opposing influences: Pure speculators will start (panicked) selling because their reason for buying was a quick profit; on the contrary, those who hold cryptocurrencies out of distrust of the state or
opposition to fiat money
, in my opinion will buy. But which ones are there more? Quite obviously, people buy cryptocurrencies for both reasons; and I doubt that anyone can know how essential either is. But I think that the economic crisis will test this. What do you think, dear readers? In which direction will the courses go in the crisis? And are my reflections on the reasons for the rise or fall of the price at all meaningful? I welcome any reasoned opinions; Thank you.

There is a bridge for squirrels in Sokolov; yes, you read that right, it's just a bridge over the road, they built it there in 2012 and it cost four mega (seriously, I'm not kidding). I can't imagine who would defend this, or even agree with it, but if any die-hard environmentalists are reading here, know that five (yes, seriously five) rodents have used the bridge during its entire existence (there are cameras installed, so it's an accurate count); that makes about eight hundred thousand crowns for one pass – great, isn't it? For that money, I would easily carry those squirrels across that road by myself; after all... who doesn't? However, the zone of absurdity still does not end, because the bombers are sitting at the Sokolov town hall until the end; when confronted with the status of the project, City Hall's response was (now hold on): "We believe this animal protection project makes sense." What to add? Well, another one of those things that would be funny if they weren't crying.

title_en: With a naked man behind bars!
text_en: A certain guy from Vizovice likes to work in his (!) garden naked; he doesn't do anything to anyone, he doesn't interfere with other people's property, he is even willing to get dressed at the request of his neighbor (that is, not forever, but if she asks him, he will get dressed for the given day as part of good neighborly relations). Nevertheless, the person in question told the television that she was afraid to invite visitors, so that they would not be disgusted by it; her worries on my head! There's a hill of fun; however, the person in question succumbed to the social climate of today's state and betrayed her neighbor to the fools... And this is where the ass ends. The uniformed monkeys informed the man that he was suspected of the crime of disorderly conduct, for which he could go to jail for up to two years. Why? Because he mowed his (!) garden naked; and because the neighborhood crack is starting. And above all, let no one defend it with the nonsense that his freedom ends where that lady's freedom begins; that border is quite clearly defined by the fence between their plots - and it was not crossed.

title_en: You have the word: social housing
text_en:
A few weeks ago, the topic of the program You Have the Word was the Social Housing Act; I only got to watch the episode now, but I was really interested. The guest of the show was, unsurprisingly, my favorite Marksová,
of
which
again
she was falling
hers
traditional
socialist
wise
; surprisingly, however, there were those who sovereignly trumped her: "I don't want housing benefits, I don't want to burden the state, and I also have my pride; give me a social apartment by law!" I couldn't believe my ears at first listen and replayed the video to make sure it was for real... and indeed. Well, apart from that it's everywhere... but there were two other people who said the same thing during the hour; Of course, Marks did not disappoint - she repeated several times that it was a matter of pride and that she understood them. What kind of propaganda did the state use to convince these people that social housing is falling from the sky? What is their pride? Totally burying your head in the sand? How do housing benefits differ from social housing?
I've always thought that renaming payroll taxes or social and health taxes to insurance won't have much of a real impact; but when I hear this and see people whose "pride won't allow" them to take housing benefit, but call for social housing, I reconsider my opinion - what those things are called has a noticeable impact in the real world. When there are people who don't get housing benefits, but do get social housing, they do it out of conviction and say that they "don't want to burden the state" (so they probably really don't know that someone has to pay for the social housing), it is probably important to solve (in my opinion, absurd) questions such as whether civil servants pay taxes; and even now I attach even greater importance to stressing that taxes are renamed protection money, that laws are enforced by the state by force, that every regulation inherently contains aggression and the like. Let's fight newspeak; let's not give it to the state for free!

Uber, Airbnb, Zonky, Doginni and many other platforms that compete with "official" entrepreneurs often move on the edge of the gray economy (or beyond); nevertheless (or rather precisely because of this) they are successful, they are winning in the market competition to the full, and the states do not know what exactly to do with them. Sometimes they prohibit them, sometimes they regulate them, but sometimes there are also judges who agree with them and support them; The "official" competition in the given fields typically hates them because they often have trouble standing up to them, which in itself says something about what customers want and don't want. Today from 16:00 I will discuss this topic in a panel discussion in Polis; among the other discussants will be, for example, the chairman of the Association of Taxi Concessionaires, Daniel Tarljovski, whom I am very much looking forward to. Come and have a look and, above all, join the discussion. I look forward to seeing you in
Parallel Polis
.

title_en: We don't work for the state!
text_en:
"Ethical hacker" crypto-anarchist Palo launches Slovak and Czech versions of the initiative
We don't work for the state
(respectively
We do not work for the state
); companies (or individuals who sell something) can apply for it, as long as they do not work for the state, do not receive subsidies and, ideally, compete with the state, or accept cryptocurrencies. Those who register determine the amount of discounts they want to provide to other registered members (three types of discounts are possible: for not receiving subsidies, for competing with the state and for accepting cryptocurrencies), then they can draw discounts from other members themselves. The minimum condition is therefore at least not to work for the state and not to receive subsidies; sign up, spread both sites and ideas of independence from the state - it makes sense! The discounts mentioned above are more of a by-product; the point is to create a platform of people who actively reject the state, compete with it, spread cryptocurrencies and cooperate on an economic basis.

title_en: Another flash of the power of propaganda
text_en: More and more often, dear readers and listeners, you write me emails discussing libertarian topics; thank you for them, they are mostly useful dialogues. Recently, in response to the lectures, an astute listener, a supporter of the so-called Zen State, wrote to me; I don't want to deal with that concept here (you can google it), I'm not a fan of it. As part of that – very interesting – discussion, the person in question declared that she identifies with the ideas of anarcho-capitalism, but does not want to call herself an anarchist, because anarchy has violent periods behind it (sic!); this very thoughtful lady (this is not irony) espouses the Zen state, but feels an aversion to anarchy for its violent history. But what about the bloody nature of states (based on violence) that killed three hundred million people in wars in the last century? Given how our debate has progressed so far, I expect the person in question will reconsider; however, that ingrained subconscious resistance to anarchy is everywhere...

Today is World No Tobacco Day; and enters into force
a totalitarian law restricting the freedom of pub owners
to decide whether smoking is allowed in their establishments or not. Most of the arguments by which this amendment was defended consisted in the fact that if we already have totalitarianism anyway, we can easily tighten it up a bit more (the pub owners are already restricted by a lot of regulations; because of the socialist healthcare system, we all bear the costs of treating smokers; the state is supposed to take care of the health of the population; "state, set up a non-smoking pub in the village" and many others); and in a similar totalitarian spirit, some town halls intend to solve the problems caused by the ban (people will go to smoke in front of pubs): For example, Prague 1 has hired anti-smoking patrol officers to go around and boo smokers (how noisy they are, where they throw their cigarettes, etc.); if you meet them, please let them eat it (without violence) so that they think carefully about what they actually do for a living.

title_en: When the EU kills freedom of speech...
text_en:
Ministers of EU member states approved a plan to force Google, Facebook and Twitter to
tougher censorship
; and they should censor the advocacy of terrorism as well as hate speech. Leaving aside the ethical side of the matter, i.e. that each of the above-mentioned companies should decide for themselves what content they want to show their users, this does not solve anything in practice; just because we forbid people to talk about a problem, it will not disappear by itself, but on the contrary, the ballast of the "underground" will be added to it, and the spreaders of similar opinions will consider themselves martyrs (and their listeners too). And while the ministers were at it, they immediately approved yet another buzz for video streaming services (such as Netflix): European films and TV shows must make up thirty percent of their content; you can't even comment decently on this anymore, because the people in question probably already screwed up in the cinema. The feeble-mindedness of this regulation is more than evident.

Minister Ťok wants to play with trains (and the government approved it in the plan for the next decade); it will cost 650 billion (please note the order of the number; it is not just "a lot", it is more than half of the state budget) and we will pay for it. Of course, there will be a trade-off for this – very fast trains will run here; the problem is that it is not at all clear who actually wants it and how much, which is characteristic of state decision-making, which is inherently burdened
impossibility of economic calculation
. What does this mean? That if we let an official, a minister or some Ťok decide whether to build trains or something else, he has no chance to do it well (even if he wanted to); because it cannot determine the subjective preferences of all taxpayers. The only way to not get it wrong is to let people decide about their money; if the track will be financed only by those who want it, it can only be created if it was really worth the cost to the people.

You won't believe it! The thief called the post office, introduced himself as a police officer, and said he was going there to disinfect the money after the chemical attack, so the manager should close the post office and let him in through the back door; this clever lady actually did, she brought him all the bills, the man (wearing a chemical suit - so the cameras wouldn't catch him) sprayed them with a sprayer and asked the postmaster to go flush the metal money down the sink, which she did, leaving him there with the money and... no surprise, she didn't find him there. A few questions come to mind: Would something like this happen in a private enterprise? For example, at a gas station... would the branch manager react the same way? I probably wouldn't rule it out completely, but if I had to choose a target as a thief, I would also choose the post office. And what role does the boundless faith in the state play in the whole case, i.e. its uniformed monkeys, to which a decent person does not contradict and does what they are told? I suspect that it is not completely negligible.

Today we pay taxes on practically everything (there is even a death tax called inheritance tax), the purchase and sale of real estate is no exception, even on this the state fattens its pockets; why? Mainly because
can; he is stronger, has a "bigger stick" and we have no way to defend ourselves
. A few years ago, the tax office changed the rules so that the tax payer was not the seller, but the buyer; it happened, and the law also granted some exceptions (for new apartments), for which the citizen naturally had to humbly apply. The requests kept rolling in, they were approved, until one day... the tax office realized that it had actually approved some of the (already approved) exemptions stupidly; so what about that? The law is the law and the subject must pay (sometimes hundreds of thousands); and even with interest and penalties (!) for late payment!! Yes, you read that right. However, our rulers are merciful, so when a subject requests (!), they will forgive him the penalty (no interest). Can you imagine the (entirely justified) uproar if a private entity did this?

You can buy goods in the regular market; it goes something like this: You conclude a purchase contract with the seller (note, the contract is not a signed paper, but an agreement; the paper is only proof that it took place), you pay him the money, he hands over the goods to you... then he has to register this transaction electronically with Babiš. In the gift market, you don't buy, you give yourself a gift; it goes completely differently: You conclude two gift contracts with the marketer (not the seller) - the subject of one is your gift of money to the person in question, the subject of the second is that the good man presents you with his goods... and that's the end of it, because no one has yet implemented electronic records of donations. Donation markets have already been successfully held in Hradec Králové and Letohrad; another fifty cities are interested in organizing a similar event. Great so far! What do you think will come next? Will it turn out to be illegal dodging? Or will EED be introduced? Or does the state cough up small fish?

The Innovation Week organized by the European Leadership & Academic Institute has just started; on their website, we can read that the Prime Minister of the Czech Republic, Bohuslav Sobotka, officially accepted the patronage of the Innovation Week of the Czech Republic 2017. Ha-Ha. That's what I call a guarantee that it just can't go wrong. It is an event focused on innovation, modern technologies, artificial intelligence and the concept of smart cities; overall, it might be nice if it was a privately funded activity, which it is somewhat, but far from completely. Why am I writing about this? Well, Parallel Polis decided to organize a lecture on the given topic and approached me to see if I would take it on, which I happily accepted; if you want to listen to me and have a little discussion on the subject, come tonight at half past seven. Although this lecture does not belong to the cycle Anarchocapitalism, it will nevertheless touch on the topic in some way. I look forward to seeing you in
Parallel Polis
.

Years ago, I bought a drive from Alza with parameters that were different from those advertised, which the seller solved by changing the product description and brazenly pretending that I was mistaken and it had always been like that (he did not respond to the evidence from Google cache); I stopped buying from them.
By repeatedly ignoring the ban on sales on holidays, they almost won me over a few months ago
; and yesterday I decided to become their customer again (and bought there straight away). Why? The owner of Alza and his wife visited Parallel Polis to discuss the state, they agreed with us on many points, they liked the idea of Polis, Freedom of Learning and my lectures... and last but not least, cryptocurrencies; what happened then Their Head of Internet Marketing announced yesterday that Alza is introducing Bitcoin payments! I hope more stores follow suit; cryptocurrencies are thus not only becoming popular, but people have more and more options where to pay with them. What about you? Are you buying them yet?

title_en: Urza in Polis: Who would build roads without the state?
text_en:
I am a month ago
lectured on public spaces and freedom of speech
; this lecture eventually led to a very interesting discussion (part on the record and part off the record), as a relatively large number of supporters of state protection, especially of various interesting buildings, showed up. The topic was very closely related to the impossibility of economic calculation without a free market.
However, since this is a very extensive issue, I was forced to divide it into several lectures; last time we didn't deal at all not only with ecology, but above all with any transit function of public space, which would include, for example, the statists' favorite roads, because the question: "And who would build roads without the state?" almost every libertarian has heard it many times. It is to her that I want to answer this evening; be sure to come, especially if you don't agree. And if you have someone around you who might be interested in the topic, or if you would like to show them an anarcho-capitalist point of view, bring them along.
After this lecture, I will be silent for quite a long time, as the exam and holidays will begin; the next lecture will be on October 18 (!) at 8 p.m. and its topic will be the social and pension system. However, it is possible that in the meantime some (rather probably more discussion) ankap meetup will take place in Polis anyway.
I'm looking forward to seeing you tonight at 8 p.m
Parallel Polis
.

Oxford University has sent out new rules to students in its regular newsletter aimed at curbing racial intolerance; is it really needed there? And if so, how do the rules help? Let's take a look at them. For example, students may not ask a student of color where they originally came from; but even "better" is that they can't even avoid eye contact! It is said to be "micro-racism". Therefore, if a man glances at a woman of another race, she must return his glances, but in the case of the same race she does not have this obligation; and this is no longer micro-racism... this is racism like a cow! Don't all those politically correct geniuses realize that these kinds of measures accentuate racial differences? Don't they understand that in this way they can make racists out of those who have never dealt with any race at all? One can only hope that other institutions will not follow the example of the University of Oxford.

Although the elections are still quite far away, they are slowly approaching; and Sobotka needs to buy votes, but why would he do so on his own, when he has the stolen money of all of us at his disposal - so he wants to increase the salaries of civil servants. It's not unlike a hood of pirates splitting it up,
what they looted
; After all, the additions should be made (apart from firefighters) primarily to policemen, customs officers and bailiffs, i.e. executive rapists, who already form the front line of state oppression and the acquisition of resources through robbery. Moreover, this act demonstrates another step in the progression of the "death cycle of democracy" I am talking about
he lectured in Polis some time ago
: Politicians promise people that they will take care of them (at someone else's expense), which if they do, the number of dependents on the state (and civil servants) will increase; an increase in dependents on the state means more votes for politicians who promise people to take care of them (at someone else's expense). The circle closes: Democracy inevitably leads to socialism.

title_en: The Pope on the libertarian invasion
text_en:
I occasionally hear a joke among foreign libertarians that I would translate roughly as follows: "Libertarians are busily plotting to take over the world and leave you alone." (You can google “libertarians diligently plotting leave you alone” in the pictures.) Guess who took this little bit seriously? Pope Franciscus. He warned the world against the invasion (sic!) of libertarian values on our culture and education system. The danger of our delusional paradigms is said to be that we are not interested in the "public good" and in our belief that "only individuals assign value to things and human relationships, ergo only individuals decide what is good and what is bad"; he said that - surprisingly - very nicely, maybe I'll use it somewhere... I understand that he doesn't like it that much, because he would prefer to have the monopoly on what is good and what is bad; and his church always got along better with the state than with the libertarians xD
I am a Christian, but not a Catholic, because I am building a personal relationship with the Lord, for which I do not need a mediator in the form of a priest and certainly not a pope; in such moments I am glad for it, because the Pope's speech does not evoke a dilemma in me, but an infinite joy. Why joy? Dear ones, the head of the church, which surely has over a billion sheep, is talking about us! That means we do what we do well! As Gandhi said, "First they will ignore you. Then they will laugh at you. Then they will fight you. Then you will win." And this Pope's speech is the first swallow of that third phase; if the late Rothbard had lived to see it, he would surely have been glad. So let us continue our efforts; let's write, talk, spread, explain, try to understand people and not be rude to them, let's do our best. For this is the way to freedom; i don't believe i'll live to see a free market society, but i'll do my best... get involved too!

Who decides whether we deny a woman who wants a child the possibilities of modern medicine? The state, how else... and the powers that be have determined that if the person in question is not married, she is unlucky. František Adámek, a deputy from the left-wing ČSSD, tried to change this – unfortunately unsuccessfully; Jitka Chalánková from the so-called right-wing TOP09 was most strongly opposed, as she herself is married, has four children, and would like to impose her values on others, and the state gives her that power. Her reasoning: "The right to a child is not a basic human right." Well, how about? Does this mean that what is not a "fundamental human right" is prohibited by the state? She and other members of parliament agreed that it was not a medical issue, but an ethical one. Well of course! It is whether people are free to enter into voluntary transactions or the state will come in and start prohibiting them; the ethical question is: "Is it legitimate for Mrs. Chalánková, together with the other deputies, to decide from a position of power who and how is allowed to reproduce?"

title_en: You have the word: Become a cyber spy
text_en:
Almost every episode of "You Have a Word" is a massacre (except for the boring ones about diets and the like); mostly statism and the results of indoctrination by state propaganda abound there, but in the last part about cyber espionage, to those classic bon mots ("Whoever has done nothing wrong, has nothing to fear.") there was added lying manipulation of such dimensions that it surprised me (and I think similarly everyone who has at least a little idea about network security). A proponent of government wiretapping of citizens' network communications argued that foreign hackers could attack our power plants, chemical plants, water plants, and other strategic targets; someone from the audience and the presenter said that it is of course possible, because today everything is controlled via "those computers". It was simply a classic professional discussion in which all knowledge is drawn from hacker action movies; Of course, I don't blame anyone for ignorance, the problem is that in a democracy everyone has a voice.
No matter how skilled a hacker is, he can only attack "those computers" he can physically connect to over the network. So if the computer is not connected to the Internet, the person concerned is out of luck; as one of my teachers used to say: "The best firewall is a meter of air." (This statement no longer has as clear a point in the days of Wi-Fi as it did in his youth.) Of course, those who deal with the security of a nuclear power plant know this; so critical systems run offline. Unfortunately, this did not come up in the discussion for long, until after a while the tragic representative of the Pirate Party spoke uncertainly, and embarrassedly objected; however, the professional uncertainty emanated from it so much that the opponent wiped it out with the Stuxnet virus (attacking industrial systems running on Simatic), which is a completely irrelevant argument (monitoring network communication does not protect against a virus transmitted from a flash drive to an offline machine). But the Pirate was so insecure (he had been wiped out by the given opponent before) that he preferred to leave the topic alone.

title_en: Who doesn't crack like he doesn't live (EET edition)
text_en: You can't teach an old STBák new tricks; but he can teach the young. For example, a twenty-three-year-old man from Domažlice called the emergency line 158 because he could not find the fiscal identification code (confirmation that the sales were electronically recorded) on his receipt for a transaction for 12 (!) crowns. Can you imagine what goes through the mind of such a person? How does he think? What did he feel during that event? For what reason did he do it? I can think of several possibilities, I can't agree with any of them; and I would really like to know how many such people live among us... unfortunately even that one seems more than enough to me. I will not, however, class this story among those which would be laughable, if they were not, of course, to cry; Why not? Because in the end it was a joke after all: The uniformed monkeys came there, found the fiscal identification code on the receipt, the crooks showed it and he walked away in shame; this story was worth the money it cost me in taxes xD

In the days when Stoky was quite in its infancy,
we were discussing the law prohibiting sales on holidays
; it was still in the draft stage at the time, but passed as expected. Well, now it bears fruit! ČOIka had a head start on Easter Monday, as it checked almost three hundred shops, three of which were "illegally open" (we should start getting used to this bizarre phrase, which would be laughable, if not crying). they now face a fine of up to one million crowns (5 million for repeated violations). And you know what? All three shops had been vandalized; I wonder what kind of a whore a person has to be to do something like that, and I hope their identity gets leaked somewhere eventually. Anyway, the state introduced this law on the grounds that families should be together on holidays, because politicians know best what is good for them; yes, it is ordered to strangers... but what if the state started at home? For example, those fiddling controllers from ČOIka...

title_en: Urza in Polis: Public Space and Freedom of Speech
text_en:
A fortnight ago I
lectured on weapons
; even staunch anti-gunners turned up, which I very much welcome, and I find it very surprising that their views did not remain unchanged throughout the evening. The subsequent debate was very interesting.
The topic of today's lecture will be public space and freedom of speech in a stateless society; what do these two seemingly unrelated topics have in common? In fact, more than most people think, they are indeed closely related; and in the evening I will explain how exactly. We will talk about parks, squares, forests, so-called "public interests" and many other related things (among which the freedom of speech is primarily included); definitely come and discuss, especially if, in your opinion, we need a state to manage these spaces. And if you have friends or acquaintances who don't agree, or who might be interested in the topic, don't hesitate to bring them along!
The next lecture, to which you are all cordially invited, will exceptionally not be held in a fortnight, but in a month (May 17 at 8 p.m.); its theme will be: "Who would build roads without the state?"
I'm looking forward to seeing you tonight at 8 p.m
Parallel Polis
.

title_en: I have a right to a pub
text_en: Unfortunately, the ban on smoking in pubs has passed and there is nothing we can do about it, because the laws in practice are constantly increasing, but with exceptions, no one cancels them, ergo, we thus solemnly join the "developed" countries of the EU, which are often argued against; however, even more common is the argument, which I call at work: "I have the right to a pub," which is often explained with the words: "There is only one pub in our village." The best answer to it came from Stok's comments from the author of TaxationISTheft: "So what? If I go to a bookstore and they don't have the book I want, should I start asking the state to make it there?" It is precisely such a senseless demand even in the case of those pubs; not to mention a pretty accurate summary of the current state of the sprawling state I read recently, I don't even know where: "I wouldn't want to own a pub. The idea of someone getting drunk in it, lighting a fire, and me kicking them out before giving them a receipt is a real nightmare."

title_en: The best president is a bad president
text_en: In my opinion, the position of the president of the Czech Republic has an amazing ratio of prestige to real power; the head of state is a media-exposed figure, but he doesn't have that much power (not that he doesn't have any at all, for example, he appoints the members of the Banking Council of the CNB) - in other words, given how much he is seen, he can't do that much damage. That's why I think it's not so bad from a libertarian point of view if the president is already a total badass; why? It provokes people, to whom it is easier to explain the absurdity of democracy and state propaganda; for example, such a Zeman represents from this point of view a president who constantly does exactly what I want him to do - namely, shame. But his election period is slowly coming to an end, and I really would not like to see any Karl (the same evil, which looks more acceptable at first glance); however, according to my information, a candidate will be presented soon, who should playfully trump Zeman in embarrassing... and whoever thinks it's not possible, let them watch the media xD

title_en: Discussion in Polis: State versus Labor
text_en:
Today at 4 pm I will participate in a panel discussion in Paralelní Polis; the topic will be the recent events at the Rohlik.cz company, where on March 10, foreign police raided on suspicion of illegal employment and took away 85 people without charge, thereby paralyzing the company's operations. Come too, you're all invited, whatever your views; in addition, you can get coffee or beer for bitcoins (and if you don't have BTC, you can buy them directly on the spot) with the certainty that the transaction will not be electronically recorded.
Go outside.

Two weeks ago I
lectured on drugs
; the hall was packed again, for which I thank all of you who came. I am really glad to be able to impart the ideas of a free society to other people; I am grateful for anyone who listens to me and at least thinks about what I say. And I will continue to try my best not to disappoint you xD
Tonight I'm giving a lecture on the topic of guns, which is a rather stylish follow-up to drugs; however, unlike the last lecture, we will not discuss weapons from a technical point of view, but this will be replaced by many interesting statistics and hard data. But that's not all! We will focus on the effect of weapons on the psyche of decent people and criminals; we will talk about the differences between an armed and an unarmed society, not forgetting their relationship to the government. Finally, we will open up the topic of heavy weapons (a lot of heavy ones - fighter planes, battleships, tanks and artillery) and their place in a stateless society. Be sure to come and discuss - especially if you're pro-regulation; and bring your friends with you, ideally those who have never heard of anarcho-capitalism, but might be interested in the topic.
In addition, you are all invited to a lecture that will take place in two weeks (April 19 at 8 p.m.); its theme will be public spaces and freedom of speech.
I'm looking forward to seeing you tonight at 8 p.m
Parallel Polis
.

title_en: Consequences of the raid in Mironet
text_en:
It is May 2000; uniformed monkeys forcefully (against the law) break into the Mironet company, confiscate computers, accounting and accuse the owner of software piracy, only to find out after two years that... sorry like, a bug crept in, you're innocent, sir, so goodbye. However, the person in question is not a sheep and tries to defend himself against this will; he is suing the state for 626 million, which is like a fuck off, you get 23 megabytes and still be happy, keep quiet and shuffle your feet, filthy subject, says the High Court in Prague. Case continues, lawsuit, dismissal, statute of limitations, appeal, it can be found on the Internet (including hateful comments); But you know what I find most interesting about all this? Absolutely no one considers the absurdity of a situation where some entity (the state) damages someone and then the same entity (the state again) judges the case; if it was a private company that would judge its own disputes, that would be a roar!
However, state propaganda is strong...

title_en: Election 2017: Another crackdown on property rights
text_en:
For the first time this year, the pre-election campaign will be governed by the latest amendment to the electoral law; the head of the Office for Financial Control of Political Parties, Vojtěch Weiss, declared that anyone who wants to stick their own (!) poster with a political theme on their own (!) fence, shop window or window (that is, not only the promotion of a political party or movement, but also its defamation) must register in his office's tampering database - those who do not do so will be
sanctioned
a fine of ten to one hundred thousand crowns. That registration is also not a piece of cake, one either needs a transparent account, a website and other essentials for it, or one has to be registered by a political party; this will especially affect those who do not want to do a campaign, but an anti-campaign (for example, various haters of Babiš); I'm wondering if this also applies to Stoky, which is certainly not a poster or a large-scale device, but I don't know if it is a "communication medium" according to the law... what do the lawyers here think about it?
And now in Stoká we will once again visit the waters where there are things that would be laughable if they weren't crying: Deputy Speaker of the Chamber of Deputies Jan Bartošek (KDU) declared: "I find it strange to interpret the law in such a way that everyone who places a banner on the fence must register as a supporter." The head of the Constitutional and Legal Committee of the House of Representatives, Jeroným Tejc (ČSSD), responded: "It is not possible to interpret the law ad absurdum and ask people not to be able to express their opinion. [...] But it is up to the authorities how to interpret the law." And you know what? The two geniuses approved the moronic law (and in addition to their parties ANO and Úsvit - let's point to them); that's how law-making works in our country (and unfortunately not only here): A bunch of incompetent idiots approve something, somehow imagine it in practice, but when they find out that another incompetent bureaucrat puts the law into practice differently, they sigh that it's up to them, because "the law is the law" (yes... and where does it come from).

title_en: Internet or electricity can be, EET must be
text_en: Based on the fact that most people have an Internet connection, Babiš introduced a general obligation to register sales; unfortunately, this also applies to the minority who have to manage it somehow. For example, the ruins of the Cimburk castle are located in deep forests, where they have not only Internet, but not even electricity; however, the state commanded, so the subject has no choice but to submit. Connectivity itself isn't that much of a problem, electricity is; therefore, it was necessary to purchase a generator to the ruins and haul canisters of fuel there, as a result of which the entire treasury came to some sixty thousand - then the increase in the entrance fee was surely a coincidence, because the two things are obviously not related. In connection with similar cases, I always enjoy it when somewhere Babiš exclaims how the establishment of EET is a negligible amount; sure, for the vast majority of people it can be, but that is no justification for the brutal bullying of that minority, even though democracy stands for it.

Two weeks ago I
lectured on the topic of education
; I consider the lecture to be very successful, because probably the most people arrived so far (certainly over one hundred and fifty), so not only the chairs ran out, but also the place on the floor and the stream (which was exceptional, not normally) was watched by thousands of people. Thank you all for your attention; especially to those who came and of them especially to those who discussed.
Tonight I will lecture again; the topic is likely to cause some controversy again, as we will be talking about drugs. We will discuss drugs themselves, their effects, dangers and risks, because although we learn in public education that drugs are bad, there is basically nothing about them themselves, so there are many myths circulating in society (some of them demonize drugs, others downplay them; in my opinion, these two phenomena are very closely related and you can learn why at the lecture); but of course I will also deal with the state's attitude towards drugs, towards our freedom and the drug war, which has been raging without visible results for many years, during which it has ruined countless human lives.
I also cordially invite everyone to the next lecture, which will take place in a fortnight (April 5 at 8 p.m.); her topic will be guns in a free society.
I'm looking forward to seeing you tonight at 8 p.m
Parallel Polis
.

The state has invented that it is simply good for many disabled children to go to normal schools; however, some parents have the audacity to think they know their child better than the official, which is why they refuse to integrate them. And it is precisely these brats that the socialite will take to task; why? Well, because refusing inclusion is against the child's interest... and who judges what is the child's best interest? Yes, that's right - the state, who else. Not that I think inclusion is bad in all cases, however, it should not be decided by the government, but by children, parents and schools;
education should be voluntary
– and that comprehensively (so no one should deny anyone the opportunity to get an education, or force them to get an education; and the exact same thing should also apply to educational institutions), while the last institution that should interfere in this is a band of robbers – called the state – living off the money.
Let's prevent the indoctrination of our children
, as we can.

title_en: The new Freedom of Learning website
text_en:
In
Freedom of Learning has finally launched a new website
; and I would like to use this opportunity to recommend Stok readers to familiarize themselves with the interesting ideas that we spread in Freedom of Learning - you can start, for example
manifesto
, in the creation of which I also participated and I fully identify with him (especially with his fourth point). Why do I find the ideas of freedom of learning (now with a small s) so crucial? In my opinion, state education is one of the key – and I think even the most important – sources of state power; yes, sure, it is carried out by the police and courts, however, the reason why it is so widely accepted by people lies precisely in the propaganda that we are all exposed to since childhood, when our minds are still being formed, and as a result it is very difficult to resist it. Let's not expose our children to the same and try to prevent the state from indoctrinating them!

title_en: The state crushes the Czech roll
text_en:
The company Rohlík.cz delivers food to people that they order via the Internet; receives and processes three to four thousand orders in Prague every day (I saw an advertisement on one of their cars that said they had already delivered over a million of them). Something like this is clearly a great initiative, because the customers get food at favorable conditions (otherwise they wouldn't order it), the employees earn the best they can within their means (if not, they work elsewhere) and the business owners also get their money's worth; as long as they don't hurt anyone, that is
clearly beneficial
completely regardless of what some politicians or officials think about the conditions under which people work there, as long as they do so voluntarily (and of course regardless of whether they pay taxes or obey other laws, as long as they do not harm anyone). Why should anyone be bothered by this? For what reason should anyone object?
However, the armed fist of the state decided to crush Rohlík.cz, because it does not like that foreigners work in their warehouses under conditions that, in the opinion of officials, contradict the laws; a lot has already been written about why the Benga behave disgustingly as always (first they arrested dozens of people, thereby paralyzing the company's activities, then they legitimized them and found out who actually broke the law and who didn't - even the innocent were therefore restricted in their freedom). However, the criticism that the state is going too hard seems insufficient to me; I see the biggest problem in the fact that such things happen at all, and people who voluntarily cooperate for the benefit of everyone, without harming anyone, are persecuted for their activities by idiots, who already parasitize on their activities, which is all defended by the fact that something is in the laws. Something like this should definitely not be an argument for using violence against someone who has done nothing to anyone and, on the contrary, is beneficial.

March 17-19 is LibertyCon, an annual event organized by Students for Liberty; registration closes on March 12th, so be sure to sign up if you're interested. We can look forward to a whole range of interesting lectures and people; more information can be found at
event pages
– in my opinion, its visit is definitely worth considering.

Lecture a fortnight ago
on the topic of democracy, it was very successful; a lot of people came (maybe a hundred and fifty) and the response was great. Thank you! Again, it was a very interesting discussion, especially since the rejection of democracy is quite a controversial issue in today's society; a lot of people came to the lecture who had never been to one before, which I am very happy about.
The next lecture is tonight, and I consider it the most important of the series; the topic will be education, which in my opinion is the main reason why people so widely accept the state without really thinking about it. We will talk about the already mentioned state propaganda, but also about various models of education, most of which are not legal in the Czech Republic; and finally we will talk about the separation of education from the state and free market education. The lecture is really key, so please come and bring your acquaintances (ideally non-libertarians - it's already going pretty well and I lecture to most people who don't know anything about anarcho-capitalism).
In addition, you are all invited to the lecture that will take place in two weeks (March 22 at 8 p.m.); its topic will be drugs (both the drugs themselves and the state's approach to them).
I'm looking forward to seeing you tonight at 8 p.m
Parallel Polis
.

title_en: We bought a lift for a disabled person
text_en:
Kevin Preiß is a wheelchair-bound young German libertarian; however, since his home is not barrier-free, he has been able to go out for years only if his loved ones take him there and back. The lifting platform that would solve the situation costs a quarter of a mega (that is, in crowns); and although the state presents itself as an entity that cares for the disabled, it has kicked Kevin out (well... it would have paid him the lift if it had cost half, which would have been possible, but in another house; it won't even pay him half that way). When my ex-girlfriend found out about the situation (she lives in Germany and knows a lot of libertarians there), she thought of doing a fundraiser... most of the needed amount was raised in three days, a quarter mega within a week; Kevin gets a lift, problem solved.
Although libertarians are often accused of being callous and unwilling to help others, I think the opposite is true; not only because I myself devote quite a bit of my resources to help those who need it (in my opinion), and I am far from alone among libertarians in this approach, but above all it makes sense - when you think that the weak should be taken care of by the state, you don't have that much motivation to do it personally (of course, it is individual and there are many of those motivations), while if you live in the belief that solidarity should be voluntary, you simply have a tendency to be simply voluntarily solidary (again, not without exceptions). This won't just be the case for libertarians, though; if solidarity is not enforced by the state, people will feel more responsible for the state of the world around them... when there is no possibility of calling a politician to solve problems, the tendency to solve them by oneself will increase.

We have over a hundred golf courses in the Czech Republic and more are constantly being built; however, the number of players is decreasing, which logically puts golf resorts in financial trouble. Whoever thought that the solution would be to let the unneeded go bankrupt while the popular ones prosper is probably a little old-fashioned; current politics understandably dictates: "Let's give the successful and subsidize the unsuccessful!!" That's what motivates people; and so the EU pours hundreds of millions of crowns in subsidies to these failed golf course operators. Remember that the next time you hear from someone how the balance of money that we send to the EU and that we get back is favorable for us; yes, it comes out that way in accounting, but the money collected from taxes appears on the outgoing side
under threat of violence
, while nonsense is being financed on the income side. It's like someone taking a thousand from you to buy us something you absolutely don't want, don't need, and can't sell for two thousand; will you thank him?

Most of us are probably familiar with Gore-Tex; amazing (and quite expensive) clothing material, which, although waterproof, is breathable and therefore breathable - absolutely priceless for chundras (similar materials are used not only for jackets and trousers, but also for shoes). I applied some myself; and I was lucky because in my tramping days there wasn't yet a wise almighty EU to ban it. But now the situation has changed and the ban is on the table; well, finally - what else would we do? Reasons? Toxicity (so now I'm seriously worried about what years of wearing Gore-Tex will do to me) and ecology - it takes too long to decompose. Well, even if, I really wonder what it will do to ban this; we produce an incredible amount of glass and plastic that will decompose...well...maybe never, while banning Gore-Tex and similar materials, which are produced like spitting in the sea compared to the above, will save it exactly. Logical...

title_en: The state destroyed, the state subsidizes
text_en:
Small grocery stores are dying; dozens to hundreds of them are closed every year in the Czech Republic. Why? Although there are undoubtedly more reasons, one of the indisputable ones is the regulations that increase operational costs intolerably - hygiene regulations, occupational safety, employee protection, inspection reports and many others, plus all the red tape that follows; you can't just open a shop and start selling, the law forbids that. Of course, the same laws apply to supermarkets, but they have entire accounting, legal and HR departments that deal with it; as a result, the exact same regulations affect small players much worse, because the difficulty of the duties associated with it is certainly not linear with respect to profit or turnover, so larger entities are favored by the state (small shops simply cannot afford to allocate even one person to take care of these things).
Current solution? The state subsidizes these small establishments; just like Ronald Reagan said: "If it moves, tax it. If it keeps moving, regulate it. And when it stops moving, subsidize it." A reasonable solution? Cancellation of regulations (
ideally also taxes
) and bureaucratic duties associated with it; small shops can then
to compete freely in the free market
and see what people actually want. And what about Miloslav Hlavsa, director of the cooperative network Konzum? "I don't like subsidies." Great so far; unfortunately, the person in question continues: "Operating food stores in small villages is not a business and should be included in the law as a public service." As an entrepreneur, he does not want subsidies; however, he misses the good old pre-revolutionary practices. What to say to that? The whole thing is so absurd that I don't even know; but if the state did not distort the market, who would the politicians actually save?

Uniformed monkeys Ondřej Bína and Přemysl Rückl stopped a van driver in Českolipska because his rear light was not on; they did so in heavy snow in a completely demented place (downhill road in serpentines), where the driver was afraid to stop, lest someone take him down. He slowed down, flashed his blinkers, making it clear he wanted to stop, but that wasn't enough for the cops; Přemysl Rückl justifies it as follows: "The car should stop immediately, not after two minutes. And where we choose a place for it." They overtook him and stopped; the Essenbák driver asked if they could go to a safer place, for which the person in question scolded him. When the driver wanted to call 158, the uniformed bandit pulled him out of the car, sprayed him with tear gas, knocked him to the ground and kicked him; the official explanation is that they were afraid he wouldn't reach for a gun, they suspected he might be a robber and should have stopped immediately. Vermin! Compared to that, I am
recently escaped
still good enough.

Some time ago, the regulatory authority forced operators to increase LTE coverage for high-speed Internet; God? Eeee... semi. Oddly enough, it cost something, which was reflected in the prices; the office does not agree with that. What to say about that? It would be laughable if it weren't for crying. But now the Minister of Industry and Trade, Jan Mládek, will go to hell; he will look at the discounts. He wants to prohibit operators from offering discounts to clients by law (which, by the way, most of them enjoy); wtf? Yes, just make it more expensive in the name of the law, let it be fair. Motivation? So here I am not exceptionally betting on the old well-known good-naturedness in combination with stupidity; I consider more likely the scenario that one of the big operators does not like the current market situation and wants to get rid of discounts, however, if he did it himself, customers would go to his competition, so he pulled the strings and wants to ban it across the board. After all, we have the state to protect us from those evil corporations!

Two weeks ago, the topic was mine
lectures in Parallel Polis
culture, art and we also touched on the protection of monuments and works of art; since the period of exams and viruses was over, over a hundred people showed up again. Considering the topic, I was very pleased to see how many of the attendees were artists who had a lively discussion with me; many of them came to my lecture for the first time, so I was busy re-explaining the basics of the Austrian school of economics, so as not to bore those who already know them as much as possible.
Today I am lecturing again and the topic (lectures and subsequent discussions) will be democracy; how do people perceive her? Why is it so often considered a synonym for freedom or even goodness? We also talk about protecting the "weak" from themselves; in connection with this, I will also try to prove the thesis that democracy naturally leads to socialism. And finally, I would like to say a few words about elitism. Since today's topic is quite broad and general (controversial as well), I think it could interest almost anyone; this talk is definitely a great place to take someone you'd like to start asking questions about libertarianism.
Furthermore, you are all cordially invited to the next lecture, which will take place in two weeks (March 8 at 8 p.m.) and which I consider to be the most important of the entire cycle; its topic will be education.
I'm looking forward to seeing you tonight at 8 p.m
Parallel Polis
.

TOP09 started a debate about when and under what conditions the Czech Republic will be ready for a four-day work week; Kalousek conditions this by improving labor productivity, while the unions above all demand that the reduction of working hours should occur across the board for everyone, and the biggest problem for them would be if it happened only in certain industrial sectors, but the furthest away is of course the favorite Stok Marks, which long ago founded a working group called Work 4.0 for this purpose and is about to visit Germany, where the debates on this topic are said to be further. For now, I'm just shaking my head and wondering why these bombers should decide this? What if we would rather abolish the entire Labor Code and leave working hours and all other requirements to the agreement between employers and employees? At least unions would regain their original meaning and stop being just a group promoting their interests through legal (but illegitimate) violence.

title_en: We do not cook for refugees!
text_en:
For the second time, ČOIka has fined the Grand Italia pizzeria from Hrušovan nad Jevišovka in South Moravia (with an amount in the tens of thousands), because the owners dared to put up a sign stating that they do not cook for immigrants. In addition, I would like to note a few things (I will start from the least important and continue to the most important): First, I consider the actions of the restaurant owners to be quite stupid and as a guest I would probably go elsewhere; secondly, many of their customers see it differently, support the restaurant and even want to pay the fine; thirdly, I would be quite interested in whether the people in question seriously broke the law, when technically they only threatened to break it with the sign, which is probably not allowed anymore; and finally, fourthly, regardless of whether the law was broken, I find it grossly immoral and unjustifiable for the state to force someone to serve and cook for someone they don't want to serve.
The real problems in the Czech Republic associated with migration (especially due to the real absence of a larger number of immigrants) are paradoxically not caused by immigrants, but by the state, which interferes with people doing what they want in their own way and for their own sake; let anyone who doesn't want to serve immigrants not to serve them, because there are plenty of people here who will gladly serve them (and we won't interfere with them, of course). Let everyone be free to decide whether they want to be a xenophobe, a racist, an Islamophobe, or an Islamophile; as long as no one initiates violence against others, it is basically only and purely their business. What will be the result of forcing people who obviously do not want migrants here and hate them to cook for them? Will they perhaps start to like them or respect them more? Not by mistake! Quite the contrary – they will be all the more angry that the state is imposing on them. Even leaving aside whether the fines are crap (which they are), they won't do any practical good either.

The Libertarian Institute seeks to spark a public debate about freer education; they are trying to do this through a petition. Although I cannot agree with its wording in some points, because
in my opinion, education should be completely separated from the state
(you can read more about it on the website
Learning freedoms
, of which I am a member), I have signed it; why? First, because I find even the state described by the petitions to be better than the present; and secondly because the goal
Libertarian Institute
it is primarily through this petition to start a discussion (in which, if successful, we can also present more free-spirited opinions). The whole event is just starting, many signatures have not yet been collected, so even yours can make a difference; and even if the event is not successful, with your signature you can at least motivate its authors - the Libertarian Institute - to continue their work. If you are interested in at least reading the petition,
click here
! Thank you.

A fortnight ago we were on
lecture in Parallel Polis
they talked about firemen; due to the exam and virus period, a little less people came than to the first lectures, however, according to the organizers, it was still a "blow" by Polis standards (perhaps a hundred people). As always, a few socialists and left-wing anarchists also arrived, who are always warmly welcomed; thank you to everyone who came, or who promoted the lecture.
Today's topic (also for the subsequent discussion) will be culture and art in the free market; we will talk about how artists would create without state subsidies, how theaters and other cultural stands would survive, but we will also focus on the protection of works of art and monuments, which is also under the control of the state today. Of course, everything will be presented in the context of the previous lectures; I am going to apply the conclusions we reached earlier to this issue as well. After the lecture I will of course be happy to answer all your questions, which is something I enjoy perhaps even more than the lecture itself; so don't hesitate and come! If you have any acquaintances who might be interested in the topic, be sure to bring them along.
Furthermore, you are all cordially invited to the next lecture, which will take place in two weeks (February 22 at 8 p.m.); its theme will be democracy and responsibility.
I'm looking forward to seeing you tonight at 8 p.m
Parallel Polis
.

The Communists (now I mean the officially recognized and declared ones) decided to be bombers to the end and came to the House with an old hit - the anti-parasitism law, yes indeed! It hasn't been here for a long time. The chairman, Comrade Filip, justifies it as follows: "This is a simple amendment to the Criminal Code, which introduces a new criminal offense that responds to a serious problem in society." Politicians from other parliamentary parties (led by Kalousek) laughed at him. And you know what's the saddest part? That Philip is consistent and logically right; unlike those who laugh at him. If we want a welfare state, such a law unfortunately makes sense; because he is really responding to a serious problem in society - a serious problem created by the welfare state. The best (and only meaningful) solution is, of course,
separation of the state from the social security system
; or we can invent laws to combat vermin.

The state has noticed that there are cryptocurrencies; and reacted classically in his own way - the first regulation regarding their purchase and sale. Exchange offices and other service providers that can be paid for with virtual currencies (there are over 80 places in Prague, where you can buy food, accommodation, school fees or veterinary treatment with bitcoins) are now obliged to find out the identity of those with whom they trade in cryptocurrencies. The next planned step is to make the buyer (!) responsible for VAT if he bought in cryptocurrency and the seller did not pay the tax. Bitcoin and other virtual currencies are, of course, a pain in the ass for the tax office, because they can be used to easily mask a financial trace and the state no longer has all the property of its subjects in the palm of its hand; and the more popular these currencies become, the more they will become resisted. So let's get ready to present Bitcoin as the currency of child porn traffickers and the like; we will still enjoy it.

Although most of the recent terrorists profess Islam, this time a (literal) Islamo-killer attacked – he shot up a mosque in Quebec, Canada; it shows the quite unsurprising truth (which Breivik also showed some time ago) that a terrorist does not have to be a Muslim (although the lying president claims the opposite and many idiots repeat it after him). Most people just aren't totally deranged dorks who would be satisfied with shooting innocents, but every now and then there is a flawed piece like that; he then looks for all sorts of convenient excuses to do it - and Islam is one of them. But those who do not have Islam can do otherwise; someone attacks an abortion clinic, another sets fire to a police car, another throws a Molotov cocktail at a baby, finding an enemy is so easy when you have it in your head and you're hungry for blood... and whoever doesn't even have enough invention to create an ideological enemy, he just shoots up a school... or a pub.
The stupid thing is that, like the Islamobites, they tend to be ecstatic about every Muslim attack and many are almost happy about it, mainly because it supports their worldview, now one can observe again in the camp of the sun-lovers the association of terrorists with DJ Trump and Marine Le Pen, whom the person admired; yes, this terrorist was anti-immigrant and shot up a mosque, but neither Trump nor Le Pen are really responsible for that (and I say that, even though I loathe both of them). Responsibility for actions rests with the one who commits them; when someone presents me with evidence that DJ Trump helped him with this, I will be the first to condemn him, but the reality is that he probably didn't even know the young man, so it's hard to blame him for looking up to the fool in him. Dangerous rogues were, are and will be; luckily there aren't many, but there are a few, so let's put up with it, be ready to defend ourselves, but let's not make up nonsense and limit freedom in their name.

Until now, Czech schools were financed according to the number of students; however, the deputies voted that from September the money would be distributed according to the lessons learned (by the way, the presentation of the law was accompanied by hysteria, which included topics such as the tradition of humanism, the genocide of the Indians, European values, the Thirty Years' War, the atrocities of Christianity, the harmfulness of multicults and chocolate - the papalists took it from the ground). What will this change bring? Does anyone know? No. Everyone has an opinion, but real results are unpredictable; it can help and harm, probably one way for some and another that way. The declared goal is to help rural schools with few pupils, which will probably happen, but if costs are maintained, quite logically at the expense of schools with a large number of students (extra money for small schools will be missing somewhere). The question, of course, is: Is it desirable? And the answer? Unfortunately, no one can even know this; and what's worse, we won't even know in the future.
the only way
how to find out what is desirable
, consists in leaving people a free choice - let everyone decide which school to go to (and if to school at all; we also have
unschooling
) wants to send his child and how much he wants to pay for it; until we leave these things to the free market, where everyone can best decide how they want their resources to be used, we are completely blind, unable to perform an effective economic calculation. Not to mention that funding is one of the smallest problems in the case of education; the state education system primarily deforms our children through indoctrination, exposes them to massive pro-state propaganda and instills in them from an early age the feeling that
submission to imposed authority is desirable
. If someone wants to educate in an authoritarian way, that's basically their business, but let them do it through the schools
he doesn't even expose the children of the rest of us
.

The subject
last lectures
, which I had at Polis a fortnight ago, was money; again, you came in large numbers, the hall was crowded (again at least some 150 people, which basically borders on the capacity of the room), even some leftists, socialists, anarcho-communists and the like arrived on this controversial topic. Thank you to everyone who came or promoted the lecture in any way.
Today from twenty o'clock in the evening I will give a lecture again, the topic will be firefighters in the free market; we will talk about how they could function without state coercion, as well as why and what is harmful about the use of force to enforce that (not only) firefighters are a service provided by the state. In addition, of course, as always, we will also deal with broader contexts and more general principles related to the topic; after the lecture I will be happy to answer all your questions, which I enjoy immensely. title_en: Twenty-two years since the death of Murray Newton Rothbard
text_en: Today is exactly twenty-two years since one of the greatest thinkers, economists, philosophers and geniuses - Murray Newton Rothbard, the "father of anarcho-capitalism" left this world at the age of 69; his life's work was a consistent and logical introduction to the consequences of two trends that were seemingly not very related: anarchism and the Austrian school of economics. Anarchists were often wrong in economics, and the proponents of the Austrian school of economics did not apply their (correct) conclusions to the state; Murray Newton Rothbard corrected both and came to a brilliant conclusion: "Capitalism is the fullest expression of anarchism, and anarchism is the fullest expression of capitalism. Not only are they compatible, but you can't really have one without the other. True anarchism will be capitalism, and true capitalism will be anarchism." This knowledge and full understanding of it changed my life greatly; Thank you, Mr. Rothbard.

I have a hospital not far from where I live; this hospital is famous for how bad it is, not to mention the personal experiences of my loved ones suggest that (visibly drunk doctors and such). Fortunately, I personally rarely use the services of doctors, but recently I found myself in a condition (poisoning) where a visit to the hospital was necessary; for obvious reasons, my girlfriend drove me about 30 kilometers to a better hospital (which is almost every one). It took the doctors about eight hours to fix me, so there were quite a few medical staff around me; however, without exception, their first question after looking at the card was not about my health, but about why I'm not in the hospital where I live (I don't think they always ask, but this time they couldn't catch up). Each time, I was told that not like this, and they wrote (with exclamation marks) in my discharge papers that I should go to the place of residence for the inspection.
Can you imagine this in a private company? Can you imagine employees who reproachfully ask customers why they didn't go to a competitor? Understandably difficult; entrepreneurs are passionate about customers, they fight for them, they try to please them, and when they have a lot of them, they do everything to keep them. Hospital
in our socialist healthcare system
however, they do not have this motivation; the boys represent nothing but the current and the necessity to do something. I believe that the repeated calls for me to go to the competition vividly illustrate and symbolize something much deeper, the whole attitude is reflected in them; if you tell a businessman that his competition has disappointed you, you go to him, he will typically be happy, but a socialist thinks differently. And now consider what pervades the effort to discourage customers; unfortunately, it's not the doctors' fault, they act rationally, the whole state juggernaut that more or less forces them to act like that is faulty.

In my efforts to show people the benefits of a free society and the inherent evil that lies in states as such, I mainly come across propaganda and indoctrination on the subject of "the state is necessary", where this firmly rooted thesis often completely overwhelms any logical arguments, which are then swept off the table a priori; however, there is also the popular and ubiquitous "it wouldn't work" argument, which I have mentioned many times before and would now like to discuss in a little more detail.
Before I get into that, I can't help but mention one observation I've made over the years of debates about freedom: Against the general distrust of people in freedom in the real world stands a fairly significant confidence in the freedom of the Internet in the virtual world by the same people. Did you notice that? When politicians come up with regulations outside the Internet, they are often supported in activities that limit freedom of expression (and not only that); however, when it comes to Internet censorship, most people are far more sensitive. Why do you think this is so?
One explanation occurred to me - while the real world is so over-regulated that no one can even imagine it without regulations, the Internet is currently quite free and everyone can see that there is no doom and things work even without a central authority. The amount of regulation outside the Internet has exceeded all limits, so that people have been forced to integrate it into their lives, which the majority of the population can no longer imagine well enough without them; rather, it requires a huge amount of imagination and the necessity to accept the fact that the outcome cannot even be predicted well enough, because the free market is unpredictable, so the most daring ideas will be just one of many hypothetical versions of the future.
In connection with this, an urgent question arises: How much do people fundamentally reject freedom and how much change as a result of state propaganda? In an unfree world, these two things can merge - the one who is an enemy of change can appear to be an opponent of freedom, which of course also applies vice versa. What role does fear of the unknown play? Everyone can see that a free Internet does not mean the end of civilization; however, many are convinced that a stateless society would bring about the end of civilization. Do you think that if these people were able to imagine some alternatives, that would change their attitudes?

How to do it? Well, I'm spending the holidays with my family and loved ones, and we're discussing what "should" be done for Christmas; no one is forced into anything. Whoever wants to go get a tree, it will happen; whoever wants to bake cookies, bakes; whoever wants to cook dinner will cook; whoever wants to buy gifts, will buy them; most of it is usually done by someone... and what does no one do? And now I am not talking about the sacrifice of Jesus, but about changing the meaning of pagan holidays to Christmas despite the fact that all the interesting astronomical phenomena around the year zero that could be the Bethlehem comet, whether it was 1P/Halley or not, did not take place in winter; that's something like changing Czech Statehood Day to Tax Abolition Day... and there's still a long way to go.
I also like the "consumer" part of Christmas - tinsel, debauchery, good food and other pastimes; moreover, during them there is a huge amount of voluntary exchange, which symbolizes capitalism. I thank the libertarian Robert Higgs for the inspiration to write this text.
Dear readers, have you ever heard or used any of the following arguments?
1/ Look around you, there is a state in every society; Do you know of one that isn't there?
2/ The state is a thousand-year-old institution, it has existed since time immemorial; if it's so bad, why aren't stateless societies emerging?
3/ Without states, people would behave like animals, be dangerous and unable to take care of themselves; they need their rulers!
4/ Without states, economic collapse would occur; the economy stands and falls by laws.
5/ The abolition of states would cost great bloodshed; then they would still spawn again at the cost of more blood.
6/ Free people in various parts of the world are even worse off than the citizens of our state; and they should be happy for what they have.
7/ Conditions in the States may improve; rather than abolishing states, let's try to reform them.
8/ A world without states is nothing but a utopia; it can never work, which is clear to all but a few naive fools.
Let's go back in time a few hundred years and look at a few arguments against the abolition of slavery:
1/ Look around you, there is slavery in every society; Do you know of one that isn't there?
2/ Slavery is a thousand-year-old institution, it has existed since time immemorial; if it's so bad, why don't neo-slave societies emerge?
3/ Slaves would behave like animals without their masters, would be dangerous and unable to take care of themselves; they need their slavers!
4/ Without slavery there would be an economic collapse; the economy stands and falls with slavery.
5/ The abolition of slavery would cost great bloodshed; then it would still spawn again at the cost of more blood.
6/ Free people in different parts of the world are even worse off than our slaves; and they should be happy for what they have.
7/ The conditions of slaves may improve; rather than the abolition of slavery, let us try to improve their living conditions.
8/ A world without slavers is nothing but a utopia; it can never work, which is clear to all but a few naive fools.
These are real arguments of real people (A. Lincoln, G. Washington, T. Jefferson, G. Fitzhugh, T. Carlyle and many others).
How "strong" does the first eight arguments appear compared to the second? And how many more years will pass before people find them just as absurd?

If you drive more slowly, you have more time to react to the situation around you; this is definitely true if you are going that way by your own decision. But what if you are forced to do so under the threat of a fine? An Australian study led by Dr. Vanessa Bowden shows that volunteering matters here too; eighty-four drivers (who did not know what was being tested on them) were allowed to drive in a simulator where they had to drive through places with a speed limit of 50 km/h - while they knew once that they would be fined for exceeding the limit by 1 km/h, the second time by 6 km/h and finally by 11 km/h. Result? Well, the more restrictive limits forced the driver to watch the speedometer more and less of the surroundings, ergo they were demonstrably more likely to overlook what was happening around them; and what's the use of a shorter braking distance if you can't see that you have to brake? However, the uniformed monkeys don't care; their job is to collect dashes for fines...
The order was clear: He must not pass at any cost!
